articles.title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11228-6AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Developing artificial intelligence (AI)-native experimental laboratories for autonomous scientific exploration with minimal human intervention represents a long-standing goal.
Although autonomous experimental systems are emerging1,2,3,4, especially in chemical and materials science, they remain largely confined to domains with singular objectives, well-defined workflows and simple instrumentation.
This limitation may reflect an ‘add-on’ architecture that uses AI as a task-specific tool rather than providing it with a global understanding of experiments, especially under engineering-oriented circumstances.
Here we present AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments.
Through the co-design of models, experiments and instruments, AutoDNA realizes the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.
The system autonomously orchestrates over 20 types of instruments across more than 11,000 steps to execute core nucleic acid operations including synthesis, transcription, amplification and sequencing, while human intervention is limited to hardware maintenance tasks, such as reagent and labware replenishment.
Across four representative applications, AutoDNA matched expert-optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis yields, accelerated concurrent protocol execution by 3.
2-fold, completed an end-to-end DNA data storage cycle with exact recovery of the original digital content, and identified and validated a clinically detected KRAS G13D mutation.
AutoDNA establishes a blueprint towards science-as-a-service, accelerating biological discovery and advancing various applications in synthetic biology and information storage.

articles.title: Space CISOs Sound Alarm on Starlink Disruption in Ukraine, Urge Clear Service Terms and Sovereign Control - Via Satellite
articles.summary: Space CISOs Sound Alarm on Starlink Disruption in Ukraine, Urge Clear Service Terms and Sovereign Control  Via Satellite
articles.full_text:
RESTON, Va. — Space industry CISOs weighed in on the recent service disruption that left Ukrainian forces without connectivity to SpaceX’s Starlink and its military variant Starshield during combat operations with Russia, in a Monday discussion during CyberSat. Without knowing the details of the service agreement, some CISOs condemned the action and highlighted the impact it will have on governments’ continued pursuit of sovereign satellite services.
“It was a crappy thing for them to do,” said Victor Einfeldt, director of IT Security at Iridium. “You don’t play games with human lives in the middle of a war and take away service without communicating it to them first. That can’t become the standard from which we operate our satellite constellations and services.”
With more nations actively building or considering sovereign constellations for mission-critical operations, Einfeldt suggested that sovereignty may soon be defined by “who owns the kill switch.”
Vantor CISO Norm Laudermilch pointed to the severity of the outage. “We’re not talking about an outage here, we’re talking about a change to a critical operational service that a customer was relying on for their mission,” he said.
Laudermilch expects the Starlink disruption will drive competition as customers look for resilience and layered capabilities. “Instead of having one satellite internet provider maybe I need three,” he said. “And maybe I need to design into my end system the ability to route between those three or automatically fail over when one service [degradation] happens.”
There was general agreement that sovereignty does not require every nation to build its own constellation, but that commercial solutions need clear mission expectations between the customer and service provider.
“You can build these sovereign commercial partnerships — and we’re doing it with IRIS² — and give the entity what they need in order to operate,” said Vinit Duggal, SES CISO and vice president of Network Engineering.
Sovereign entities can maintain control and asset visibility, even in a managed service, Duggal added. “The control is still with the sovereign partner,” he said, noting the IRIS² service “kill switch” and payloads will be under the control of the EU partner. SES leads both the Medium-Earth Orbit (MEO) and user terminal component of IRIS², with initial operations planned to begin by 2030.
Agentic AI for Black Hats and Red Teams
In a wide-ranging discussion on cyber issues for the space industry, CISOs also explained why agentic artificial intelligence is better than a security patch, how to defend orbital data centers, and the growing importance of network sovereignty in commercial managed services.
Agentic AI is a double-edged sword that is accelerating threat actors’ capabilities on one side, but also giving organizations a tool to remediate vulnerabilities before they’re found in the wild.
“If you’re still defending things in the traditional way of scanning the network for vulnerabilities and working with system owners to patch, you’re not doing it right anymore,” said Laudermilch. “You’ve got to be defending at machine speed.”
Vantor, which operates a Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) imaging constellation and AI-driven spatial intelligence software, has adopted an “agentic defense factor” in its security operations center (SOC).
The CISOs acknowledged the need to accelerate response time in the aftermath of the PHP web scripting language vulnerability, discovered using AI, and announced by U.S. cybersecurity agencies in an Oct. 21 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) report.
“The community did a good job circling the wagons and getting an understanding of where and how it was vulnerable,” said Duggal. Some 70% of the internet runs on PHP and impacted companies were told to take sites offline for patching. SES, which operates a multi-orbit constellation of 120 satellites and over 100 teleports, had an idea of its exposure and responded without any material impact to the business, Vinit said.
Laudermilch added that agentic AI has “primed the pump” for attackers to act as soon as vulnerabilities come to light. “Within 48 hours of that CVE being announced, we were seeing four to five hundred thousand attacks a day looking for [exploits],” he said of Vantor.
Defending Orbital Data Centers
On orbit data centers have triggered waves of investment and engineering effort, but security is not yet where it needs to be to defend those assets, according to CISOs.
“We are not ready,” Duggal said when asked if the industry is prepared to secure future on-orbit data centers. He cited significant engineering and cybersecurity challenges before data centers in space become a reality. With the rise of on-orbit data processing, Duggal highlighted the growing risk of on-orbit “stalking,” which has been attributed to several Russian and Chinese spacecraft. When users rely on satellites to process intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) data in space, “it just becomes the juicy target for foreign operators, and then it becomes a resiliency issue,” Duggal said.
Intrusion detection, which is a baseline for terrestrial data center security, is another challenge on orbit. Operators will not have real-time access to intrusion detection and response data for a spacecraft, noted Laudermilch, which leads to the conclusion that the spacecraft will have to manage those functions itself.
“We are in the infancy when we’re looking at onboard, IP-layer detection and response,” said Laudermilch. “We have to evolve that technology.”
Vantor is developing its next generation imaging spacecraft, Vantage and Pulse, with automated onboard detection and response. The satellites are scheduled for launch between 2027 and 2029.
Einfeldt reiterated that orbital data centers should follow similar logical security controls as data centers on the ground and also focus on link security to prevent interception. Commercial or military-grade encryption are becoming more common in the satellite control plane but link-layer encryption has not historically been a commercial requirement. Einfeldt also raised questions about encryption for optical inter-satellite links (ISLs) in the future, though the narrow, directional beams are widely considered secure against existing interception methods.
The CISOs overarching message was to build security from the outset and manage risks across network layers and physical boundaries, especially with the rise of onboard compute. “We have to be very conscious about moving workloads into space,” said Laudermilch. “You also need to move all the security intelligence that we use to detect and respond to malicious behavior into space too.”

articles.summary: Diffusion Sources Market To 2035: Growth Driven by Sub-10nm Node Ramp and Wide-Bandgap Semiconductor Expansion - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Diffusion Sources market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global diffusion sources market is a critical enabler of advanced semiconductor manufacturing, providing high-purity dopant materials that underpin the fabrication of integrated circuits, power devices, and photovoltaic cells. As of the 2026 edition, the market is characterized by high technological barriers, concentrated supply chains, and demand intrinsically tied to capital expenditure cycles in the semiconductor and solar sectors. The industry is undergoing a phase of consolidation and technological transition, driven by the shift toward smaller process nodes below 10nm and the rise of wide-bandgap semiconductors such as silicon carbide and gallium nitride.
These trends are fueling demand for ultra-high-purity and next-generation source materials, including gaseous, liquid, solid, and spin-on dopants. Geographically, consumption is heavily concentrated in East Asia, mirroring leading-edge foundry and memory production, while supply chain localization efforts are creating regional champions. The competitive landscape is oligopolistic, with stringent safety and purity requirements creating high entry barriers.
This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market's current state, projecting trends, competitive dynamics, and strategic implications through 2035, offering stakeholders a data-driven view of market evolution, risk mitigation, and opportunity capture in this strategically vital industry.
The baseline scenario for the diffusion sources market through 2035 anticipates sustained growth, albeit with cyclical fluctuations tied to semiconductor capital expenditure cycles. The market is projected to expand at a moderate CAGR, supported by the relentless progression of Moore's Law and the increasing complexity of chip architectures. Demand will be primarily driven by the ramp-up of sub-10nm logic and memory nodes, which require ultra-high-purity dopant sources with precise delivery systems.
Additionally, the accelerating adoption of wide-bandgap semiconductors in electric vehicles, 5G infrastructure, and renewable energy will create new demand for specialized dopants, particularly for silicon carbide and gallium nitride processes. The market's value growth will outpace volume growth due to the rising share of premium, high-purity products and the increasing complexity of source formulations. However, the outlook is tempered by supply chain fragility, volatile raw material costs, and tightening environmental regulations governing specialty gases.
Geopolitical tensions and trade policies may further disrupt supply chains, prompting localization efforts and regional capacity investments. Overall, the market is expected to remain oligopolistic, with leading players investing in R&D and capacity expansion to maintain their positions, while regional champions emerge in response to supply security concerns.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Ramp-up of sub-10nm logic and memory nodes requiring ultra-high-purity dopant sources
- Expansion of wide-bandgap semiconductor (SiC, GaN) production for EVs, 5G, and renewable energy
- Growth in solar cell manufacturing, particularly high-efficiency cell architectures
- Increasing complexity of chip designs driving demand for precise doping and advanced source formulations
- Rising capital expenditure in semiconductor fabs globally, supported by government incentives
- Technological transition toward spin-on dopants and ion implantation sources for advanced processes
Potential Growth Constraints
- Stringent safety and environmental regulations governing toxic and pyrophoric gases
- Volatility in raw material costs and supply chain disruptions
- High entry barriers due to complex synthesis and purification technologies
- Cyclical nature of semiconductor capital expenditure impacting demand stability
- Geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions affecting global supply chains
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Semiconductor Manufacturing (estimated share: 55%)
Semiconductor manufacturing remains the dominant end-use sector for diffusion sources, accounting for the majority of global consumption. The ongoing shift to smaller process nodes below 10nm, coupled with the adoption of 3D transistor structures such as FinFET and gate-all-around, is driving demand for ultra-high-purity dopant gases and liquid sources. These advanced nodes require precise control over dopant concentration and profile, which necessitates high-performance diffusion sources. Additionally, the increasing complexity of memory and logic chips is leading to more doping steps per wafer, further boosting consumption. Demand-side indicators to watch include fab construction spending, wafer starts, and technology node transitions.
The sector's growth is also supported by government incentives for domestic semiconductor production, particularly in the US, Europe, and Japan, which are expected to increase regional demand for diffusion sources. However, the cyclical nature of the semiconductor industry may cause short-term fluctuations. Current trend: Growing demand for ultra-high-purity dopants driven by sub-10nm node ramp and 3D device architectures.
Major trends: Transition to sub-10nm and gate-all-around architectures, Increasing doping steps per wafer for advanced logic and memory, Rise of 3D NAND and DRAM with complex doping requirements, Government incentives driving fab construction in new regions, and Growing demand for high-purity and low-metal dopant sources.
Representative participants: TSMC, Samsung Electronics, Intel Corporation, GlobalFoundries, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology.
Solar Cell Production (estimated share: 20%)
The solar cell production segment is a significant consumer of diffusion sources, primarily for doping processes that form the p-n junction in crystalline silicon cells. As the photovoltaic industry shifts toward higher-efficiency architectures such as TOPCon and heterojunction (HJT), the demand for advanced dopant sources, including boron and phosphorus oxychloride, is increasing. These architectures require more precise doping and often employ diffusion sources with lower contamination levels to achieve higher conversion efficiencies. The growth of solar cell production is driven by global renewable energy targets and declining costs of solar modules.
Demand-side indicators include solar installations, cell production capacity, and technology mix shifts. The sector is expected to see robust growth through 2035, particularly in Asia-Pacific, which dominates global solar manufacturing. However, oversupply and price pressures in the solar industry may impact the adoption of premium dopant sources. articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check



A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.



While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.



Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.



Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave.



—Amit Katwala



Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test



At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”



One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.”



But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks.



So one month in, who’s on board?



—James O’Donnell



This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

Quote of the day



“Don’t spend money unduly by asking a human expert to enter into a debate with a robot expert.”



—Steven Benmor, a family lawyer, tells the Wall Street Journal that clients increasingly need to pay human experts to correct advice they’ve received from chatbots.



One more thing







The noise we make is hurting animals. Can we learn to shut up?



As human society has expanded, animals have started struggling to hear one another. For many birds, the noise has grown so loud that they’ve begun to sing with faster trills. Now, their mating calls aren’t as effective. 



The growing hubbub can also increase bird-on-bird conflict, and entire species that can’t handle urban clamor simply leave town for good. But there are technological solutions to the noises hurting animals—and they could help humans, too.



Read the full story.



—Clive Thompson

articles.title: Nvidia tells data center partners to cut China exposure, limits RTX chip sales to mainland - Data Center Dynamics
articles.summary: Nvidia tells data center partners to cut China exposure, limits RTX chip sales to mainland  Data Center Dynamics
articles.full_text:
Nvidia has told its data center partners to reduce their exposure to customers in China.
The GPU giant has told cloud computing clients to sell at least 51 percent of their services to non-Chinese companies, the Financial Times reports. Nvidia told customers its new restrictions verbally, and not in written documents.
The new rule only covers future contracts and not existing leases. With restrictions on access to Nvidia hardware in China, many Chinese companies have leased compute in Malaysia and Indonesia. Such deals could face limits under Nvidia's rules.
Local cloud providers are struggling with the new requirements because it is “difficult to find enough non-Chinese clients outside the US”, one Singapore-based group told the FT. “If strictly implemented, it will definitely hurt business.”
This week, Oracle reportedly dropped a $7bn deal with Tencent, which would have seen the Chinese cloud provider access as many as 100,000 Nvidia GPUs. The deal fell apart amid pressure on Oracle from US officials, as well as pressure on Tencent from Chinese officials to support domestic chips.
Nvidia has already more than halved the number of Asian customers authorized to buy its AI chips. This year, it created a “white list” of companies that have passed tougher compliance checks, aimed at limiting the export of GPUs to China.
While B300s are banned from export to China, the less powerful RTX Pro 5500 workstation graphics card is cleared for shipping to the country. However, Bloomberg reports that Chinese AI developers expect to receive only one percent of the chips they have ordered in the coming months.
Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese AI and cloud firms have in total ordered about six million RTX Pro 5500 chips, but will only receive a few tens of thousands over the next four months.
The low shipment number is due to capacity constraints, with Nvidia currently ramping up production. Should export controls not change, Chinese hyperscalers estimate they could receive around 700,000 RTX Pro 5500 units by the end of 2027.
“Unfortunately, US firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly half a decade ago, and China’s own limits on US imports,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Bloomberg.
The news comes following the revelation that US agencies are investigating whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the victim of a Chinese spy plot, with Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) accused of working for the Chinese state.
The Megaspeed exec has been accused of sending information to China, while the Singapore-based company has been accused of sending GPUs to China. It has denied the allegations.

articles.title: Kamau Therapeutics Releases Encouraging Sickle Cell Clinical Data Ahead of ASH Meeting - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
articles.summary: Kamau Therapeutics Releases Encouraging Sickle Cell Clinical Data Ahead of ASH Meeting  Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
articles.full_text:
Kamau Therapeutics, a California biotech company co-founded by Stanford University physician-scientist Matthew Porteus, MD, PhD, has emerged from stealth with the release of preliminary clinical data on its first cohort of gene-edited patients with sickle cell disease (SCD).
The findings, part of a trove of abstracts that will be presented at next month’s American Society of Hematology (ASH) conference, show precise correction of the SCD mutation in the β-globin gene in three SCD patients as well as restored expression of adult hemoglobin (HbA). In contrast to FDA-approved Casgevy, which overcomes the SCD mutation by switching up expression of fetal hemoglobin (HbF), Kamau is employing a direct replacement of the SCD mutation using homology-directed repair (HDR) of the β-globin gene.
All three patients are currently transfusion-independent and have not experienced any pain crises since receiving their gene-edited hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). In addition to the predominant HbA profile being restored, Kamau reports that the sickle hemoglobin (HbS) level fell below 20% of total hemoglobin in the two patients who have reached the 6-month post-infusion mark.
Porteus told GEN he was “very encouraged” by this early readout of Kamau’s RESTORE trial. “These were the target results that we were expecting once we got HDR to work in engraftable HSCs,” Porteus said. “We are now full speed ahead on enrolling more patients and moving to talk to the FDA about the registration trial design.” The Phase I/II RESTORE trial is enrolling some 15 participants.
Between the abstract submission and next month’s presentation at ASH, Porteus said Kamau has “further data that gives us confidence in the safety, efficacy and sustainability of the approach.” Porteus says that the updated data will be included in the ASH talk, which will be given by John DiPersio, MD, Director of the Center for Gene and Cellular Immunotherapy at Washington University School of Medicine, on December 14 in New Orleans.
“Achieving hemoglobin levels above 10 g/dL, with sickle hemoglobin below 20% and adult hemoglobin predominant, in patients who also remain free of vaso-occlusive events, is an encouraging early signal,” DiPersio said in a press release. “Seeing that profile alongside stable engraftment of corrected cells is what we would hope to see from a durable correction of the underlying mutation.”
Vali Barsan, MD, co-founder and CEO of Kamau Therapeutics, said his team applies “process engineering to HDR, nature’s own high-fidelity repair pathway.” The HDR pathway “can implement corrections we design directly into a patient’s own stem cells,” Barsan continued. “That has been the promise of gene editing from the beginning, and these data are early clinical evidence that it can be realized.”
Direct deposit
Porteus, who is head of R&D of Kamau, has been steadfast in his determination to translate some of the basic insights he helped define regarding DNA repair and recombination into the clinic, especially for the benefit of patients with SCD. He said his new company adopts a twin-stranded approach: reduce production of pathogenic HbS and restore the body’s own production of normal HbA. Kamau’s gene replacement strategy is a 1:1 exchange of the faulty HbS allele with a healthy HbA copy, rather than a gene addition strategy.
“We developed nula-cel to work in a patient’s own stem cells, enabling those cells to produce adult hemoglobin under the body’s normal regulation,” Porteus said. The nula-cel therapy directly corrects the SCD mutation in the β-globin gene. That is in contrast to the HbF switching approach taken in Casgevy, the gene editing therapy sponsored by Vertex Pharmaceuticals and CRISPR Therapeutics, approved in late 2023.
A major question is whether Kamau’s HDR strategy will offer any long-term clinical advantages compared to Casgevy. Porteus believes it might. “Since we see a greater reduction in HbS than the HbF [switching] approaches, we think that it will prove better at preventing the myriad of multi-organ damage that the disease causes,” Porteus told GEN. For example, “it has been shown that exchange transfusion, in which the target is to keep HbS below 30%, is better at preventing stroke or recurrent stroke than upregulation of HbF.”
In addition, Porteus said, “evolution has selected a tunable HbA as the solution to oxygen delivery to tissues under various conditions, whereas HbF is not tunable in its oxygen unloading. This may result in better long-term organ health.”
Of course, Kamau still faces some very stiff headwinds en route to commercial viability. In December 2024, Editas Medicine suspended its own gene editing asset for SCD after it was unable to find a pharma partner to move the therapy to approval despite strong clinical data.
Porteus notes that in his reading of Editas’ published data, “it did not appear the clinical results were improved over Casgevy.” Moreover, there are encouraging signs that the gene therapy approaches approved in 2023 are beginning to reach patients. “That Lyfgenia is, and Casgevy will soon be, profitable as patient infusions logarithmically increase quarter-over-quarter, while only addressing a tiny portion of the [SCD] patient population, gives us conviction on the commercial upside,” Porteus told GEN.
“The demand is there and we will be part of the solution to meet that demand,” Porteus insists. And as the CAR T commercial market demonstrates, “being first to market helps but the ultimate winner is best in indication.”
ASH anticipation
DiPersio’s presentation at ASH next month will be entitled: “First Clinical Results of Precise HBB Gene Correction by Homology Directed Repair in Patients with Severe Sickle Cell Disease: Safety and Efficacy from Phase 1A of the RESTORE Study” (NCT04819841). He will present results on three SCD patients treated with Kamau’s revised manufacturing process (V2.0) for nula-cel, along with continued follow-up of the first patient ever treated with nula-cel four years ago, under the auspices of Graphite Bio, Porteus’ previous company. Graphite Bio halted its SCD clinical trial in late 2022 and subsequently disbanded.
The ASH data “provide early clinical evidence that precise HDR-mediated correction of the native HBB gene is feasible,” Porteus said. “We look forward to learning more as the RESTORE trial progresses.”
All three V2.0 treated patients achieved transfusion independence before they were released from hospital, achieving neutrophil engraftment at a median of 21 days. In the two patients with more than six months of follow-up, total hemoglobin exceeded 10 g/dL, with relatively low levels of HbS (17.6% at 12 months and 19.1% at 8 months) and high HbA (77% at 12 months and 67% at 8 months).
Bone marrow HDR allele frequencies stabilized at approximately 20%, consistent with durable engraftment of gene-corrected HSCs. Single-cell analyses showed more than 90% of circulating red blood cells contained protective levels of HbA. There were no serious adverse events related to nula-cel or the multistep gene-editing process V2.0-treated patients, but some consistent with the busulfan conditioning and stem-cell transplantation.
Off-target gene editing remained low and unchanged, Kamau said. HDR allele frequencies exceeded the 20% target in all three patients (32–38%). HSC mobilization required a median of just 1.3 apheresis cycles to reach target cell dose.
Nula-cel, which has received Fast Track and Orphan Drug designations from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), is an ex vivo approach. Kamau engineers a patient’s own stem cells outside the body, verifying each cell product’s quality, potency, and safety, before reinfusing the HSCs into the patient. Kamau claims this offers a measure of control that would not be possible using an in vivo gene editing approach.
Kamau is funded by a group of investors including Khosla Ventures, Cormorant Asset Management, NEVA SGR, Draper VC, Modi Ventures, and Regeneron Ventures. The company’s leadership team also includes chief technology officer Ramji Krishnan, PhD, who brings experience in CMC leadership at BMS/Celgene, and autologous HSC gene therapy experience at Rocket; chief medical officer Jacob Garcia, MD, previously at Juno/BMS; and chief business officer Reza Afkhami, formerly with Global Blood Therapeutics, where he helped manage the company’s 2022 acquisition by Pfizer.

Newsletter Signup - Under Article / In Page

The latest advances in cardiovascular medicine will take center stage at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago from November 6 to 9. Bringing together researchers, clinicians, and industry leaders from around the world, the meeting will showcase new clinical findings and emerging approaches to tackling some of the biggest challenges in cardiovascular disease.
This year’s program will highlight the growing diversity of strategies being explored, from RNA-based therapies and in vivo gene editing to new ways of targeting cardiovascular inflammation and the metabolic risk factors that drive heart disease. Several companies are also set to present clinical data that could offer new insights into the potential of these approaches, including treatments aimed at triglycerides, transthyretin amyloidosis, and cardiometabolic disease.
However, the meeting comes against a backdrop of mixed results for the field, with recent setbacks in major cardiovascular trials underscoring just how difficult it is to translate promising biological targets into meaningful clinical benefits.
In this article, we look at some of the key biotech developments, companies, and clinical data to watch at AHA Scientific Sessions 2026.
Table of contents
- The next generation of cardiometabolic medicines on show at AHA Scientific Sessions 2026
- New therapeutic modalities open up more opportunities in different cardiovascular disease indications
- Tackling cardiovascular inflammation and other emerging risk factors
- AHA Scientific Sessions 2026: A test for the next generation of cardiovascular medicine
The next generation of cardiometabolic medicines on show at AHA Scientific Sessions 2026 Back to Top
Cardiovascular drug development is increasingly looking beyond traditional cholesterol management, with companies exploring new ways to tackle the range of metabolic factors that contribute to heart disease. Elevated triglycerides, remnant cholesterol, and obesity are all emerging as important targets, while advances in RNA therapeutics and gene editing are opening new possibilities for addressing cardiovascular risk at its biological roots. Several of these approaches will be featured in the late-breaking science program at AHA Scientific Sessions 2026, offering a snapshot of where the next generation of cardiometabolic medicines could be headed.
Targeting triglycerides and cholesterol through new mechanisms
While low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol – colloquially known as “bad cholesterol” – has long been the central focus of cardiovascular prevention, there is now a growing interest in addressing other atherogenic lipoproteins, particularly triglyceride-rich particles and their remnants, which can contribute to residual cardiovascular risk even in people who are already receiving standard cholesterol-lowering treatment. This, therefore, creates an opportunity for companies to develop therapies that act on different metabolic pathways.
One company to watch here is Marea Therapeutics (a subsidiary of Lisata Therapeutics), which is developing MAR001, a monoclonal antibody designed to inhibit angiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4), a regulator of lipid metabolism. The candidate has already demonstrated strong phase 1 and 2a results, and the company is due to present data at AHA Scientific Sessions 2026 from its phase 2b trial, which is evaluating the treatment in adults with elevated triglycerides and remnant cholesterol. The findings will be part of a late-breaking science session dedicated to new approaches to cardiometabolic risk reduction on November 9.
RNA interference (RNAi) company Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals is also pursuing this area, with two sets of data scheduled for presentation. One concerns ARO-DIMER-PA, the first dual-functional investigational RNAi therapy for the treatment of mixed hyperlipidemia, a common blood fat disorder characterized by elevated levels of both LDL cholesterol and triglycerides. The asset is designed to silence two genes involved in lipid regulation: PCSK9, which influences LDL cholesterol levels, and APOC3, which plays a role in raising triglycerides. By targeting both pathways with a single molecule, the approach aims to reduce multiple types of atherogenic lipoproteins in people with mixed hyperlipidemia. The company will present detailed results from its phase 1/2a study at AHA Scientific Sessions 2026.
Arrowhead will also share a pooled analysis of its phase 3 SHASTA-3 and SHASTA-4 trials of plozasiran, an RNAi medicine that targets APOC3. The analysis will examine triglyceride lowering and the potential to reduce acute pancreatitis risk in people with severe hypertriglyceridemia. Although plozasiran is already approved under the brand name REDEMPLO in several countries for familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS) – a rare, inherited genetic disorder that prevents the body from breaking down dietary fats – these data could provide further insight into its potential in a broader population with severely elevated triglycerides.
Can gene editing transform cardiovascular risk reduction?
RNA-based therapies will not be the only genetic approach attracting attention at AHA Scientific Sessions 2026. Gene editing could also offer a way to make durable changes to the pathways driving lipid disorders, potentially reducing the need for repeated treatment.
CRISPR Therapeutics will present phase 1b data for CTX310, an investigational in vivo CRISPR/Cas9 gene therapy designed to edit the ANGPTL3 gene in the liver. ANGPTL3 is involved in regulating lipid metabolism, and inhibiting its activity has been shown to lower several types of blood lipids. CTX310 is being developed for conditions including heterozygous and homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, mixed dyslipidemias, and severe hypertriglyceridemia.
The presentation, scheduled for the November 9 late-breaking session, will offer an early clinical look at whether a one-time gene-editing treatment can safely and effectively target this pathway in people with severe hypertriglyceridemia. The approach is particularly interesting because it aims to produce a lasting effect rather than relying on regular dosing. Additionally, it is an in vivo gene therapy, which is an approach that has attracted a lot of interest from big pharma; the swing toward in vivo therapies from ex vivo has been a key trend in the cell and gene therapy field in recent times. However, questions around safety, durability, and the long-term consequences of permanently altering a gene will be central to determining whether this strategy can translate into routine cardiovascular care.
CTX310 is part of a broader cardiovascular gene-editing pipeline at CRISPR Therapeutics. The company is also developing CTX340, which targets the angiotensinogen gene as a potential treatment for hypertension, and CTX321, which targets lipoprotein(a), another risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Together, these programs illustrate how gene editing could eventually be applied to several major drivers of cardiovascular risk.
The expanding overlap between obesity and cardiovascular disease
The growing recognition that obesity is closely linked to cardiovascular health is also shaping drug development, with companies increasingly looking beyond weight loss alone to investigate whether metabolic medicines like GLP1s can improve health in other ways.
Eli Lilly will present results from ATTAIN-OSA, a trial evaluating its oral GLP-1 receptor agonist orforglipron in people with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea. While sleep apnea is not itself a cardiovascular disease, it is associated with increased cardiovascular risk, making the findings relevant to the wider relationship between obesity and heart health.
Boehringer Ingelheim, meanwhile, is due to report results from SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT, a cardiovascular outcomes trial of survodutide, which is a dual GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist, in people with obesity. The study is particularly notable because it examines cardiovascular outcomes directly, rather than focusing solely on changes in body weight or metabolic measures.
These presentations reflect a broader shift in the field; as obesity medicines become more sophisticated, their potential role in reducing the wider burden of cardiometabolic disease is coming into sharper focus. The results from both trials could help clarify how far these treatments might extend beyond weight management.
New therapeutic modalities open up more opportunities in different cardiovascular disease indications Back to Top
Beyond cardiometabolic risk factors, advances in drug development are creating new opportunities to treat cardiovascular conditions that have historically been difficult to manage. RNAi, gene editing, and more targeted small molecules are among the approaches being explored, with companies increasingly looking to intervene in the underlying biology of specific heart diseases. At AHA Scientific Sessions 2026, two indications in particular will offer a glimpse of this progress: transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM).
New approaches to tackling transthyretin amyloidosis
ATTR-CM, a progressive condition in which misfolded transthyretin (TTR) proteins accumulate in the heart, has become an increasingly active area of cardiovascular drug development. articles.title: Drone warfare in space: Swarms of autonomous, laser-shooting cubesats could defend Western satellites in orbit - Space
articles.summary: Drone warfare in space: Swarms of autonomous, laser-shooting cubesats could defend Western satellites in orbit  Space
articles.full_text:
In May 2026, four Russian military satellites came close to ICEYE-X36, a private synthetic aperture radar satellite widely believed to be providing battlefield intelligence for Ukraine, in an apparently aggressive and risky "grey zone" maneuver that spooked many in the space industry.
Close enough to jam or interfere with the satellite's signal, blind it with a laser, fire a metal dart at it or, simply, force it to maneuver and burn fuel, the satellites' seemingly intimidatory behavior has increased the West's desire to develop defensive technology for satellites. In October 2026, it was reported that one of those same four Russian satellites passed within 500 meters (1,650 feet) of the same ICEYE satellite.
Now, U.K. startup Shield Space is racing to apply the lessons of drone warfare in Ukraine to develop swarms of up to 100 very small, low-cost, attritable drone-like autonomous spacecraft called cubesats. Released by a car-sized carrier in Earth orbit, these microwave-sized spacecraft will act as interceptors to protect Western satellites, and their deployment will mark a next step in the evolution of orbital warfare. Shield Space says that these space drones will use "effectors" like lasers or microwaves, or "kinetic standoff" techniques, to defend Western satellites even if controllers lose contact with them.
"We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million [$134 million US], which is how [much] you would pay for one satellite previously," said Graeme Ritchie, co-founder and CEO of Shield Space.
Launched in 2023, NASA's civilian project Starling demonstrated that a swarm of four small satellites can cooperate and operate autonomously in space on a civilian science mission without relying heavily on real-time commands from ground control. But that seems like a far cry from the adversarial or defensive missions Shield Space and its competitors imagine. It is telling that the leading space powers appear not to have demonstrated swarm combat in space — although they tend to be reluctant to reveal their space warfare capabilities.
In the fourth quarter of 2027, Shield Space plans to take this next step in space warfare's evolution by demonstrating rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) with two very small spacecraft. This effort, named Project Broadsword, will launch on SpaceX's Transporter-21 rideshare mission. It will send up an 8U cubesat and a smaller 3U target craft, which Shield Space plans to maneuver from 100 kilometers (62 miles) apart to within 100 meters (330 feet) of each other and, through four stages of autonomy, from human-in-the-loop to "approximately" fully autonomous. (A cubesat unit, or U, is a cube that measures 10 cm, or about 4 inches, on a side.)
The gaps between a true satellite-defense capability and this demonstration appear to be great, in terms of the technological and practical challenges of squeezing propulsion and power systems, AI compute power, sensors, the lasers the swarm needs to communicate and weapon systems onto small, lightweight maneuvering satellites. But it is a gap that Shield Space believes it can bridge through the purchase of relatively cheap off-the-shelf technology rather than more expensive bespoke designs.
"Yes, it's a problem because of size, weight and power," Ritchie told Space.com. "We've had to totally innovate from scratch some elements of the mission… but we have only got roughly 100 cm by 100 cm [40 by 40 inches], so saving space or having systems that are already completely integrated is the main aim."
"We have commissioned EnduroSat to build us an autonomous 8U cubesat that has chemical propulsion and its own imagery-collecting capability, which we will put our software on," said Dan Molland, co-founder and CTO of Shield Space, "and which we will then use to conduct our RPO.
"The good thing about cubesats is they're very standardized and they're very off the shelf," he added. "There's always some level of adjusting you've got to do, but these cubesats are a lot more plug and play than more conventional platforms, which are usually all custom-built."
Yet to focus on the technical issues may be to miss the point. "It takes an extraordinary amount of data to train the models and algorithms to achieve a fully autonomous mission," said Ritchie, "and the problem [unlike in the Ukraine war] is that data is not readily available.
"We can train AI using synthetic data, but it's just not quite good enough for space. It's incredibly important to gather data from missions like this if we really want autonomous missions in the future."
There is also the complexity of the AI needed in a war-fighting system. "Starling is a really great example," Molland told Space.com. "With Starling, you're essentially just asking a guidance system to make sure you stay within a given range of this or that satellite… But if you are controlling a swarm to deliver [a] military mission, you have a much more complex set of questions."
It also comes with the challenge of ensuring that AI complies with any rules of engagement.
But Ritchie and Molland believe these technical challenges can be overcome, and they have an aggressive schedule of demonstrations planned that they think will prove it.
Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. and author of the book "War in Space: Strategy, Spacepower, Geopolitics" (Edinburgh University Press, 2020), is more cautious about Shield Space's plans for the evolution of space warfare.
"They remind me of a late Cold War missile-defense scheme called Brilliant Pebbles," he told Space.com. "It was one of the more advanced research and development programs in the Strategic Defense Initiative."
The plan was to defend the U.S. against Soviet intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) by using thousands of small autonomous orbiting interceptors to destroy them by collision.
"With enough investment, a lot is feasible," Bowen said. "But you're looking at many years of development and testing, solving the problem of testing kinetic weapons in space without leaving debris, and finding someone to buy the system."
It is clear from Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine that the future of warfare includes swarms of low-cost autonomous drones — and Shield Space is already planning an aggressive schedule of missions to prove that this pattern applies to the final frontier as well.
According to Ritchie, the startup hopes to quickly go from the first RPO demonstration to testing two full-sized 16U cubesats. It will then move on to a full carrier of 10 such cubesats, and then to a "super carrier" of 10 carriers, which will be deployed across multiple orbits.
"We then get towards our future vision, which we call space-based carrier strike," said Ritchie. In this scenario, "responsive launch or pre-positioned carriers will give us an ability to protect and defend entire orbits, should you choose."

articles.title: Graphene armor boosts sodium-ion anodes - Metal Tech News
articles.summary: Graphene armor boosts sodium-ion anodes  Metal Tech News
articles.full_text:
Metal Tech News - November 3, 2026
Seeking to overcome one of the persistent limitations of sodium-ion batteries, researchers at Fudan University in Shanghai, China, have developed a graphene-protected electrode that demonstrates rapid charging and extended lifespan in laboratory testing, offering a potential path toward more durable, high-power energy storage.
Considered a promising alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries, sodium-ion technology relies on sodium rather than lithium to store and release electrical energy, using a metal that is approximately 1,000 times more abundant and could help reduce dependence on lithium supply chains.
Beyond the potential material cost and availability advantages, sodium-ion batteries have demonstrated strong power output, rapid charging capabilities, and reliable performance in cold temperatures, although their energy density generally remains lower than that of lithium-ion batteries, limiting how much energy they can store for a given weight or volume.
One of the challenges facing researchers has been the relationship between charging speed and battery lifespan, as moving sodium ions rapidly through an electrode can accelerate deterioration of the materials responsible for storing energy, particularly when larger amounts of active material are packed into the electrode to increase its capacity.
To address those limitations, a research team led by Yanhua Wan and professor Wei Li of Fudan University's Department of Chemistry developed a new anode structure that combined titanium dioxide with an ultrathin, graphene-like carbon coating, allowing sodium ions to move more readily through the material while protecting the electrode during repeated charging and discharging.
Published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society in October, the study involved researchers from Fudan University, Xiamen University, the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology, and Shanghai Electric Group Co. Ltd.
Rather than introducing a new battery chemistry, the researchers redesigned the structure of the anode – the electrode that stores sodium during charging – using hollow, double-layered titanium dioxide spheres assembled from nanosheets approximately two nanometers thick, each surrounded by a protective carbon coating.
Through that arrangement, the thin sheets provided shorter pathways for sodium ions to enter and leave the electrode, while the graphene-like covering improved electrical conductivity and helped maintain the material's structural integrity during repeated use.
According to Li, the combination allowed the researchers to address several limitations simultaneously, including the difficulty of maintaining rapid charging performance when electrodes contain larger quantities of energy-storing material.
"Our design combines fast energy storage with long cycle life, even when considerably more active material is packed onto the electrode," Li told Chemistry World.
In laboratory testing, the redesigned electrode retained more than 90% of its original capacity after 3,000 charging and discharging cycles at a relatively high active-material loading of 10.5 milligrams per square centimeter.
The researchers also recorded an areal capacity of 2.13 milliampere-hours per square centimeter, a measure of how much electrical charge an electrode can store across its surface, while maintaining a specific capacity of 121 milliampere-hours per gram under exceptionally rapid charging and discharging conditions.
Together, the results demonstrated that the electrode could sustain rapid sodium storage while retaining much of its capacity through thousands of cycles, including under conditions intended to more closely reflect the greater material quantities required for practical batteries.
Despite those findings, the experimental electrode remained some distance from commercial application, with additional testing needed to determine whether its performance could be maintained in complete batteries rather than individual electrode configurations.
"Practical charging speed also depends on the cathode electrode and electrolyte," Li explained. "Both must keep pace with our electrode and remain stable during repeated fast charging."
Manufacturing presented another challenge, as the researchers used established particle-forming, carbon-coating, and heat-treatment processes to produce the material, but had not demonstrated whether its unusually thin sheets and uniform protective covering could be reproduced consistently at industrial scale.
"Maintaining the same thin sheets and uniform graphene wrapping across large batches remains unproven," Li noted. "We would need to demonstrate consistent quality, yield and performance using larger equipment, while assessing energy use and processing costs."
Further testing under realistic battery operating conditions would also be necessary to establish whether the laboratory results could translate into practical energy storage systems, including larger cells containing conventional quantities of active materials.
For now, the research demonstrated how changes to the physical structure of existing electrode materials could improve sodium-ion storage performance, providing another potential avenue for developing batteries capable of combining rapid charging with longer operating lifespans.

articles.title: Nvidia Orders Data Center Partners to Limit Exposure to Chinese Customers - Breitbart News
articles.summary: Nvidia Orders Data Center Partners to Limit Exposure to Chinese Customers  Breitbart News
articles.full_text:
Nvidia has instructed data center partners worldwide to keep Chinese customers below half their cloud computing business, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
The Financial Times reports that Nvidia’s sales force and regional teams have spent the summer verbally passing along a new rule to data center partners: sell at least 51 percent of cloud computing services to non-Chinese companies. No such restriction existed before. The instructions were never put in writing, people familiar with the rules said, and they apply globally rather than just to data centers in Asia, according to two people familiar with the matter. The rule covers only future contracts; existing leasing agreements are untouched.
Sources describe the move as pre-emptive, meant to head off criticism from U.S. lawmakers and other critics of Nvidia’s approach to China before it escalates further. Washington has been trying to close off routes that let intermediaries build a black market for Nvidia chips in China, and to stop Chinese companies from reaching advanced chips indirectly through overseas leasing deals.
Breitbart News previously reported that Nvidia cut off many customers after performing an audit to ensure chips were not being moved into China through the black market:
Nvidia has taken significant steps to tighten control over the distribution of its AI chips in Asia. The AI giant has established a new whitelist of verified customers that dramatically reduces the number of authorized clients by over fifty percent. This move comes as part of an intensified effort to prevent sophisticated AI processors from being illegally smuggled into China, where U.S. export restrictions have banned the sale of advanced AI chips since 2022.
The remaining companies on the approved list have undergone rigorous compliance inspections designed to confirm they are legitimate businesses rather than shell companies created to funnel Nvidia GPUs and servers into restricted markets. Nvidia’s verification process reportedly has included sending field staff to inspect customer data centers, conducting contract verification procedures, and interviewing end users to authenticate business operations.
Nvidia, responding to the reporting, said: “Datacenters and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide. Longstanding U.S. policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can. America’s longstanding policy has always supported the build-out of American infrastructure worldwide, bringing prosperity, influence, and jobs home.”
One Singapore-based cloud provider said it was “difficult to find enough non-Chinese clients outside the U.S.” to meet the new threshold, and warned about what strict enforcement would mean: “If strictly implemented, it will definitely hurt business.”
Breitbart News recently reported that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy he developed a relationship with:
Authorities were already investigating whether Alice Huang was helping China obtain restricted advanced Nvidia AI chips before surveillance revealed she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to a report by the New York Times. The discovery raised alarms due to Huang’s central role in the global AI race as the CEO of Nvidia, which produces the most powerful AI chips in the world.
Nvidia, meanwhile, said Megaspeed is an ordinary regional customer and that Jensen Huang’s meetings with Alice Huang are routine CEO interactions with customers.
“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo told the Times.
The war to control AI between America and China becomes even more complex as the deep ties between U.S. tech giants and the Communist country become clearer. Breitbart News social media director Wynton Hall has written his New York Times bestseller Code Red: The Left, the Right, China, and the Race to Control AI to serve as the definitive guide on how the MAGA movement can create positions on AI that benefit humanity without handing control of our nation to the leftists of Silicon Valley or allowing the Chinese to take over the world.
Read more at the Financial Times here.
Lucas Nolan is a reporter for Breitbart News covering issues of AI, free speech, and online censorship.

articles.title: Poland Commands Eight Military Satellites in Orbit as Geospatial Agency ARGUS Becomes Space Command - Tech Times
articles.summary: Poland Commands Eight Military Satellites in Orbit as Geospatial Agency ARGUS Becomes Space Command  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Poland's military geospatial intelligence agency is being elevated to a full Space Operations and Environmental Support Command, Col. Leszek Paszkowski announced in a November 2, 2026 interview published by Space24.pl. The upgrade broadens the mandate of the Agencja Rozpoznania Geoprzestrzennego i Usług Satelitarnych — ARGUS — beyond battlefield reconnaissance into environmental monitoring and humanitarian crisis support.
ARGUS, established June 27, 2024 as Poland's dedicated military geospatial and satellite services agency, now controls eight military satellites in orbit: four synthetic aperture radar satellites under the POLSARIS program and four optical imaging satellites in the MikroGlob constellation, whose final units reached orbit on October 1, 2026. Combined investment across three satellite constellation contracts totals approximately €903M.
Col. Paszkowski's November interview confirms the Space Operations Command elevation will give ARGUS command authority aligned with Poland's other service branches. The environmental monitoring mission adds weather intelligence and natural disaster response to ARGUS's battlefield surveillance function, expanding the agency's value to both military and civilian national security structures.
ARGUS in NATO's Space Architecture
NATO established Combined Forces Space Component Command — CFSpCC — in February 2025 under Allied Air Command at Ramstein Air Base, Germany, giving Poland's growing satellite fleet an alliance-wide coordination framework. CFSpCC operates the NATO Space Operations Centre at Ramstein — NSpOC — which consolidates national space contributions from member countries including Poland and provides alliance commanders with fused satellite situational awareness.
The NATO Space Centre of Excellence in Toulouse reached Full Operational Capability on January 26, 2026, establishing the alliance's dedicated doctrine development and training hub for space operations. ARGUS's operational integration with CFSpCC is governed by NATO doctrine developed and disseminated through the Toulouse center.
Poland's Space Operations Center: Already Standing Watch
Poland's dedicated satellite command node — the Polish Space Operations Center, POLSpOC — reached full operational readiness on March 6, 2026, at ARGUS headquarters in Warsaw. The center serves as Poland's national interface with NSpOC and the command node for all eight military satellites now under ARGUS control.
Where POLSpOC handles the technical execution of satellite collection tasks, the Space Operations Command designation Col. Paszkowski confirmed provides the institutional command authority for ARGUS to task satellites in direct support of operational military requirements — a distinction that matters in joint operations where collection priorities must be adjudicated among competing commanders.
How SAR Satellites See Through Clouds and Darkness
Synthetic aperture radar satellites offer a surveillance capability that optical satellites cannot provide: cloud-penetrating, day-and-night imagery generated by microwave pulses bounced off the ground surface rather than reflected sunlight. Poland's POLSARIS constellation, built under a €200M POLSARIS contract with ICEYE signed in May 2025, operates at 25-centimeter spotlight-mode resolution — sufficient to identify individual vehicles and monitor equipment movements across Poland's eastern border corridor.
Unlike passive optical systems that require daylight and clear skies, SAR satellites illuminate targets with microwave energy and process reflected returns into synthetic imagery regardless of weather or time of day. Poland's four-satellite POLSARIS constellation provides multiple daily revisit opportunities over any point in its coverage area, enabling continuous monitoring rather than periodic snapshots.
POLSARIS: From Contract to Full Constellation in Under 12 Months
The first two POLSARIS satellites launched aboard the SpaceX Transporter-15 on November 28, 2025, from Vandenberg Space Force Base. ICEYE delivered a second pair of satellites to orbit on SpaceX's Transporter-16 rideshare mission on March 30, 2026. The Polish Armed Forces formally received all four POLSARIS satellites on May 15, 2026 — less than twelve months from contract signing, a deployment pace ICEYE describes as the fastest national military satellite delivery on record.
The ground control infrastructure for POLSARIS operations is housed at the WZŁ-1 facility, supporting ARGUS satellite tasking and data distribution to military end-users across Poland's command structure.
MikroGlob Completes Poland's Optical Layer
Poland's first MikroGlob satellite — PIRX-1, also designated MIKROGLOB-1 — launched July 7, 2026, aboard SpaceX Transporter-17 from Vandenberg. Three additional MikroGlob satellites — MikroGlob-2, -3, and -4 — followed on Transporter-18 on October 1, 2026, completing the four-satellite optical constellation and bringing Poland's total active military satellites to eight.
Creotech Instruments built the MikroGlob satellites on its HyperSat bus platform, developed at the company's Piaseczno facility near Warsaw, under a PLN 556.7M satellite program contract signed in December 2024, equivalent to approximately €128M at time of signing.
POLEOS: High-Resolution Airbus Satellites Coming in 2027
Poland's third satellite constellation — POLEOS — consists of two very-high-resolution optical satellites built by Airbus Defence and Space on the S950 bus. Airbus announced the POLEOS contract in early January 2023, covering the two satellites, an associated ground segment including a direct-receiving station in Poland, launch services, and operator training, with launch planned from Kourou, French Guiana by 2027. Poland has received Pléiades Neo imagery access from Airbus starting from 2023, providing high-resolution optical coverage ahead of the POLEOS satellites entering service. The two POLEOS satellites currently complete final integration at Airbus facilities in Toulouse, where they will deliver 30-centimeter optical resolution upon reaching orbit.
What Poland's Twelve Satellites Mean for NATO's Eastern Flank
Poland's eight operational satellites — four POLSARIS SAR and four MikroGlob optical — combined with the two incoming POLEOS high-resolution optical platforms create a twelve-satellite national space architecture covering a full range of imaging modes. The combined SAR and optical constellation eliminates the primary limitation each technology faces alone: POLSARIS collects through cloud cover and at night; MikroGlob delivers photographic-quality daytime optical detail; and the incoming POLEOS satellites will add very-high-resolution 30cm imagery alongside MikroGlob's wider-area coverage.
For NATO's eastern flank, Poland's emerging Space Operations Command represents the first national space command among front-line alliance members in the Baltic-to-Black Sea corridor, providing sovereign collection capability that can be tasked independently of alliance collection priorities — a strategic asset at a region where collection demand consistently exceeds available assets.
Exchange rate as of November 3, 2026: €1 ≈ PLN 4.35. All Polish zloty-to-euro conversions in this article are approximate.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is ARGUS and when was it established?
ARGUS — the Agencja Rozpoznania Geoprzestrzennego i Usług Satelitarnych (Geospatial Intelligence and Satellite Services Agency) — is Poland's dedicated military geospatial and satellite services agency, established June 27, 2024. Its mandate covers oversight of Poland's sovereign military satellite programs and provision of geospatial intelligence to Polish armed forces and NATO allies. Col. Paszkowski's November 2026 interview confirms ARGUS will be elevated to a full Space Operations and Environmental Support Command.
How many military satellites does Poland currently operate?
Poland operates eight military satellites as of November 2026: four POLSARIS synthetic aperture radar satellites from ICEYE and four MikroGlob optical imaging satellites from Creotech Instruments. Two additional high-resolution optical satellites — the POLEOS program built by Airbus Defence and Space on the S950 bus — are scheduled to launch from Kourou, French Guiana by 2027, bringing the total sovereign military satellite count to twelve.
What is the difference between SAR and optical satellites?
Synthetic aperture radar satellites generate their own microwave energy pulses and record returns from ground surfaces, producing imagery regardless of cloud cover or darkness. Optical satellites capture reflected sunlight, delivering high-resolution photographic-quality imagery but requiring daylight and cloud-free conditions. Poland's combination of four POLSARIS SAR satellites and four MikroGlob optical satellites provides continuous coverage across weather and lighting conditions that neither technology alone could deliver.
How does ARGUS connect to NATO's space coordination framework?
ARGUS contributes satellite collection through Poland's Polish Space Operations Center — POLSpOC — into NATO's Space Operations Centre at Ramstein, Germany, which operates under the Combined Forces Space Component Command, established in February 2025. The NATO Space Centre of Excellence in Toulouse, which reached Full Operational Capability on January 26, 2026, provides the doctrine and training framework governing how national space commands like ARGUS integrate into collective NATO operations.

articles.title: Nvidia Reportedly Orders AI Data Center Partners to Reduce China Exposure - CryptoRank
articles.summary: Nvidia Reportedly Orders AI Data Center Partners to Reduce China Exposure  CryptoRank
articles.full_text:
Share news:
Nvidia reportedly told global cloud partners to direct at least 51% of services to non-Chinese customers, potentially limiting Chinese access to overseas AI computing and delaying data center expansion. The guidance is described as nonmandatory by separate reporting, while a B300 server rack reportedly sold for $2.8 million in China versus about $600,000 internationally, highlighting chip scarcity and rising pressure on Nvidia’s business.
Key takeaways
- Nvidia reportedly requires majority non-Chinese AI cloud customers
- Overseas data centers face growing restrictions on Chinese demand
- China exposure adds pressure to Nvidia's struggling stock
Nvidia is reportedly directing its global data center partners to reduce their reliance on Chinese customers, potentially closing another route through which China's technology companies access advanced American artificial intelligence chips.
According to the Financial Times, Nvidia has instructed cloud computing providers to ensure at least 51% of their services go to non-Chinese companies. The newspaper cited five people familiar with the matter, describing a policy communicated verbally through sales teams rather than formal documentation.
The development comes as Nvidia stock has fallen more than 13% over the past month, with investors questioning AI infrastructure spending despite strong demand for the company's chips.
Nvidia's 51% Rule Could Reshape Overseas AI Data Centers
The reported restrictions apply globally to new cloud computing contracts rather than existing customer agreements.
Chinese companies have increasingly rented overseas computing capacity to train AI models without directly importing Nvidia's most advanced processors, which remain subject to US export controls.
Southeast Asian data centers have become particularly important because Chinese technology companies represent a substantial share of demand in several regional markets.
The new requirements could force cloud providers to find additional American, European or other non-Chinese customers before expanding their computing infrastructure.
However, separate reporting by The Information characterized Nvidia's instructions as nonmandatory guidance that has not been enforced as a strict customer-allocation rule.
That distinction matters because the financial consequences depend on whether operators must actually reject Chinese contracts.
The move also raises questions about previously reported overseas partnerships, including Tencent's $7 billion Oracle arrangement involving approximately 100,000 advanced AI chips.
Neither company has publicly confirmed that agreement, and there is no evidence Nvidia's reported instructions have changed its terms.
China's AI Chip Shortage Creates a $2.8 Million Problem
Nvidia's latest restrictions would arrive after years of escalating US controls on advanced semiconductor exports.
Its B300 chips cannot legally be sold directly into China under existing restrictions, creating substantial pricing disparities between international and Chinese markets.
According to the Financial Times, an Nvidia B300 server rack selling internationally for approximately $600,000 recently fetched $2.8 million in China.
That represents a premium exceeding 360%, highlighting the scarcity of advanced computing equipment.
Meanwhile, Nvidia has reportedly reduced its list of approved Asian AI chip customers by more than half through stricter compliance screening.
The company previously disclosed that H200 shipments to China represented less than 1% of quarterly data center revenue despite limited US export licenses.
Earlier discussions about reopening chip purchases for ByteDance and Alibaba had suggested some restrictions might ease.
However, tougher cloud access requirements could offset those potential gains.
What the China Restrictions Mean for Nvidia Stock
The immediate financial risk may fall on cloud operators that depend heavily on Chinese customers rather than Nvidia itself.
Some providers could struggle to replace that demand, potentially delaying future data center expansion and GPU purchases.
For Nvidia, the restrictions introduce another complication as the company faces a broader semiconductor stock selloff.
The company also risks encouraging Chinese developers to accelerate investment in domestic alternatives, including Huawei and Cambricon.
That trend is already visible in China's AI chip market, where domestic suppliers have gained opportunities as American export restrictions tighten.

The reported measure would limit the ability of Chinese AI developers to obtain computing power through foreign data centers, an increasingly important alternative to purchasing advanced American semiconductors directly.
The development comes as the United States seeks to maintain its technological advantage in artificial intelligence while Chinese companies pursue increasingly sophisticated AI systems despite restrictions on advanced chips.
Nvidia moves to limit Chinese access to AI computing
The Financial Times reported that Nvidia began communicating the new requirements to cloud computing providers over the summer, citing five people familiar with the matter.
The instructions reportedly apply to data centers worldwide, rather than exclusively to facilities in Asia. They affect future contracts but do not alter existing agreements.

The company has reportedly encouraged cloud providers to diversify their customers and disclose the identities of end users, but has not enforced the 51 percent threshold as a strict requirement.
The distinction leaves questions about how aggressively Nvidia intends to enforce the reported restrictions and whether they will eventually become binding conditions for its partners.
Responding to the reports, Nvidia neither confirmed nor denied the new measures. In a statement provided to Agence France-Presse, the company emphasized the importance of expanding American AI infrastructure internationally.
“America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide,” Nvidia said.
The company argued that the global expansion of data centers built around American technology is essential to maintaining U.S. competitiveness in artificial intelligence.
Beijing responded cautiously. During a Nov. 3 press conference, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said she was unfamiliar with the reported restrictions.
“We believe that all parties should engage in cooperation based on the principles of fairness, transparency and non-discrimination,” Mao said, according to the ministry’s official transcript.
The reported Nvidia guidance adds another dimension to a technology confrontation that has increasingly moved beyond conventional semiconductor trade.
Overseas cloud computing becomes a new battleground
Since 2022, Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI semiconductors to China, arguing that the technology could strengthen Beijing’s military and intelligence capabilities.
However, limiting physical shipments has not necessarily prevented Chinese developers from accessing American computing technology.
Instead of purchasing advanced chips directly, Chinese companies can rent computing capacity from data centers located in other countries. The processors remain overseas, while developers access their computational resources remotely through cloud services.
This arrangement has complicated American attempts to control the international availability of advanced AI hardware.
An April 2026 Congressional Research Service report identified remote cloud access as a significant challenge for U.S. export controls. The report noted that restrictions on transferring physical chips do not automatically prohibit every form of remote access, although existing rules can apply to certain end users and sensitive applications.
American lawmakers have attempted to address the issue through legislation.
In January, the House of Representatives passed the Remote Access Security Act, which would expand federal authority to regulate foreign access to controlled American technologies through cloud computing.
“The CCP’s AI ambitions are being fueled by its access to American chips housed in data centers located outside of China,” Rep. John Moolenaar said in a statement announcing the bill’s passage.
The legislation reflects growing concern in Washington that traditional export controls may be insufficient in an industry where computing resources can be accessed internationally without transferring ownership of the underlying hardware.
At the same time, U.S. policy has not amounted to a complete prohibition on American chip sales to China.
In January, the Department of Commerce revised its licensing policy, allowing certain Nvidia H200 and comparable processors to be considered for export to approved Chinese customers on a case-by-case basis.
“Export controls should evolve with changes in technology, while protecting national security,” said Jeffrey Kessler, under secretary of commerce for industry and security.
The competing priorities illustrate Washington’s difficult balancing act: preventing sensitive technology from strengthening potential adversaries while preserving American leadership in the global semiconductor and cloud computing markets.
Nvidia’s reported restrictions could also create commercial challenges for overseas data center operators, particularly those in Asia that depend heavily on Chinese customers.
The Financial Times reported that some providers have struggled to attract enough non-Chinese customers to meet the proposed threshold. Stricter enforcement could force certain operators to reduce their operations or reconsider expansion plans.
