- The Trillion-Dollar AI Illusion: Is the World Investing in a Revolution or a Bubble?
- Anthropic Files for Potential $100 Billion IPO Amid AI Safety Concerns
- China Pours $13 Billion Into AI Robotics as Competition With US Enters New Phase
Taiwan crackdown highlights expanding struggle over AI chips
The reported Nvidia restrictions coincide with renewed efforts in Taiwan to prevent advanced American semiconductor technology from reaching mainland China.
On Nov. 3, Taiwan News reported that Taiwanese lawmakers were considering amendments to export-control legislation that would impose tougher penalties for illegally transferring advanced semiconductors and related technology.
The proposed measures could introduce prison sentences of up to 10 years and fines reaching NT$10 million, approximately $304,500.
The legislation follows an investigation in which Taiwanese prosecutors indicted nine people in August for allegedly diverting 74 servers equipped with advanced Nvidia processors to mainland China.
The defendants included employees associated with Nvidia and server manufacturer Supermicro.
The proposed restrictions would also target attempts to circumvent export controls by routing semiconductor technology through third countries.
“Changes in supply chains and semiconductor security and resilience are happening faster,” Wang Guo-chen, a researcher at Taiwan’s Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, told Taiwan’s Public Television Service.
The case is part of a broader pattern of investigations into suspected attempts to circumvent American restrictions on advanced AI hardware.
In March, the U.S. Department of Justice announced charges against three individuals accused of participating in a scheme involving approximately $2.5 billion worth of advanced servers purchased from an American manufacturer.
Prosecutors alleged that the defendants used false documentation, intermediary companies and elaborate shipping arrangements to conceal the movement of restricted computing equipment to China.
“These chips are the product of American ingenuity, and NSD will continue to enforce our export-control laws to protect that advantage,” said Assistant Attorney General John Eisenberg.
The allegations remain subject to judicial proceedings.
Together, the investigations, proposed legislation and Nvidia’s reported cloud restrictions illustrate how the technology confrontation between Washington and Beijing is expanding across the global semiconductor supply chain.
American authorities are increasingly concerned not only with where advanced chips are manufactured and sold, but also with who ultimately controls and uses the computing power they provide.
For Chinese AI developers, overseas cloud services have offered an alternative source of advanced computing capacity as domestic semiconductor producers work to close the technological gap.
Whether Nvidia ultimately enforces the reported customer restrictions remains uncertain. Nevertheless, the development highlights a broader shift in the U.S.-China technology rivalry, in which access to computing power itself is becoming as strategically important as ownership of the chips that produce it.

Nvidia has purportedly told its data center customers that they must limit the amount of business that they do with Chinese companies in what is a new policy for the U.S. company. The move would mean that data center operators who sell their services to Chinese companies must now track what proportion of their overall business they make up, limiting them to just 49% of the total and ensuring 51% are non-Chinese outfits. The FT reports the new policy has been communicated to Nvidia's customers by its sales force and regional teams, and does not appear to have been laid out in any official form via documentation.
Notably, Nvidia's alleged new stance on Chinese customers does not only apply to data centers that are located in Asia. Instead, it applies to those based globally, and even then it only affects new and future contracts rather than any existing Nvidia hardware leasing agreements that are in place. In a statement, Nvidia notes that "American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide." The statement goes on to say that current U.S. policy "encourages" cloud providers to build on American infrastructure and to accept business from "everywhere they can."
But this latest move to restrict Chinese access to Nvidia's high-performance data center hardware comes amid ongoing tensions between the United States and China with regard to AI capabilities. Nvidia can only sell its chips to whitelisted companies, a situation that has led to a thriving black market for its wares. Earlier this year, it was found that even Nvidia's older servers have become so sought-after that their values have tripled.
Whether limitations on who Nvidia can sell its chips to have had the desired effect is open to debate, with even China's state-owned telecoms giant China Telecom having recently been found to have Nvidia hardware in its data centers. The situation wouldn't be out of place in a blockbuster espionage thriller, with Nvidia CEO Jason Huang reportedly the target of a spy plot by Chinese agents.
The reasons behind the U.S. government's attempts to limit China's access to Nvidia hardware are obvious. The aim is to stymie China's ability to advance its own AI technologies, with Nvidia chips the go-to option for AI servers and data centers around the globe. But this limitation on which customers cloud service providers can accept will put additional strain on companies that are already fighting it out for the same contracts. Reducing the pool of potential customers could potentially see a shrinking in the scale of data center operations moving forward.

articles.title: Nvidia tells cloud clients to cap China business at 49% of their services - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: Nvidia tells cloud clients to cap China business at 49% of their services  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
Nvidia spent years fighting to keep selling chips in China. Now it's reportedly telling the data centers that resell its compute to pull back from Chinese customers instead.
Nvidia has told cloud and data center clients they need to keep Chinese companies to no more than 49% of their customer base, according to the Financial Times, which Bloomberg cited in a report published November 3. The instruction reportedly went out through Nvidia's sales and regional teams rather than in writing. It applies to neoclouds and other data center operators that buy Nvidia chips in bulk and rent out the compute.
The guidance effectively asks these operators to make sure at least 51% of their services go to firms outside China. Think about that. For a chip maker that spent most of 2025 and 2026 publicly lobbying Washington to loosen export rules so it could keep selling in China, pushing its own customers to shrink their Chinese exposure is a strange kind of hedge. It suggests Nvidia itself expects the China market to keep getting smaller, messier, or more legally dangerous, not bigger.
It isn't the first move of its kind this year. In July, Nvidia cut its list of approved Asian buyers by more than half, according to the Financial Times. That came after it introduced stricter compliance checks, which sent staff into customer data centers to verify contracts and interview end users. The crackdown followed a case in March: US prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and two employees with smuggling roughly $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips into China through a Southeast Asian shell company. Restricted Nvidia B300 servers have reportedly sold for close to $1 million inside China, nearly double the US list price. That's a hefty premium. A margin like that pays for the smuggling.
Frankly, the smuggling risk alone explains a lot of this. Every chip that ends up rerouted into China through a proxy buyer can blow back on Nvidia with US regulators. The company has already watched one alleged multibillion-dollar scheme play out in federal court this year. Capping a cloud operator's Chinese customer share is a blunt way to cut off the incentive to game the system in the first place.
Beijing is reversing its own block on Nvidia's H200 chip, letting Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek buy limited numbers after keeping them out for months despite U.S. export approval. The move, capped at under 200,000 units and restricted to AI training use, looks like a stopgap while Huawei and Cambricon race to close the performance gap. - China AI chips buying restrictions - how to train frontier AI models
There's also the export-control reality underneath all of it. China and other restricted markets made up somewhere around 20% to 25% of Nvidia's data center revenue before Washington tightened the rules. Jensen Huang has said losing full access to China could cost Nvidia as much as $50 billion a year if it had competitive products to sell there. That number hasn't materialized. It can't, under the current rules. Huang has been blunt about it: he told reporters this year that US export controls "have already largely backfired" by pushing Beijing to build its own chip supply instead of slowing it down.
That domestic buildout is the other half of this story. Huawei's Ascend 910C, built on SMIC's 7-nanometer process, reportedly reached close to 40% yield this year, according to industry reporting picked up by Tom's Hardware, making the line profitable for the first time. Huawei shipped around 812,000 AI chips domestically, roughly half of all China-branded AI chip shipments tracked this year. TrendForce has projected Nvidia's share of high-end AI chips used by Chinese cloud companies could fall from around 80% to somewhere between 50% and 60%. Alibaba and Tencent have both told Nvidia they plan to buy significantly fewer chips than originally planned. Chinese regulators have reportedly pressed Alibaba and ByteDance directly on why they're still ordering Nvidia's H20 over Huawei's hardware.
Put those two trends together and Nvidia's new guidance to cloud clients looks less like aggression and more like triage. China is buying less, scrutinizing more, and building its own alternative faster than expected. Telling neoclouds to diversify their customer base isn't really about punishing China. The logic isn't hard to follow. It's about making sure Nvidia isn't left holding the compliance risk for a market that's already shrinking on its own.
Nvidia didn't respond to requests for comment cited in the Financial Times and Bloomberg reporting. Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance have not publicly addressed the specific 49% guidance.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Defends Nvidia After Spy Investigation Report. Why I’d Buy the Dip. - Barchart.com
articles.summary: Jensen Huang Defends Nvidia After Spy Investigation Report. Why I’d Buy the Dip.  Barchart.com
articles.full_text:
Megaspeed, a cloud company in Singapore, buys Nvidia's (NVDA) chips. The New York Times reported that U.S. authorities are investigating a former Megaspeed executive. She's suspected of passing information to China and helping get around U.S. rules on chip sales. The investigation has been running since late 2024 and has now been handed to the Justice Department. On Oct. 29, Huang told Bloomberg that Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed were “normal and not unusual.” He said that Nvidia has checked every one of its chips at Megaspeed and found that none of them had been sent to China illegally. He further noted that the executive doesn't even work there anymore. The very next day, NVDA stock fell about 4%, but that probably had more to do with a wider selloff in AI stocks.
Investors might wonder if any of this could hurt Nvidia's business. In my opinion, I don't think it will. As of this writing, Nvidia is among the two most valuable companies in the world, and its business continues to look stronger every quarter. In its last quarter, it made $96.2 billion in revenue, more than double what it made a year earlier. Most of that came from data centers, which made up $89 billion in revenue, up 117% year-over-year (YoY). For the current quarter, Nvidia expects about $108 billion in revenue, comfortably over the $104 billion analysts expected.
And here's the main reason I believe the investigation shouldn't hurt Nvidia's business. As I pointed out after its August report, Nvidia's $108 billion forecast doesn't even assume any data center compute revenue from China. So the business is already growing fast without selling its AI chips to China. That's why I think the dip may be a buying opportunity for long-term investors.
About Nvidia Stock
Nvidia makes the chips behind most of the world's AI. Its data center GPUs, networking gear, and software power the biggest AI systems out there. Its chips are so powerful that the U.S. limits their sale to China. This is why an investigation into a customer like Megaspeed draws so much attention. Founded in 1993, the company is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, and is led by co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia's stock is up about 9% this year, a bit behind the S&P 500's ($SPX) 12% gain during the same period. In early October, it reached an all-time high of $243.37 but has dropped roughly 17% since. Part of that drop was due to worries about Big Tech's AI spending, and the Megaspeed investigation has added to the pressure.
Nvidia's stock already looked cheap this year compared to its historical norms, and the discount looks even bigger after the recent drop. Its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) of 21.70x sits about 48% below its 5-year average of 41.67x. Its forward price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 11.85x is also about 39% below its average of 19.53x. That's a steep discount, especially for a company whose earnings are still growing fast. Analysts expect EPS to jump 95% this fiscal year and another 71% next year. At that pace, the P/E falls to just 12.70x by fiscal 2028. The balance sheet is a genuine strength as well. Nvidia holds $62.47 billion in cash against $38.86 billion in debt. Overall, I think the recent selloff in AI stocks and the investigation fears have pushed NVDA stock lower than the business deserves.
A Strong Quarter, a Stronger Outlook
In its second quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia delivered another strong report, beating analysts' consensus on both key metrics. Revenue beat estimates by about $4 billion, while adjusted EPS of $2.22 also surpassed the $2.10 analysts expected. Gross margins held at a healthy 75%, and Nvidia handed back about $26 billion to shareholders through buybacks and dividends.
Management expects even stronger growth ahead. CFO Colette Kress said revenue should grow about 70% next fiscal year, well above the roughly 45% analysts had expected. And that's with Nvidia still unable to make enough chips to meet demand.
What Do Analysts Expect for NVDA Stock?
Based on 52 Wall Street analysts, NVDA stock holds a consensus “Strong Buy” rating with a mean price target of $326.65, indicating a healthy 62% upside. So, after the stock has dipped more than 15% while the business is still booming, analysts also largely see this as a buying opportunity for investors.
On the date of publication, Jabran Kundi did not directly have a position in any of the securities mentioned in this article. All information and data in this article is solely for informational purposes. For more information please view the Barchart Disclosure Policy here.

articles.title: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling - TechCrunch
articles.summary: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling  TechCrunchHere’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch  The VergeApple Watch Always-Listening AI Features Roll Out to Select Users  GizmodoApple's Upcoming watchOS 27 Beta Will Enable Siri Recap And Live Rewind Audio Features  EngadgetApple Watch Automatically Identifies Songs Playing Around You  MacRumors
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
After just a day with Apple’s Siri Recaps feature on my Apple Watch, I can already see how its value may ultimately outweigh any creepiness factor that comes from the AI-powered audio recording and summarization it provides. However, I also see areas where AI-assisted note-taking can go too far, capturing things that aren’t worth remembering, and where there’s room for improvement.
The first two, sound and song detection, don’t represent potential privacy concerns; they are designed to detect either important sounds — like an alarm or doorbell — or identify a song using Shazam’s technology. The former helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users navigate the world, and the latter is something we’ve already done with our iPhone for nearly two decades now.
It’s the two other features, Live Rewind and Siri Recaps, that have raised concerns. The features record and then transcribe or summarize the conversations happening with and around the Apple Watch’s owner. Live Rewind lets you go back to see what was said in the past 15 seconds, while Siri Recaps summarize audio throughout your day, saving notes of the important things that were said.
Apple has taken care to ensure the privacy of these AI features by processing the audio and running AI models on-device, when possible, and by not identifying speakers, storing raw audio files, and redacting private information, like government ID numbers or personal account information.
Still, some are put off by the idea that we’re now normalizing the idea that technology is always listening.
I find myself sympathizing with both camps. I often lament that we’ve allowed technology to become so pervasive in our daily lives, but I still see the value in what Apple has built.
I haven’t yet had an appropriate time to test Live Rewind, nor do I think this will be a feature I use as often. I’m more likely to say “sorry, what?” or “can you repeat that?” if I missed something that was said, before turning to my Apple Watch for help.
But with Siri Recaps, I immediately saw how this could become a feature I rely on regularly to save important notes for later.
I was able to test the feature in a real-world scenario yesterday, when we were dropping off my teen’s car for repairs and picking up a rental. At both places, employees shared a lot of information about time frames, prices, and policies that were delivered verbally. The information came too fast to stop and write anything down. Yet when I returned to Siri Recaps later in the day, it had captured key details that I may need to refer back to.
For instance, it noted the deductible, the repair time frame, the amount of gas we had in the rental at the start, and other things I wanted to remember.
One complaint is that Siri Recaps had mixed this information with other topics that were later discussed in the home, like an errand we needed to run and what time babysitting was this week, something we were discussing in order to create an appointment on the family calendar with an appropriate alert time frame.
I think these items should have been saved in a separate note titled “family schedule and errands,” rather than in the same note with the car repairs, but under a separate heading.
Because I configured Siri Recaps to run at all times, it also captured non-essential things, like our “plan” to watch the midterms coverage on TV, which is not the kind of thing you’d normally jot down a note about. It also was a stark reminder that the feature was listening in on our everyday conversations. That’s something that could feel invasive in different scenarios, if the subject being discussed was more personal in nature.
This had me considering turning off the Recap feature while at home in the evening, so family dinner table chatter doesn’t become note fodder.
While I appreciated that the Recap picked up a reminder about an errand I needed to run from one of the family conversations, other tidbits it saved — like what we were watching on TV — would only be valuable if you were exporting a Siri Recap note to Apple’s Journal app, because it was something you wanted to record for personal reasons.
I’d like to see these sorts of extraneous details saved as separate notes — or at least as dedicated sections that could be exported or deleted on their own at the end of the day.
I’d also love to be able to swipe left on an individual bullet point to remove it from the Siri Recap entirely, rather than having to enter edit mode, place the cursor, and then start deleting the text I don’t need.
Another option I’d like to have would be a setting that would allow you to automatically export any saved Siri Recap (the ones you click the bookmark icon to save) to Apple’s Notes app, instead of that being an extra step.
These Recaps could go into their own folder in the Notes app for easy reference. I can understand why this option is not the default, given how many different ways people use a general-purpose app like Notes. However, it would be useful for those of us who want to keep Notes as the central starting point for all our jotted-down reminders and to-dos.
Though I wasn’t immediately warmed up to the idea that my Watch was always listening, so to speak, I see the value of this sort of automated note-taking in daily life.

articles.title: Nvidia Is Telling Cloud Clients to Sell at Least 51% to Non-Chinese Customers - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.summary: Nvidia Is Telling Cloud Clients to Sell at Least 51% to Non-Chinese Customers  24/7 Wall St.
articles.full_text:
Nvidia quietly told its cloud partners to limit how much business they do with Chinese customers, and the unwritten rule is already putting some smaller providers in a difficult position ahead of the company's November earnings report.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
The Financial Times reported that NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction) has been telling its cloud computing clients that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese customers. The paper cited five people with knowledge of the matter.
NVIDIA had never set a limit like this before. The instruction reportedly went out by word of mouth through its sales force and regional teams, with nothing in writing.
The stock rose 2.29% to close at $206.69 on November 3, giving the company a market value of $4.99 trillion. It then fell to $206.20 in after-hours trading by 7:59 p.m. ET. Nothing links that gain to the report. For shareholders, the question is whether a limit NVIDIA set for itself reduces export risk by more than it costs in lost rental demand.
What NVIDIA Reportedly Told Its Cloud Partners
The floor reportedly applies to clouds worldwide, beyond Asia. It covers only future contracts, so existing agreements stay in place.
Reports disagree on what the floor measures: services sold, share of clients, capacity or revenue. Some coverage described it as a 49% cap on Chinese business. No report explains how compliance would be measured or checked, when the floor would start, or which partners would be subject to it.
NVIDIA neither confirmed nor denied the report. Its statement said, “Longstanding U.S. policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can,”. It never mentioned China or a floor.
Why Rented Chips Abroad Are the Target
Many Chinese tech companies rent computing power from clouds outside China to train AI models. Washington has tried to close that path for years.
In March, ByteDance reportedly planned to use about 500 Blackwell systems in Malaysia through Aolani Cloud. Aolani said it fully complies with export rules.
Price drives the demand. A rack of B300 chips reportedly sells for about $600,000 outside China, but in October one brought 18.5 million yuan, or $2.8 million, inside China.
A Singapore-based provider said non-Chinese customers are hard to find outside the U.S. and that strict enforcement would hurt its business.
What NVIDIA’s Filing Already Discloses
NVIDIA’s latest 10-Q (its quarterly report to regulators) shows $7,880 million of revenue from direct customers based in China, including Hong Kong, in the quarter ended July 26, 2026. Total revenue that quarter was $96,221 million. For the first half of fiscal 2027, China-headquartered customers accounted for $12,430 million of the $177,837 million in total revenue. Direct China sales remain a small piece of the business.
Those figures are sorted by where each buyer is headquartered. They don’t capture Chinese companies renting capacity abroad, so they don’t tell you how much revenue this policy puts at risk.
The filing also lists $36 billion of cloud service commitments to select AI cloud partners, usually running six years. It says NVIDIA must “rely on the compliance programs of our customers and partners.”
The House passed the Remote Access Security Act by 369 to 22 on January 12, 2026. The 10-Q says the bill, which Congress is still considering, “could prohibit the provision of cloud services to any company with an ultimate parent headquartered in China.”
What Investors Should Watch Before NVIDIA’s Earnings Report
The report likely matters less to near-term results than the headlines suggest because it affects demand that NVIDIA’s own forecast already excludes. Its fiscal third-quarter guidance of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, excludes any data center compute revenue from China.
The floor protects NVIDIA’s standing with export regulators and keeps its partners’ access to its chips secure. The cost falls on neoclouds (smaller cloud providers built around NVIDIA chips) that rely on Chinese demand. NVIDIA supports some of them through those commitments.
The next check comes with results scheduled for November 17. If revenue lands within the guided range and the cloud commitments hold steady, the floor is costing little, and a cut to those commitments would likely mean partners are under financial pressure.

articles.title: Quantum Computing Continues Very Slow Progress - Bismarck Brief
articles.summary: Quantum Computing Continues Very Slow Progress  Bismarck Brief
articles.full_text: Quantum technology relies on the unique and counterintuitive properties of subatomic physics to store information, perform calculations, or sense phenomena. The interactions of subatomic particles can theoretically allow quantum computers to reach processing speeds orders of magnitude faster than classical computers on certain problems, to make entirely new types of algorithms viable as a result. Perhaps the most notable example here is Shor’s algorithm for finding prime factors of an integer, which promises to break traditional encryption schemes—especially RSA, the most commonly used worldwide—if successfully implemented on a quantum computer. Other possibilities include logistical optimization problems or accurately simulating subatomic particles involved in chemical reactions. Besides computing, militaries and intelligence agencies are interested in the possibility of using quantum phenomena to create new, more secure types of encryption, or gravitational and electromagnetic sensors that far surpass any technology available today, allowing, for example, for subterranean, stealth, or submarine structures and military materiel to be detected at a great distance.

articles.title: NVIDIA Reportedly Wants Cloud Providers to Cap China Sales at 49% in New Contracts - XenoSpectrum
articles.summary: NVIDIA Reportedly Wants Cloud Providers to Cap China Sales at 49% in New Contracts  XenoSpectrum
articles.full_text:
According to a Financial Times (FT) report on November 3, NVIDIA is asking cloud providers to sell at least 51% of the services they offer under future contracts to companies outside China. The report is based on five people familiar with the matter, and NVIDIA has not officially confirmed the policy. In the United States, a bill that would bring remote access to advanced AI chips through overseas data centers under export controls has stalled, so NVIDIA may be trying to limit Chinese companies' access to computing resources through its own sales terms.
How much impact the policy has, however, will depend heavily on how the 51% ratio is calculated. Providers whose business centers on leasing dedicated GPU clusters to a single Chinese company could be forced to rethink their business structure if a cap of 49% on China-bound services is applied. Two large usage contracts disclosed by Japan's Data Section (TSE Growth: 3905) total about $1.297 billion in usage fees over three years alone. The question is how such large contracts would be affected by the new sales terms.
What is NVIDIA's "51% rule"?
On November 3, 2026, the FT reported that NVIDIA is asking cloud providers to sell at least 51% of the services they offer to companies outside China. The requirement reportedly applies to contracts signed from now on, not to existing ones. It is also said to be communicated verbally through NVIDIA sales representatives and regional teams rather than in writing. According to two people familiar with the matter, it covers customers around the world, not only data centers in Asia. The FT says this is the first time NVIDIA has imposed this kind of sales restriction.
NVIDIA neither confirmed nor denied the report in response to AFP, instead stressing the importance of U.S. AI infrastructure remaining competitive in global markets. The company said that if data centers and clouds built on U.S. chips do not win globally, the United States will not win the AI race either. China's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she was not aware of the report and expressed hope that companies from all countries can operate in a fair, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment.
The biggest unknown right now is the scope over which the 51% ratio is calculated. Whether it is judged contract by contract or against a cloud provider's overall revenue or service volume changes which providers would be affected. It is also unclear what the ratio is based on: revenue, contract value, compute usage, or something else. Because no formal written notice has been confirmed, how enforceable the condition is, and what happens in case of violation, is also unknown.
According to NVIDIA's Form 10-Q for the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue from China (including Hong Kong) for the three months ended July 26, 2026 was $7.88 billion, about 8.2% of total revenue of $96.221 billion. However, this regional revenue is classified by the headquarters location of the direct customer and does not necessarily match where the product is ultimately used. For example, if a Chinese company rents GPU compute from a cloud provider outside China, it may not be counted as China revenue in NVIDIA's statistics.
In its earnings, NVIDIA guided to third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $108 billion (plus or minus 2%) and said it does not assume any China data center compute revenue. But that outlook does not show the scale of Chinese companies' use of compute through overseas cloud providers either. In other words, NVIDIA's regional revenue alone cannot reveal how many transactions would fall under the reported 51% rule.
Why remote access from overseas is hard to catch under U.S. export controls
Since November 17, 2023, the United States has in principle required licenses to export advanced computing items to companies headquartered in countries in export-control Country Group D:5, which includes China, or in Macau. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) made clear in its May 31, 2026 guidance that this requirement remains in effect. Even if a covered company is located in a third country, the license requirement applies if its headquarters or ultimate parent is in a D:5 country or Macau.
The BIS guidance also explains that data center operators legitimately doing business under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) need not stop using, storing, disposing of or maintaining existing equipment because of the guidance, until further notice. In other words, the guidance mainly addresses to whom regulated advanced computing items may be exported. It does not explicitly name as a direct target the arrangement in which a non-Chinese company holds GPUs in a third country and a Chinese company rents that compute over a network.
That said, using this structure does not guarantee export controls can be avoided. Legality depends on the parties, the end use, license conditions and other factors. NVIDIA itself explains in its Form 10-Q that the U.S. government has set conditions on export licenses for certain countries and has already restricted the ability of foreign companies to build large GPU clusters and offer them as services. Existing export controls can also affect transactions routed through overseas clouds.
To clarify rules on such remote use, the Remote Access Security Act is under consideration in Congress. H.R.2683 would, under certain conditions, bring within export controls the act of foreign persons accessing items under U.S. jurisdiction from outside their physical location via network connections such as the internet or cloud services. It contemplates cases where the Commerce Secretary determines there could be a serious risk to national security or foreign policy, and it does not impose a blanket ban on all remote access.
The bill passed the U.S. House 369 to 22 on January 12, 2026, but it has remained referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs since the following day. As of November 3, the U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo) record shows no further progress. Until a legal framework directly regulating remote access is in place, a situation has emerged in which NVIDIA is limiting Chinese companies' use through the terms on which it sells to customers.
What matters here is that NVIDIA is not merely selling GPUs but is deeply involved in building out AI cloud providers' infrastructure. In the Form 10-Q, it refers to a new business model with some AI cloud providers, and its maximum exposure on debt guarantees related to land, power and buildings for AI clouds reaches $3.5 billion. NVIDIA, which is involved not only in GPU supply but also in financing data center businesses, is in a position to influence business operations through its transaction terms with customers. If the 51% rule is actually applied, it could narrow the routes by which Chinese companies use overseas compute through such relationships.
How would the 51% rule affect large contracts?
An example of a business that could be affected if the policy is applied is the AI data center business run by Japan's Data Section. On July 10, 2025, the company announced that it had procured GPU servers with 5,000 NVIDIA B200 chips for an AI data center to be opened in Osaka Prefecture, and had indirectly signed a usage contract with one of the world's largest cloud service providers through its business partner NowNow Japan. The contract runs three years, with annual usage fees of $135.342 million and a three-year total of $406.026 million. Converted at the exchange rate at the time (¥144.01 per dollar), the company put the amount at about ¥58.471 billion, and the contract can be extended by two years at the company's discretion. The customer's name has not been disclosed, citing the customer's wishes and confidentiality obligations.
On October 3, 2025, Data Section further announced that it had won the order for its second project, in Sydney, Australia, from the same customer as the first Osaka project through a similar commercial flow. The original plan was to use 10,000 NVIDIA B200 chips, but on December 19 the GPUs were changed to B300 and the contract was re-signed. The revised usage fees are $297 million per year and $891 million over three years, equivalent to about ¥139.115 billion at the exchange rate at the time (¥156.15 per dollar). Separately, the contract provides for a $74 million setup fee for building the customer's dedicated GPU cluster.
Combining the three-year usage fees for the two projects gives $1.297026 billion. The breakdown is $406.026 million for the first project in Osaka and $891 million for the second in Sydney, excluding setup fees and fees for the extension period. The counterparty for both contracts is the same undisclosed single company.
In December 2025, the FT reported that China's Tencent was using Data Section's compute through a third party. However, Data Section has not disclosed the name of its counterparty, and it has not been independently confirmed that the customer in the disclosed contracts is the same as Tencent. It is also unclear whether Data Section itself counts as a "cloud customer" in NVIDIA's terms.
It therefore cannot be said that the 51% rule applies directly to Data Section's business. Still, for the two disclosed contracts alone, the counterparty is a single company, accounting for 100% of the customer mix by contract value. If that customer is a Chinese company and the 51% rule is applied contract by contract, similar new contracts could run afoul of a condition holding China-bound services to 49% or less. If the ratio is calculated across a provider's entire business, deals with other customers would also have to be taken into account.

articles.title: Pouch Cell Cases Market To 2035: EV Battery Demand Drives Growth - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Pouch Cell Cases Market To 2035: EV Battery Demand Drives Growth - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Pouch Cell Cases market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global pouch cell cases market is a critical segment of the advanced battery supply chain, providing flexible, sealed enclosures for lithium-ion and other advanced cells. As of 2026, the market is defined by its essential role in enabling high energy density and design flexibility for battery packs. The market's trajectory is intrinsically linked to the unprecedented global transition to electric mobility and the parallel expansion of stationary energy storage systems. The automotive sector, particularly battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, consumes the largest volume of pouch cells, directly driving case demand.
Concurrently, the imperative for grid stabilization and renewable energy integration is fueling substantial investment in energy storage systems, a major secondary market. This dual-engine growth scenario is creating both immense opportunities and complex challenges related to supply chain resilience, material innovation, and cost optimization. From a supply perspective, the market features a concentrated yet competitive landscape where specialized material science firms and vertically integrated battery component manufacturers vie for share.
Production is geographically aligned with major battery gigafactory clusters, predominantly in Asia-Pacific, with growing capacity in Europe and North America. The forecast period to 2035 will be characterized by intense innovation in barrier properties, thermal management integration, and sustainable material sourcing. Strategic success will hinge on deep partnerships with cell manufacturers, scalability, and the ability to navigate evolving regulatory and trade environments. This report provides a comprehensive, data-driven analysis of the market landscape as of 2026, projecting trends, competitive dynamics, and strategic implications through to 2035.
The baseline scenario for the pouch cell cases market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust expansion, primarily driven by the accelerating adoption of electric vehicles and the build-out of stationary energy storage capacity. The market is expected to register a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 12.5% over the forecast period, with the market index reaching 325 by 2035 (2025=100). This growth is underpinned by the fundamental advantages of pouch cell architecture—lightweight construction, high energy density, and design flexibility—which make it the preferred choice for many automotive OEMs and consumer electronics manufacturers.
The automotive segment is projected to remain the dominant end-use sector, capturing an increasing share of demand as global EV penetration rises. However, the pace of growth will be tempered by supply chain constraints, particularly in the availability of high-quality aluminum foil and specialized polymers, as well as by the capital-intensive nature of scaling production. Geographically, Asia-Pacific will maintain its leadership position, supported by the presence of major battery manufacturers and a mature component supply ecosystem.
Europe and North America are expected to witness faster growth rates, albeit from a smaller base, as new gigafactories come online and regional supply chains are localized. The market outlook is also shaped by ongoing technological advancements, such as the development of thinner, more durable laminate films and integrated thermal management features, which are expected to open new application avenues and enhance product value.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Rapid expansion of global electric vehicle production, particularly battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, which rely heavily on pouch cells for their high energy density and design flexibility.
- Significant investments in stationary energy storage systems for grid stabilization and renewable energy integration, creating a substantial secondary market for pouch cell cases.
- Continuous demand for thinner, lighter, and more compact consumer electronics, driving innovation in pouch case materials and designs.
- Technological advancements in laminate materials and sealing technologies that enhance barrier properties, thermal management, and safety, expanding application scope.
- Government policies and incentives promoting electric mobility and clean energy adoption, particularly in Europe, China, and North America.
- Growth in e-mobility applications such as e-bikes and e-scooters, which require lightweight and cost-effective battery solutions.
Potential Growth Constraints
- Volatility in raw material prices, particularly aluminum and specialized polymers, impacting production costs and profit margins.
- Complex and capital-intensive manufacturing processes for high-quality pouch cases, requiring significant investment in precision stamping and coating technologies.
- Stringent safety and performance standards for battery components, necessitating extensive testing and certification, which can delay product launches.
- Competition from alternative battery form factors, such as cylindrical and prismatic cells, which may limit market share in certain applications.
- Supply chain disruptions and logistical challenges, including trade restrictions and geopolitical tensions, affecting the availability of key materials and components.
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Electric Vehicle (EV) Batteries (estimated share: 45%)
The electric vehicle battery segment is the largest and fastest-growing end-use market for pouch cell cases. Pouch cells are favored by many automotive OEMs for their high energy density, lightweight construction, and flexibility in pack design, which allows for optimized space utilization and improved vehicle range. As global EV production accelerates, particularly in China, Europe, and North America, demand for pouch cell cases is set to surge. Key demand-side indicators include EV sales volumes, battery capacity per vehicle, and the share of pouch cells in total EV battery chemistries.
Through 2035, the segment will be driven by the transition to higher-nickel cathode chemistries and the development of solid-state batteries, which may require advanced pouch designs. The trend toward larger cell formats and integrated battery packs will also influence case specifications, with a focus on thermal management and safety features. Major automotive OEMs and battery manufacturers are investing heavily in pouch cell capacity, ensuring sustained demand for cases. Current trend: Rapid growth driven by global EV adoption.
Major trends: Shift toward higher energy density cells requiring thinner, stronger laminates, Integration of thermal management features into pouch cases, Development of solid-state battery compatible pouch designs, and Increasing cell size for cost reduction and simplified pack assembly.
Representative participants: LG Energy Solution, SK On, CATL, AESC, and Northvolt.
Consumer Electronics Batteries (estimated share: 25%)
Consumer electronics, including smartphones, tablets, laptops, and wearables, represent a mature but consistently growing market for pouch cell cases. The demand is driven by the relentless pursuit of thinner, lighter, and more powerful devices, which require compact and flexible battery solutions. Pouch cells enable manufacturers to design sleek products with longer battery life. Key demand indicators include global shipments of consumer electronic devices, average battery capacity per device, and the adoption of fast-charging technologies. Through 2035, the segment will see gradual growth, with innovation focused on improving energy density and safety.
The rise of wearable devices and IoT applications will create new opportunities for small, custom-shaped pouch cases. However, the market is also subject to product lifecycle fluctuations and intense price competition, which may pressure case manufacturers to optimize costs while maintaining high quality. Current trend: Steady growth with focus on thinness and lightweight.
Major trends: Ultra-thin and flexible battery designs for wearables, Increased adoption of fast-charging, requiring enhanced thermal stability, Custom shapes for space-constrained devices, and Growing demand for high-capacity batteries in premium smartphones.
Representative participants: Samsung SDI, Amperex Technology Limited (ATL), Murata Manufacturing, LG Chem, and Panasonic.
Energy Storage Systems (ESS) (estimated share: 15%)
The energy storage systems segment is a rapidly expanding market for pouch cell cases, driven by the global push for grid stabilization and renewable energy integration. Pouch cells are increasingly used in stationary storage applications due to their scalability, high energy density, and declining costs. Demand is fueled by utility-scale projects, commercial and industrial installations, and residential storage systems. Key demand-side indicators include renewable energy capacity additions, government incentives for storage, and the levelized cost of storage. Through 2035, the segment is expected to grow at a high CAGR, supported by the transition to clean energy and the need for grid flexibility.
Technological trends include the development of long-duration storage solutions and the use of pouch cells in modular, containerized systems. Safety and cycle life are critical factors, driving innovation in case materials and designs. Current trend: Accelerating growth due to renewable integration.
Major trends: Growth in utility-scale battery storage projects, Increasing use of pouch cells in modular ESS containers, Focus on long cycle life and safety, and Development of cost-effective, large-format cells.
Representative participants: Tesla, Fluence, Sungrow, BYD, and Saft.

articles.title: Global satellite race accelerates amid connectivity boom and sovereignty concerns - Consultancy-me.com
articles.summary: Global satellite race accelerates amid connectivity boom and sovereignty concerns  Consultancy-me.com
articles.full_text:
The number of satellites orbiting Earth could increase more than eightfold in the coming years as major technology and space companies, alongside governments, accelerate plans to build large-scale satellite constellations. The expansion is set to reshape the global connectivity market, intensify competition for spectrum and raise important questions around national sovereignty.
That are the central messages in a new whitepaper from Detecon, a leading consultancy in the ICT and telecoms market. The report examines the emerging competitive landscape and the regulatory challenges facing governments as satellite technology becomes an increasingly important part of digital infrastructure.
The scale of the anticipated expansion is big. According to Detecon’s analysis, more than 11,907 satellites have already been launched for low Earth orbit (LEO) and medium Earth orbit (MEO) internet, Direct-to-Device (D2D) and Internet of Things services.
If all planned satellites were deployed, this number would rise to more than 97,000.
The competitive landscape remains heavily concentrated. Starlink, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, has approximately 10,000 satellites in orbit and accounts for 84% of all launched LEO and MEO satellites.
However, a growing group of competitors is preparing to challenge its position. Amazon Leo has plans for 3,236 broadband satellites and 5,105 D2D satellites, while Blue Origin’s recently announced TeraWave constellation comprises 5,804 planned satellites.
China is also positioning itself as a major competitor. Its planned programmes include Qianfan (Thousand Sails), with 15,000 announced satellites, Guowang with 12,992 planned, and Honghu-3 with 10,000. Other initiatives include Logos Space in the US and the European Union’s IRIS programme.
The geographical distribution of this expansion is particularly revealing. Detecon’s projection estimates that the satellite population could grow from 13,141 to over 103,000 in a few years, an eightfold increase.
While the US currently accounts for 89% of the satellites in the analysis, its projected share will fall to 65%, or close to 67,000 satellites. China’s share is expected to rise from 4% today to 26%, positioning it as a significant challenger to US dominance. The EU’s projected share is anticipated to drop slightly.
Sovereignty becomes a strategic consideration
Beyond commercial competition, the expansion raises questions about who ultimately controls critical communications infrastructure in space. Detecon’s authors argue that satellite sovereignty has no universally accepted definition and should be assessed across three dimensions: military use, government funding and secure government communications, and potential deployment in military conflict zones.
The EU’s IRIS programme illustrates the strategic importance of sovereign infrastructure. Designed for civilian, government and potential military applications, the planned constellation will comprise 18 MEO, 264 LEO and 10 Very-LEO satellites.
Yet building independent infrastructure is financially and technically challenging. Many countries cannot afford their own constellations and will need to rely on foreign providers. This creates a delicate balance between expanding connectivity and maintaining control over critical national infrastructure.
Market access and regulation will shape the next phase
Detecon expects the competitive landscape to increasingly reflect geopolitical divisions. Western markets may favour providers from allied countries, partly due to national security and privacy concerns, while China is likely to serve its domestic market and support Chinese commercial interests abroad.
Other countries will largely determine access through their national regulatory frameworks, with established Western operators likely to gain an early advantage in shaping market conditions.
For regulators, the challenge is to ensure that foreign satellite providers compete on fair terms with domestic telecommunications operators. This includes reconsidering licensing requirements, spectrum allocation, interference management and spectrum fees. Satellite operators should not gain an unfair advantage by avoiding obligations imposed on terrestrial mobile providers.
The report identifies four areas requiring regulatory attention over the next 12–24 months: satellite spectrum access, proportionate spectrum fees, domestic market access and licensing frameworks. It also highlights the importance of developing clear rules for D2D services, which could either complement existing mobile networks or become direct competitors.
Key takeaways
Ultimately, the next phase of the satellite race will be determined not only by technological innovation and the number of satellites launched, but also by the regulatory and geopolitical conditions governing their use. Governments that establish clear, investment-friendly frameworks while protecting national interests will be better positioned to benefit from the expanding space-based connectivity market.

articles.title: The Starlink Slowdown and an Adapting Ukraine - Defense Security Monitor
articles.summary: The Starlink Slowdown and an Adapting Ukraine  Defense Security Monitor
articles.full_text:
Starlink and its use in the current war in Ukraine have been receiving a lot of press lately. The slowdown of Starlink across the country drastically reduced the fighting power currently available to Ukraine. This has therefore had an effect on the defense capabilities that Ukraine has at its disposal. It does seem, however, that Starlink has now returned to stable speeds.
What is the issue?
Starlink brings internet to all corners of the globe. Even in places where terrestrial internet has been dominant, there has still been a rise in Starlink users. For Ukraine, Starlink is a lifeline connecting many destroyed areas to the internet. It is used on the front lines for communications, and even the Russians have used it.
Traditional communications are one aspect, but Starlink has been used to control interceptor drones that have been destroying jet-powered Shahed loitering munitions. Starlink was not available in Ukraine at speeds going over 100mph, which drastically limited the effectiveness of these weapons.
Ukraine has been striking everything from airbases to oil refineries; however, Starlink is not used to control these drones, as Starlink does not work over Russia. If Ukraine cannot use Starlink to guide its drones for deep strikes, there are other options available. Airborne relays through mothership drones can extend the range of drones without using space-based communications. Terrain matching can also be used by uploading satellite maps to drones, which they in turn follow. AI can also be used to navigate, identify and engage targets. Wild Hornets, a company in Ukraine, is actively trying to mitigate the need for Starlink through various means.
Poland pays for commercial Starlink for Ukraine; however, this apparently does not include the use of Starshield satellites, which is the military-grade version of the constellation. Starlink has no peer in terms of sheer number of satellites in LEO (Low Earth Orbit). To give perspective, about 8,000 objects had been launched to orbit since Sputnik and before Starlink. Starlink alone has launched about 13,000 satellites. The constellation is therefore unmatched in terms of numbers, and with that comes massive data capacity and exceptionally low latency that users can tap into worldwide.
The slowing down of Starlink had a definitive effect on counter-drone operations in Ukraine. With that being said, Ukraine has been on the cutting edge of warfare technology since the start of the war. If Starlink is now an unstable communications platform for Ukraine, then the country will adapt as it always has, but that will take time.
Carter Palmer has long held a keen interest in military matters and aviation. As an analyst for Industrial & Marine Turbine Forecast, Carter specializes in examining key gas turbine programs for electrical power generation, mechanical drive, and marine propulsion applications. He is also responsible for updating the reports and analyses within the Space Systems Forecast – Launch Vehicles & Manned Platforms and Space Systems Forecast – Satellites & Spacecraft products.

articles.title: Intel 14A moves closer to production as PDK 0.9 becomes available — plans to release PDK 1.0 in the first quarter of 2027 - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Intel 14A moves closer to production as PDK 0.9 becomes available — plans to release PDK 1.0 in the first quarter of 2027  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
Intel Foundry last week made available its Intel 14A process design kit (PDK) version 0.9, an important milestone in the development of this next-generation manufacturing technology. The company says that the production node is reaching performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, and the results are backed by silicon validation. Intel plans to release PDK 1.0 in the first quarter of 2027, which will validate the technology's readiness for high-volume manufacturing (HVM).
14A PDK v0.9 is here
A process design kit contains transistor models, design rules, and other information that enables chip designers to develop products for a particular manufacturing process using electronic design automation (EDA) tools. The accuracy and quality of the PDK are crucial for modelling how chips will perform once manufactured, and the release of PDK 0.9 is particularly important because it provides customers with a representation of Intel 14A based on actual silicon measurements rather than on theoretical models or simulations. At this stage, customers can proceed with product development with greater confidence that the technology will meet their requirements when it comes to performance and power consumption.
Intel says that PDK 0.9 lets customers develop designs intended to enter risk production around the time the process is certified, which — provided that PDK accurately reflects the characteristics of manufactured silicon — in many cases enables chip developers to greatly reduce the number of silicon revisions between initial tapeout and mass production. Of course, availability of PDK 0.9 does not indicate that Intel 14A is ready or even close to mass production, as the company expects to validate HVM readiness only with PDK 1.0, sometime in Q1 2027. Again, this does not mean that 14A will enter mass production in early 2027, as Intel itself expects to begin mass production using its 14A process technology in 2028, following risk production for its own products in the second half of 2027.
"From a customer perspective, the PDK 0.9 gives customers the confidence to design products on Intel 14A, as the technology is reaching the industry-standard performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, supported by silicon-backed validation," said Ben Sell, corporate vice president and general manager of front-end technology development at Intel Foundry.
Building on top of 18A
Intel 14A builds on top of architectural foundations introduced with Intel 18A but incorporates several substantial enhancements. These include 2nd Generation RibbonFET 2 gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, PowerDirect backside power delivery (which delivers power right to the transistor source/drain regions without using intermediate connections like TSVs used by PowerVia), and Turbo Cells (high-performance standard cells designed to accelerate timing-critical paths in CPUs and GPUs), which provide chip designers with additional ways to increase performance and optimize power efficiency. Since Intel has previously outlined advantages of these technologies, the latest announcement does not provide updates regarding transistor performance, power consumption, or transistor density figures for Intel 14A.
Beyond improvements to transistor, power delivery, and interconnect technologies, Intel is applying manufacturing experience gained during 12 months of Intel 18A production to accelerate maturation of 14A. Specifically, the company says it has increased investments in inline defect detection, modeling, and simulation to identify potential manufacturing problems earlier in the development cycle. These initiatives are intended to improve manufacturing yields, process variability, ultimately transistor performance, and reduce production cycle times. Intel also says it has introduced several strategic initiatives to accelerate technology development, although it does not quantify their impact.
New collaboration model
Another important change concerns Intel's relationships with equipment and materials suppliers. The company says it has revised its collaboration model to involve technology development teams and external suppliers earlier in the process development cycle. The goal of such close collaborations is to address manufacturing defects and improve equipment capabilities before they become obstacles for yield improvements after the technology enters mass production. Intel also conducts regular yield summit meetings with suppliers to accelerate progress on critical development objectives.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
"This has required evolving our collaboration model with equipment and material suppliers, and earlier engagement from our [technology development] leaders with suppliers to drive improvements in defects and equipment capabilities," Sell said.
A bonus of such early collaboration is that equipment and materials suppliers may incorporate Intel's requirements into their standard products and development roadmaps. This could give Intel an advantage over competitors, which would have to either adapt their manufacturing processes to equipment optimized around Intel's requirements or work with suppliers to develop alternative solutions from scratch.
Historically, Intel frequently set the direction for semiconductor manufacturing technologies as other chipmakers subsequently adopted similar approaches. One notable exception was immersion DUV lithography, which Intel adopted after TSMC, which led the development of immersion DUV lithography. By engaging equipment and materials suppliers earlier, Intel could regain some of its historical influence over the development of industry-standard manufacturing solutions, though the importance of this should not be overestimated.
Expanding design ecosystem
Meanwhile, Intel continues to expand the design ecosystem for its 14A technology. Cadence and Intel have established a design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) collaboration focused on next-generation AI-driven design tools and intellectual property, whereas Keysight, Siemens, and Synopsys have announced design-tool certifications for the process. Intel is also working with other software developers and IP providers to validate design flows and reusable building blocks required by prospective foundry customers.
Intel says it is encouraged by customer feedback regarding the progress of 14A development. However, the company has not identified any customers that have committed to manufacturing products using the technology, disclosed customer tape-outs, or announced specific manufacturing agreements, which is normal for the foundry industry. For Intel Foundry, attracting external customers remains particularly important because development costs of modern leading-edge process technologies can only be recoupled when they are used to make hundreds of millions of chips, way more than Intel sells these days. Meanwhile, the commercial success of Intel Foundry with advanced manufacturing technologies depends not only on transistor performance and manufacturing yields, but also on its ability to deliver predictable development schedules.
Looking ahead, Intel intends to continue improving performance, yields, variability, and manufacturing cycle times of 14A, though for now the company does not disclose any actual goals. Intel also plans additional process enhancements and performance refinements for 14A-E and 14A-P nodes after the initial technology becomes available. However, exact schedules for these nodes are not known at the moment.
"Our next major milestone is the Intel 14A PDK 1.0, expected in the first quarter of 2027," said Ali Farhang, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel Foundry's design technology platform organization. "I am looking forward to sustaining this level of quality across future releases and continuing to earn our customers' trust by delivering on our commitments with a customer-first mindset."
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Dismal Run Might Be Coming to an End. Grab NVDA Stock While It’s Still Around $200. - Barchart.com
articles.summary: Nvidia’s Dismal Run Might Be Coming to an End. Grab NVDA Stock While It’s Still Around $200.  Barchart.com
articles.full_text:
The artificial intelligence (AI) trade has whipsawed this year, and so has its flagbearer Nvidia (NVDA). The chip-designing giant hit its record highs last month and has since lost 15% from those levels. As of last week’s closing prices, the stock’s year-to-date returns trail both the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index ($IUXX) and the diversified S&P 500 Index ($SPX).
Nvidia’s performance would seem at odds with its financial results, though. For instance, its revenues more than doubled in the most recent reported quarter, and its guidance for fiscal Q3 implies they will nearly double again. For the next fiscal year, Nvidia guided a 70% revenue growth, which is astonishing considering the high base. Moreover, at a time when companies are hard-pressed even to guide for the next quarter, Nvidia went out of its way to provide a forecast for the next fiscal year.
Following Nvidia’s fiscal Q2 earnings release in August, I noted that despite the strong growth and reasonable valuations, Nvidia wasn’t a “buy.” With NVDA coming off those levels, let’s explore the stock's outlook.
Why Has NVDA Stock Been Falling?
The recent weakness in NVDA could be attributed to the weakness in the AI trade. Incidentally, all the Magnificent 7 names, which happen to be Nvidia’s biggest customer set, plunged following their September quarter earnings, in part due to growing anxiety over their AI capex. Since much of this capex lands in Nvidia’s coffers, the stock too fell alongside. To make things worse, Intel’s (INTC) tepid Q4 guidance led to a sell-off in other chip stocks, which also put pressure on NVDA.
On a broader level, there are concerns over the sustainability of Nvidia’s growth since customers like Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL) and Amazon (AMZN) are working on their own chips. They are not only using them internally but also aggressively scouting third-party customers. Selling chips to third parties would help hyperscalers justify their burgeoning AI capex and offset some of their cash burn.
Then there are fears over “circular financing” and off-balance-sheet financing. So, we have Nvidia investing in companies that buy its chips, while cloud companies like Amazon, Microsoft (MSFT), and Alphabet — the three biggest players in that order — are investing in AI startups that have developed into their biggest cloud customers, driving much of the incremental growth. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is dismissive of the very term circular financing and, during the Q2 call, said that he regrets not investing in these companies early, terming it an “once-in-a-generation opportunity,” at least a section of the market is getting apprehensive over such transactions.
Off-balance-sheet financing is another concern, and Nvidia has been providing credit guarantees for its customers’ data centers. There are reports that Nvidia is in talks to provide credit guarantees to Nscale for a data center that Anthropic would use. Such deals add a layer of risk for Nvidia investors and would be catastrophic if AI actually turns out to be a bubble and goes bust. That, however, is not my base case assumption, and while there are visible signs of exuberance in AI, the technology holds a lot of promise.
How to Play NVDA Stock?
I believe the sell-off in NVDA stock has gone a bit too far and see the recent pullback as a buying opportunity, particularly as the company heads into its Q3 earnings call. While Nvidia’s recent quarterly earnings have been followed by a decline in its stock price despite the company delivering a “beat and raise” quarter, the setup looks nice to me ahead of the Q3 report.
At around the $200 price level, Nvidia is offering an attractive entry point with a price-to-earnings multiple of around 23x. While Nvidia has had a dismal run this year, I believe the stock should make up for it in the final two months of the year, and I see it ending the year higher than these levels.
On the date of publication, Mohit Oberoi had a position in: AMZN, GOOG, NVDA. All information and data in this article is solely for informational purposes. For more information please view the Barchart Disclosure Policy here.

articles.title: Sodium-ion batteries overcome lifespan vs charging conundrum with graphene armour - Chemistry World
articles.summary: Sodium-ion batteries overcome lifespan vs charging conundrum with graphene armour  Chemistry World
articles.full_text:
Chemists have developed a graphene-armoured anode designed to overcome sodium-ion batteries’ trade-off between charging speed and lifespan.
Interest in sodium-ion batteries has grown in recent years as researchers seek more sustainable alternatives to lithium-ion technology. Sodium is approximately 1000 times more abundant than lithium, potentially easing supply-chain constraints and reducing battery costs, although overall environmental impact depends on other components in the battery, supply chains and manufacturing. Sodium-ion batteries also offer several advantages, including high power output, rapid charging and reliable operation at low temperatures. However, sodium-ion batteries currently still exhibit lower power density and energy density than their lithium-ion counterparts.
Researchers in China have now addressed this trade-off by using ultrathin nanosheets of titanium dioxide wrapped in a graphene-based protective shell to create a battery anode. This offers a potential route to high-power sodium-ion batteries, with the key advance being not a new battery ingredient but a structural design that combines fast charging and long life under more demanding electrode conditions.
This architecture, says Wei Li at Fudan University, China, does several jobs at once. The nanosheets allow sodium ions to move in and out easily, helping the electrode charge and discharge quickly, while the graphene coating improves electrical conductivity and helps protect the anode’s structure. ‘Our design combines fast energy storage with long cycle life, even when considerably more active material is packed onto the electrode,’ he adds.
In tests, the electrode retained more than 90% of its capacity after 3000 cycles at a relatively high active-material loading. ‘Practical charging speed also depends on the cathode electrode and electrolyte,’ says Li. ‘Both must keep pace with our electrode and remain stable during repeated fast charging.’
The anode was made using established processing steps: forming the particles, coating them with carbon and heat-treating the material. ‘However, familiarity does not establish industrial scalability,’ says Li. ‘Maintaining the same thin sheets and uniform graphene wrapping across large batches remains unproven. We would need to demonstrate consistent quality, yield and performance using larger equipment, while assessing energy use and processing costs.’
Tengfei Song, a research fellow at the University of Birmingham, UK, who was not involved in the study, agrees. ‘This is a strong piece of fundamental research,’ he says. ‘The authors show that careful nanoscale and interfacial design can give a titanium dioxide anode unusually fast sodium-ion storage kinetics and very long cycle life, even at relatively high mass loading. However, I would see it mainly as a high-power materials concept rather than a commercially ready anode material.’
Although the material’s large surface area helps it store sodium quickly, it could make manufacturing more difficult and costly at scale, Song adds.
‘The main next step would be testing under more realistic full-cell conditions,’ says Song. This would mean testing the material in larger batteries, using practical amounts of active material and without the need for extra sodium to compensate for early losses. A test cell to emulate a normal battery environment would help establish whether the anode’s fast charging and long cycle life translate into useful energy storage in a practical battery, he concludes.

articles.title: Epileptic seizures nearly vanish after people receive experimental gene therapy in their brains
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03566-2A clinical trial in three people tested a combination of gene-laden viruses and a drug.
articles.full_text:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
and JavaScript.
Three people with epilepsy resistant to drug treatment saw the number of seizures they had per month fall by more than 90%, after gene-laden viruses were infused directly into their brains as part of an early-stage clinical trial1.
In each participant, the gene therapy was precisely targeted to a small patch of brain tissue that was the source of their seizures. The viruses carried a gene that makes neurons sensitive to a specific drug, which works like a dimmer switch for the therapy. By combining gene therapy with a drug — an approach known as chemogenetics — researchers can adjust a treatment’s potency, which is not possible with other types of gene therapy. The trial participants did not experience serious side effects.
The results were reported today in The New England Journal of Medicine byYang Dai, a neurosurgeon at Xuanwu Hospital of Capital Medical University in Beijing, and his colleagues. “It’s exciting that there’s such a dramatic effect, and that they see very few side effects,” says Matthew Walker, a neurologist at University College London who was not associated with the study.
But he cautions that the study is small. He is also concerned about the long-term use of the drug that participants took after receiving the gene therapy. High doses of the drug, an anti-psychotic called clozapine, have been associated with cardiovascular problems and other negative effects. “In the future, hopefully there are going to be better drugs” for this form of treatment, says Walker, who is the co-founder of the start-up company Focalis Bio in Canterbury, UK, which is also developing gene therapies for epilepsy.
Direct to the brain
The three trial participants were adults with a common form of epilepsy caused by hippocampal sclerosis, a type of scarring in a region of the brain called the hippocampus. The participants had this scarring on only one side of the hippocampus. All three had been diagnosed with epilepsy 10–25 years earlier and had developed resistance to at least two anti-seizure drugs. They also had at least two seizure episodes per month, on average, over the three months before they enrolled in the trial.
The experimental treatment uses a virus called adeno-associated virus 9 to deliver a gene to neurons in the affected area. The gene was engineered to produce proteins specifically in excitatory cells — the ones that are involved in seizures.
The gene instructs neurons to produce a receptor that binds to clozapine. Clozapine acts like a switch and activates these receptors, reducing the activity of the targeted neurons, the authors say. That reduced activity helps to suppress the abnormal electrical activity that triggers seizures.

articles.title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
articles.summary: Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.
One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects.
In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.Read full article
