articles.title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
articles.summary: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent,…
articles.full_text:
Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.



Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.



Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself. 



Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether. 



The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.



That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana. 



The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.



Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.





A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere. 



It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red. 



This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices. 



Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat 



In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge served hungry students steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. The students loved them: 92% of those who tried them wanted them on the menu. Few could guess that mushrooms had been mixed into the meat.



Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the biggest challenges of the climate crisis: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef.



Joyn is among a wave of startups creating “blended meat,” which combines plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat.



Get a taste of the startups betting on greener beef.



—Meghan McCarron







This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration



More than 5 million people have an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) called geographic atrophy, in which retinal cells die off. Until now, no treatment could restore their vision. A system called PRIMA changes that.



It combines a retinal implant with camera-equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients could read, do crosswords, and use their phones.



Find out how the sight-restoring implant works.



—Linda Marsa



MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here



In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.



At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.



This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.



This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 Democrats have dealt tech billionaires a major midterm setbackThe results could bring tougher scrutiny of AI and data centres. (CNBC)+ Musk poured millions into Texas, but both his candidates lost. articles.title: AMD's record quarter: Data center business doubles, while gaming craters
articles.summary: AMD's gaming revenue fell 40 percent in an otherwise record $13.4 billion quarter.
articles.full_text:
AMD reported third-quarter revenues on Tuesday with a record $13.4 billion, an increase of 45 percent year over year, as data center business nearly doubled and the company's gaming segment cratered.
AMD CFO Jean Hu said, "We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The middle point of our guidance represents approximately 66% year-over-year revenue growth, primarily driven by the acceleration of our Data Center segment." AMD says its Q4 revenue projections are up another 27 percent from this quarter's results. As reported by Tom's Hardware, Intel's Q4 guidance places revenue estimates between $15 billion and $16 billion. That means that if both companies land where they expect to at the end of the fourth quarter, AMD would exceed Intel's revenue for the first time in history.
The data center segment of AMD's business was up 97 percent year over year, with a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributes the growth to demand for its EPYC line of enterprise server CPUs, along with the launch of the Instinct MI450 series GPUs. Sales of AMD Ryzen mobile chips led growth in the Client business, which includes desktop Ryzen processors and posted $2.95 billion in revenue, up 7 percent year over year.Read full article

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone strikes spur hasty Russian plans for underground data centers
articles.summary: Russia tries to fix exposed digital infrastructure as data center war backfires.
articles.full_text:
Russian tech companies are scrambling to harden and hide their data centers underground after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged facilities housing AI supercomputers and disrupted cloud services for millions of Russian users. Meanwhile, the Kremlin is requiring data center owners to reserve computing capacity for emergency state needs and has even authorized possible use of foreign data centers.
These consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine come as the Russian military has bombarded Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles nearly night and day in recent months, along with specifically targeting Ukrainian data centers since late September. But Ukraine has retaliated with its own drone strikes on military and infrastructure targets across Russia, degrading or knocking out data centers operated by Russian tech giant Yandex, the state-owned bank Sberbank, social media site VKontakte, and the Russian Ministry of Finance.
Now, state-owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has raised the possibility of moving some Russian data centers underground in talks with the nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti. The industry publication Data Center Dynamics also pointed to a recent proposal by a Russian regional governor to build data centers within open-pit coal mines while planting green public parks above as camouflage.Read full article

articles.title: AI on the Ballot
articles.summary: Data Centers were on the ballot, and they lost in a major way; what does it mean if American opposition to building is permanent?
articles.full_text:
Listen to this post:















Log in to listen











From Bloomberg this morning at 2 a.m. Central:




Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in a midterm election landslide that amounted to a rejection of President Donald Trump following widespread voter discontent with the economy and the war in Iran. Across the country, Democrats scored victories in GOP strongholds, flipping at least seven Senate seats and winning House races in districts Republicans easily carried in 2024. Several news organizations projected that Democrats would win the House, while Decision Desk HQ projected they took the Senate.




I have no doubt that Iran and the economy played significant roles in this election; what stood out to me, however, was very much Stratechery fodder. Specifically, I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite.



Meanwhile in Texas, from Yahoo Finance:




A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state’s first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies. The state is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers…Hinojosa, Texas’ first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030.




Republican incumbent Greg Abbott, I would note, already declared a moratorium on new data-center permits in September; that’s how much of a hot-button issue this is, including in the state that is the biggest opportunity and beneficiary of the data center buildout. So yeah, this is a Stratechery topic of concern.



The Data Center Veto



Earlier this year, while writing about data center opposition, I said:




There really wasn’t widespread opposition to data centers when they were being built for the Internet generally; indeed, local governments would compete for them, eager for the economic benefits that came during their construction and the long-term tax benefits once they were operational. In other words, it seems pretty clear that the current wave of opposition can’t be divorced from AI — you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race.



I do not, I don’t think, need to explain to you why this is not a very compelling message, and, in the very long run, I do think that humans will have economic value. At the same time, it’s hard to explain the huge amount of investment that is going into AI, not just at the model level but also in terms of data centers, without admitting that a big part of the thesis is that AI can not just increase the top line for companies, but also increase the bottom line — i.e. replace the jobs of some number of humans. Again, I’m generally an optimist here, but this already happened with the first wave of IT.



That leads to an interesting contrast to globalization: when companies were closing down American factories and laying off workers and moving operations to China, none of the affected towns or workers had a say. They just suddenly no longer had a job, and a huge number of cities across the Rust Belt no longer had a reason to exist. People simply had to move, or worse, retreat to things like alcohol or drugs. AI, however, is the opposite: building data centers requires permission, which is to say that people actually have a say. Again, I am not at all saying that these people are well informed about data centers, or about the economic impact on their communities, much less the economic impact of AI generally; what I am noting is that people who didn’t have a say in globalization are suddenly finding they do have a say about AI, and it’s not a surprise they are expressing their disapproval by blocking data centers.




That message was loud and clear last spring; now it is deafening, and it’s tempting to say that tech, particularly the frontier labs, have no one to blame but themselves. In fact, however, some of the biggest culprits may, in the long run, be some of the biggest beneficiaries of the anti-data center wave.



My thesis — driven not just by national results and the Texas governorship, but also the fact that, as this thread documents, nearly every relevant local ballot measure opposing data centers won or is winning (the only exception so far was in North Dakota) — is that the constraint on AI dispersion has shifted once again. First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified. The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all. Not only is it harder to solve, but it actually interferes with solving the other constraints. Many of the theories about AI assume that it becomes a commodity; I think it’s just as likely we are looking at scarcity for much longer than we expected, which will have ripple effects on everything.



Ten Takes



To that end, here — with the caveat that nothing leads to hot takes you regret like an election — are ten perspectives on what a permanently impaired ability to build might mean. To be clear, I’m not declaring permanency — look at how our elections swing back and forth — but it’s worth considering what the implications might be if Americans don’t change their minds about data centers.



1. The AI Trade Got It Right



The most obvious reason why the stock market has been rocky over the last few weeks is the tightening of credit markets, which I wrote about this summer. We are, needless to say, full on into the equity funding era (and while I’m here, I haven’t written about Anthropic’s updated S-1, but it strongly affirms my initial analysis). At the same time, it seems clear that this outcome is very bad for the AI trade in the short term, but much of the pain may have already been endured.



2. Neoclouds on the Edge



The Neoclouds have been at the forefront of credit concerns, and from a certain perspective, being unable to build data centers has a silver lining in that they couldn’t get the money to pay for them anyways. Moreover, Neoclouds with facilities that are already permitted now have an asset that is going to be scarcer than expected. At the same time, it’s Neoclouds that need new sites and new permits, even as they are likely to have much less political sway than the hyperscalers — who already have more sites they can repurpose or rebuild. It was already getting harder to get capital, relative to the hyperscalers; now you have to layer on that it’s going to be harder to get permission, too.



3. Hyperscalers Are Winners



The downside for the neoclouds is upside for the hyperscalers, who are more likely to grow their share of AI compute than they were before. Moreover, investors may be pleased if the hyperscalers’ ambitions are somewhat curtailed; political opposition is an excuse to moderate spending, knowing that everyone else is in the same boat.



4. Nvidia’s Mixed Bag



Nvidia will almost certainly be a short-term loser. Fewer data centers mean fewer Nvidia chips generally, and a weakened Neocloud set is particularly harmful not only because Neoclouds almost exclusively use Nvidia full-rack systems, but also because Nvidia is back-stopping a huge number of them. It’s the hyperscalers, meanwhile, who are Nvidia’s biggest long-term threat, given their scale and ability to invest in their own chips.



At the same time, a constrained world makes Nvidia’s offerings more compelling. CEO Jensen Huang actually spent an entire keynote making this point back in 2025; I wrote in an Update:




When Huang says “iso power” he means that power is the constraint; the question is how many tokens can you generate given a fixed power envelope, and Blackwell can generate a lot more. These were the numbers Huang gave for a 100 MW data center:







What this means is that the first order of business for an ASIC maker is to match that level of efficiency. That, though, means keeping up with Nvidia’s product development cadence; The Information has a post about Amazon offering instances using its latest Trainium ASIC at a significant discount to the H100. Huang, though, spent this keynote insulting the H100! You can almost hear him speaking to Amazon directly: you spent all this money, and are offering these huge discounts, just to entice developers to lock themselves into an inferior chip, even as reasoning models are going to swamp your available power generation…



Huang is issuing a challenge to every cloud provider tempted to make an ASIC: do you really think that you can keep up with this, and risk running out of power capacity because your chips aren’t efficient enough? Don’t even try.




A world without power or data center constraints is one where it is, in the very long run, very difficult to maintain Nvidia’s margins; once those constraints start to bite, however, an advantage in tokens/megawatt is worth a lot of money. Go back to my point about the hyperscalers: one way to generate more tokens is to build a new data center; another way is to rebuild a data center with new Nvidia chips.



5. Advantage China



China is the inverse of the scenario that Huang laid out: the country has plenty of power and the ability to build a lot more, but they don’t have leading-edge chips. Some of the advantages of leading-edge chips

articles.title: Hard X-ray attosecond metrology
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11245-5Metrology techniques are developed to characterize and control attosecond hard X-ray pulses, directly measuring a 170-attosecond duration and enabling ultrafast studies of electronic dynamics in quantum systems.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Sub-ångström spatial resolution combined with attosecond temporal resolution enables direct observation of electron motion in matter1. Attosecond hard X-ray pulses generated at X-ray free-electron laser sources provide the requisite spatiotemporal sensitivity, yet their application has been limited by the absence of precise pulse metrology and control. Here, building on a broadband X-ray split-delay line, we establish metrology of attosecond hard X-ray pulses. Field-correlation measurements provide the first time-domain characterization of the pulse coherence time and demonstrate attosecond synchronization between the generated pulse pairs. By exploiting non-sequential two-photon absorption as a nonlinear probe, intensity autocorrelation quantifies the average pulse duration directly in the time domain to be 170 as. The demonstrated experimental tools and techniques enable systematic attosecond time-resolved experiments, including X-ray pump–X-ray probe spectroscopy and diffraction, and open a pathway to probing electronic phenomena with unprecedented spatial-temporal resolution.

articles.title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11224-wLongitudinal tracking of endothelial cells shows they can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 and form new functional vessels, challenging conventional views of the essential role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and providing insight into resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival1.
Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells2,3.
The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic.
However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported4,5.
Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe–HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development.
These Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs.
Vegfr2KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs.
However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis.
Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss.
These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3.
VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs.
Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth.
Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs.
This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis.

Similar content being viewed by others
Main
VEGF is frequently targeted in clinical settings to suppress tumour angiogenesis, metastasis and retina disease6. However, resistance to VEGF-blocking antibodies arises over time, which limits the effectiveness of such treatments4,5,7,8. By contrast, resistance to loss of VEGF signalling has not been reported during physiological vascular development.
Embryos or postnatal tissues lacking activity of the VEGF signalling pathway in all cells fail to develop vessels3. VEGFR2 (encoded by the Kdr (also known as Vegfr2) gene in mice) is the most important VEGF receptor and has been shown to be essential for angiogenesis in all vascular development contexts studied so far1,9. Germline mutants for this gene completely lack blood vessels and die very early during embryonic development2, and mouse embryos chimeras formed by wild-type and Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) progenitor cells cannot form endothelial cells (ECs)10. Conditional deletion of Vegfr2 with Tie2–Cre after endothelial differentiation11, or in postnatal tissues with Cdh5–CreERT2, also strongly impairs angiogenesis12, without any evidence of genetic compensation or resistance.
Despite a large body of literature showing that VEGFR2 is essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, migration and survival, previous studies involving deletion of Vegfr2 in all ECs (Vegfr2iDEC) during embryonic or postnatal organ development could only analyse its effect on angiogenesis for a relatively short period of time. Its essential role in vascular development and hence in tissue development and organ function causes severe impairment of angiogenesis and premature lethality of Vegfr2iDEC embryos and postnatal animals; thus, such studies have been unable to determine whether ECs can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 over time or make certain organ vascular beds in the complete absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling.
Here we used iFlpMosaics13 and iSuRe–HadCre14 to mosaically induce and longitudinally track Vegfr2KO ECs, enabling us to assess the role of this gene during the entire embryonic and postnatal vascular development of different organs. We found that despite its essential role during the initial wave of embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is dispensable for many subsequent angiogenic processes originating from veins. Vegfr2KO ECs expand and out-compete wild-type ECs in venous vessels, which serve as a continuous source of these mutant cells for angiogenesis in most organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) showed that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time through upregulation of ligands for other VEGF receptors and through increased expression of venous-specific genes, particularly Nr2f2. Targeting these adaptive and resistance-associated molecular mechanisms prevents expansion of ECs following prolonged loss of VEGFR2 signalling.
Vegfr2 KO ECs can form new vessels
Given the essential role of VEGFR2 in early angiogenesis and embryonic development, we induced mosaic loss of VEGFR2 with iFlpMosaics13 to investigate whether mutant cells could adapt and form new vessels over time.
This technology enables FlpO-dependent ratiometric induction and tracking over long periods of time of cells expressing MTomato-2A-Cre (knockout for any floxed gene) or MYFP (wild type).
To induce these mosaics, we used the Apln-FlpO allele, which is expressed in the first angiogenic and sprouting ECs at embryonic day 8.
5 (E8.
5) and throughout vascular development.
In female embryos, the X-chromosome-located Apln–FlpO allele is mosaically silenced15 and expressed only in a fraction (23–50%) of ECs, generating relatively few mutant and wild-type cells, which we found to be compatible with embryonic development (Fig.
1a and Extended Data Fig.
1a).
Analysis of major organs of Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic mice showed that ECs with full loss of VEGFR2 (Vegfr2KO-E8.
5–P7) were able to survive and proliferate during embryonic development and until postnatal day 7 (P7), with only a relatively minor competitive disadvantage (2–7-fold) compared with wild-type cells (Fig.
1b).
This competitive disadvantage was more pronounced in the lung and kidney endothelium and less so in brain ECs (Fig.
1b,c and Extended Data Fig.
1a–c).
As Apln-FlpO is constitutively active and can drive recombination at later stages of embryonic development, we also induced Vegfr2 deletion using 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at E10.
5 and E12.
5 in embryos carrying Cdh5-CreERT2, iSuRe-HadCre and an iMb2-Mosaic16 control reporter that recombines independently of Vegfr2 deletion (Extended Data Fig.
2a–c).
This resulted in a maximum of 1–6% recombined ECs, as opposed to 23–50% with Apln-FlpO.
However, this recapitulated the trend in which brain ECs were least affected by VEGFR2 loss, followed by those in the heart, liver, lung and kidney (Extended Data Fig.
2b,c).

Vegfr2 KO ECs can form arteries
VEGFR2 activity is essential for NOTCH activation and the development of arteries17,18,19. Arteries are formed by tip ECs20, which have the highest level of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling and guide vascular growth. Our high-resolution spatial zonation data with long-term iFlpMosaics showed that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were significantly enriched in veins and surrounding capillaries, and avoided angiogenic front capillaries or tip ECs, but were able to form arteries (Fig. 1d; see also Extended Data Fig. 3a for the heatmapping method).
To complement these results, we intercrossed the Vegfr2 floxed allele with Cdh5-CreERT2 and iSuRe-HadCre14 alleles to ensure fast (24 h; Extended Data Fig. 3b,c) and effective mosaic genetic deletion and full loss of VEGFR2 protein and downstream targets in ECs (Cdh5 expressing), after a single injection of 4-OHT. Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs were located mainly in veins and surrounding capillaries, as well as in the more proximal and mature segments of retina arteries (Fig. 1e). This indicates that when Vegfr2KO ECs are induced in the initial retina sprouting plexus at P1, they can make arteries forming from P1 to P3. However, owing to their inability to continue to sprout and form tip cells at the leading edge, they cannot participate in the subsequent arterial development process occurring from P3 to P7, which in the retina is dependent on incorporation of new tip cells21.
Notably, compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1−P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front capillaries (Fig. 1f,g) and were still able to make arteries. This suggests that embryonic Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs can adapt to long-term loss of VEGFR2 and contribute to venous vascular growth, tip cells and arteries at postnatal stages.
Vegfr2 KO ECs expand in veins
We next investigated how Vegfr2KO ECs could compete with wild-type cells and contribute to growing vascular networks over long periods of time, given the proposed important role of this pathway in EC proliferation1,22. During angiogenesis, there are two main locations for EC proliferation: the capillary angiogenic front and veins (Fig. 2a). We found that the surviving Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs proliferated (as determined by Ki-67 detection) as well as wild-type cells in postnatal brain, heart and lung vessels (Fig. 2b).
Venous ECs provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis and these migrate against the blood flow to capillaries and then towards arterial vessels20,23,24. When we induced Vegfr2KO ECs for longer periods of time, from P1 to P20 (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20), we observed that mutant cells stayed in the vein stem, where they proliferated and gradually outcompeted wild-type cells, which moved outwards towards the VEGF-rich leading edge and adjacent capillaries (Fig. 2c). This preferential occupation of the venous stem niche by Vegfr2KO ECs allowed them to continue proliferating for longer periods

articles.title: [不同来源] Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
articles.summary: And what that could mean for physical Switch game costs.
articles.full_text:
For years, the AI industry's insatiable demand for memory and storage has had plenty of knock-on effects on the price and availability of PC components like RAM, SSDs, and GPUs. Now those shortages are also squeezing the supply of ROM chips that power physical Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges.
Chip manufacturer Macronix announced in its third-quarter earnings report that the company's production of ROM chips "has reached its end" and that it will begin "gradually decoupling from the game industry," as reported by Taiwanese news site BigGo Finance. That could be an issue for Nintendo, which analyst David Gibson notes uses Macronix as its "main memory chip maker" for physical game cartridges.
That ROM production—which has shrunk 39 percent in the last year and now represents just 5 percent of Macronix's business—is being crowded out by production of more lucrative, in-demand chips like NOR- and NAND-based memory and eMMCs, the company said. With Macronix's production capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month—and $1.2 billion in planned new capacity taking a year or more to spin up—less profitable ROM chips are taking up wafer space that can earn more through other types of chips.Read full article

articles.title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
articles.summary: Researchers say group may have been Kremlin-sponsored in search of diplomatic targets.
articles.full_text:
Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday.
The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.
Wielding DarkSword
One of the impersonated sites was america250.org, belonging to a non-partisan group of lawmakers, business executives, and at least one former member of the Trump administration. The attackers registered america250[.]holiday and used it as a reverse proxy to america250.org. The imposter website delivered content from the real one that added malicious JavaScript into it.Read full article

articles.title: Uranium cubes reveal why the German nuclear project failed
articles.summary: "Our calculations suggest Heisenberg significantly underestimated the materials required."
articles.full_text:
During World War II, physicists on the Manhattan Project worried that the Nazi German nuclear program might achieve the first nuclear bomb before the US and its allies. That's not what transpired, but historians have debated just how close the Germans came to achieving criticality in their last attempt at building a reactor: the B8 pile. Werner Heisenberg, who led that effort, claimed that they were close and had only needed a little more uranium. But according to  a paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus, that was not the case: the project simply didn't have sufficient uranium and heavy water to build a working bomb, given the design they were using.
This particular research started in 2013, when University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth—a co-author on the new paper—received the gift of a mysterious heavy metal cube from a friend. He instantly recognized it as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists in their unsuccessful attempt to build a working nuclear reactor. Only 14 such cubes are known to exist today.
In 2019, we reported on Koeth’s quest to track down the cube’s origins, as well as several other similar cubes that had somehow found their way across the Atlantic. At the time, Koeth and his partner in the quest, then-graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert, had tracked down ten such cubes around the US. For instance, the Smithsonian Institute had a German uranium cube in storage. They tracked a third cube to Harvard University, where it was regularly passed around to students in introductory physics classes as a curiosity.Read full article

articles.title: Toothbrush that emits electricity may more effectively prevent gum disease
articles.summary: A toothbrush with bristles that produce electricity as they bend has shown promise for reducing plaque and gum inflammation
articles.full_text:
A new and improved toothbrush could help avoid trips to the dentistWestend61/Alamy



A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes. When put to the test, it led to more than twice the reduction of plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding as conventional toothbrushes.



“The concept is great,” says Nicholas Jakubovics at Newcastle University, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.”



	
		
			Read more
			How regrowing your own teeth could replace dentures and implants
		
	



Oral diseases, such as tooth decay, affect nearly half the global population. Brushing regularly can help remove plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria that forms on teeth. These bacteria can produce acids that cause cavities and irritate gums, sometimes leading to tooth loss.

	
		
							
					Advertisement				
						
				
			
		
	





But even thorough brushing can leave behind bacteria deep in plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to grow back within hours. Researchers have previously developed toothbrushes with antibacterial metal nanoparticles, including silver and zinc, embedded in their bristles, although their long-term effectiveness is uncertain. Others have designed ionic toothbrushes that use electric currents to help loosen plaque, but they are dependent on batteries.



Now, Yanhui Lu at Peking University in China and her colleagues have turned to studies showing that so-called piezoelectric materials fight bacteria in infected wounds and medical implants. These generate electric charges under pressure, prompting Lu’s team to develop toothbrush bristles made from piezoelectric plastic.




	
		Free newsletter
		
			Sign up to Health Check		
		
					
		
			
				Sign up to newsletter
				
					
				
			
		
	
	
		
		
			
							
		
	




The idea was that, as the bristles bend during brushing, they would generate electricity, triggering chemical reactions that produce molecules called reactive-oxygen species that damage bacteria, while the bristles physically remove plaque.



The researchers made two sets of bristles of different thicknesses, both of which met Chinese national standards for softness and strength. Laboratory tests confirmed the bristles generated electricity under pressure, particularly the thicker ones. The team also detected reactive-oxygen species on the brushes, which remained soft and retained their electrical properties after three months of use.



Next, the researchers exposed two common oral bacteria to their bristles and nylon ones, which are used in standard toothbrushes, in laboratory experiments, including simulated brushing movements. The thicker piezoelectric bristles were particularly effective, killing about 53 per cent of Streptococcus mutans, which causes cavities, and 78 per cent of Porphyromonas gingivalis, which contributes to gum disease, compared with just 9 and 8 per cent, respectively, for nylon bristles.



The team also grew plaque from human mouths on pieces of cow enamel and brushed them for 3 minutes. The new toothbrushes removed more than 99 per cent of the plaque, compared with about 80 per cent for conventional nylon brushes.









Finally, the team tested the toothbrushes in 109 adults with dental plaque and gum inflammation, who were randomly assigned to use either a piezoelectric or nylon toothbrush twice daily for three months. Dental examinations revealed reductions of roughly 40 per cent in plaque build-up, gum inflammation and bleeding among those using the piezoelectric brushes, compared with around 15 per cent for those using conventional brushes.



Genetic sequencing of the dental plaque from the piezoelectric group also revealed a decline in the relative abundance of harmful bacteria and an increase in some potentially beneficial bacteria.



Larger studies now need to establish whether the toothbrush actually prevents issues like cavities and tooth loss, says Jakubovics.



	Journal Reference:
	
		Science Advances
				DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg5744

articles.title: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
articles.summary: It won't win the specs race, but it will actually fit in your hand.
articles.full_text:
The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today's world of gargantuan glass slabs. Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one? Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics.
The company's cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it's probably "enough" for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button.



Specs at a glance: Enough Phone ($399 for a limited time, $599 MSRP)




SoC
MediaTek Dimensity 7500


Memory
8GB


Storage
128GB with microSD


Display
5.3-inch 1520x720 HD+ LCD


Cameras
Sony IMX766 50 MP, 32 MP selfie


Software
Android 17 or OdysseyOS


Battery
3500 mAh (removable)


Connectivity
5G, LTE, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth, NFC, SIM+eSIM


Measurements
133×64×12 mm



With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it's a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. articles.title: A dyslexia diagnosis can help struggling children, but what about the rest?
articles.summary: Children who struggle to read and are diagnosed with dyslexia can get additional help, but those who can't afford a test or don't meet the criteria get left behind. Surely there is a better way?
articles.full_text:
Shutterstock/Jakub Krechowicz



In years gone by, children who struggled to learn to read and spell were labelled “stupid”, “lazy” or “dim”. Today, of course, we are much more enlightened – now we label many of these children as “dyslexic”. But perhaps this label is still a bad idea.



Picture two 9-year-olds reading at the level of an average 6-year-old. One gets a diagnosis of dyslexia. This positively affects her wellbeing. Her teachers now understand she has dyslexia and that she can get tailored help.



The other child isn’t so lucky. Maybe his parents can’t afford a dyslexia test – in the UK, assessment isn’t available on the NHS and can cost several hundred pounds. In the US it could set parents back thousands of dollars. Or perhaps he was tested but the result was negative. Until very recently, this outcome was common for already disadvantaged children, because the official definition of dyslexia included the idea of “discrepancy” – that reading problems should be unexpected given a child’s other cognitive abilities. Assessing ability using IQ tests can also be biased against those from lower socioeconomic groups or learning to read in a second language. By extension, this second child is just bad at reading or lazy, or both, and not eligible to receive extra help with reading.

	
		
							
					Advertisement				
						
				
			
		
	






Two children with the same learning difficulty. One gets help, the other does not




Two children with the same learning difficulty. One gets help and understanding and the other doesn’t, all because of a label. Yet this label is based on a questionable assessment. Despite trials using a wide range of cognitive processes, researchers have been unable to find meaningful ways to identify dyslexia.



So, why not just help all children who struggle to read? Each has a unique combination of risk and remediation factors, but all will benefit most if we intervene when the problem first shows up, instead of waiting years for them to fail and then receive a diagnosis. Our newfound understanding of what is happening in their brains even suggests some surprisingly simple ways to help. Giving every child the best possible chance to overcome their challenge is what matters, not the label we attach to them.

articles.title: The DNA is backwards on The Selfish Gene’s cover – again
articles.summary: Feedback notes with weary inevitability that a 50th anniversary edition of Richard Dawkins's classic work features a double-helix twisting the wrong way – not for the first time
articles.full_text:
Josie Ford



Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more



Don’t get it twisted



Feedback is not young. We have been here on the back pages for many years, endlessly pushing a boulder up a hill and trying to take joy in the effort. This means, every so often, we are forced to repeat ourselves – because the world repeats itself.



With a due sense of ennui, we turn our world-weary eyes to the cover of the new 50th anniversary edition of Richard Dawkins’s popular science classic The Selfish Gene. The title, written in all-caps, takes up most of the cover. The “I” in “SELFISH” has been replaced by a colourful little drawing of a DNA double helix.

	
		
							
					Advertisement				
						
				
			
		
	





Alas, something is awry. Geneticist Simon Fisher pointed it out on Bluesky: “You know a gene is selfish when its DNA twists the wrong way, as demonstrated by the left-handed double-helix proudly adorning the 50th Anniversary Edition of the multimillion copy bestseller on this topic.”



Yes, once again we have an example of a DNA molecule being drawn, essentially, backwards. In reality, it is a right-handed double helix, but the one on the book cover is left-handed. It’s twisting the wrong way.



Feedback’s mind’s eye immediately cast itself back to March 2025, when we covered a Lego model that included many scientific and technological objects, including a sadly left-handed DNA.



It turns out that The Selfish Gene‘s art has been wrong for at least a decade. Patrick Goymer, an editor at PLOS One, shared the cover of the 40th anniversary edition on Bluesky, and it has the same left-handed DNA in place of the “I”. Feedback notes that our own copy is the 30th anniversary edition, and the DNA is correct. At some point since 2006, the DNA on the cover has flipped into a mirror universe.



This little mistake would be doubly embarrassing if, say, the Nobel prize in chemistry had recently been awarded for research into these sorts of mirror molecules. Can you imagine?



Coca-Cola faecaloma



Sometimes a scientific paper has a title so vivid, so immediate, that Feedback just has to write about it. Such is the case with a paper published in Cureus, titled: “Massive fecaloma dissolved by Coca-Cola: A case report”. It was sent to us by Australia reporter Alice Klein, who either has a truly terrible browser history or makes extensive use of a VPN.



A faecaloma, for those not yet blessed with the knowledge, is a large lump of impacted faeces trapped in a person’s rectum. In this case report, the faecaloma had a maximum diameter of 12.2 centimetres.



Readers anxious to see a dramatisation of such a condition are advised to try series two, episode five of The Pitt, in which one of the patients has impacted faeces that the doctors must manually dislodge. Based on our own personal experience, we do not recommend watching this sequence over dinner.



Back in the real world, the doctors reported that they tried “conservative management”, which apparently consisted of “polyethylene glycol, senna, mineral oil, and sodium phosphate enemas”. But the faecaloma didn’t budge, so they turned to a more drastic solution.



The authors tell us that “isolated case reports have described the use of Coca-Cola enemas for fecaloma dissolution with favorable outcomes”. This is because “Classic Coca-Cola acts as a mucolytic agent [it makes mucus less thick and sticky], a source of carbonic acid, and an effervescent solvent”. Hence the doctors administered two 1-litre Coca-Cola enemas, which shrank the faecaloma enough to resolve the situation.



Feedback has a number of thoughts, such as: would Pepsi work as well? What if the doctors had first inserted Mentos? We are also not sure we ever want to put Coca-Cola into our mouth ever again: if it can be used to destroy a faecaloma, we dread to think what it might be doing to our teeth.



@2, Brute?



Some weeks ago, Feedback began investigating unfortunate technology-induced truncations and abbreviations. These truncations have gone on for a long time and there is no end in sight.



Stuart Arnold was bemused to find Facebook recommending a post about an obsolete form of aircraft called a Rotodyne, which never made it past the prototype phase. It is best described as “a plane, but stick a set of helicopter rotors on top”. Unfortunately, due to the character limit in the Facebook feed, the post was cut off as follows: “designed to take off vertically, then fly faster and fart…” “It’s probably a good thing that the program was cancelled,” says Stuart.



Secondly, David Smith encountered a related problem: tech-induced rudeness. Because his name is a common one, he has long struggled to find unique identifiers for email addresses and such. Imagine his surprise when he joined a large organisation and found he was only the second person there with that name. This seemed like (minor) good news, but he swiftly discovered a downside to being the second David Smith. “The part of the email address corresponding to ‘2@’ has to be pronounced very carefully,” he says.



And finally, Andy Howe reminds us that Trinity Hall, one of the Cambridge colleges, “is colloquially abbreviated as Tit”. He tells us: “This was particularly unfortunate for an archaeology student who saw his name listed in a society’s membership records, followed by the descriptor ‘Arch Tit’.”



Got a story for Feedback?



You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist.com. Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website.

articles.title: Why don’t dogs look up when a low-flying plane passes overhead? Part 6
articles.summary: This question was posed as part of New Scientist’s Last Word series, in which readers give scientific answers to each other’s questions. Here’s what our readers had to say
articles.full_text:
Liz Hughes
Bath, UK
Referencing David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel’s work on the development of the visual cortex in animals, I believe the answer lies in the dog’s upbringing.
Advertisement
Hubel and Wiesel worked extensively on kittens, finding that if certain visual cues were removed from a kitten’s environment in the period when the animal’s brain was wiring its visual pathways, it wouldn’t be able to see those things once they had completed their development. In experiments, kittens brought up in a box containing only horizontal striped lines couldn’t see chair legs or other vertical objects in a normal environment.
So, if a dog wasn’t brought up in an environment that included objects at different heights, then its brain would potentially never be able to recognise that there is an aircraft overhead. And with the cacophony of other motorised and industrial sounds in our world, it is likely that the aeroplane would blend into the background.
Peter Seligman
Melbourne, Australia
We had a kitten that leapt up at a jumbo jet. It missed! And I have seen a cat catch a bird in mid flight. It began its leap in anticipation of the bird’s position.

articles.title: Why do people look better in a mirror than in a photograph? Part 3
articles.summary: This question was posed as part of New Scientist’s Last Word series, in which readers give scientific answers to each other’s questions. Here’s what our readers had to say
articles.full_text:
Why do people appear younger and better-looking in a mirror than in a photograph? (continued)
Kevin Wooding
Via Facebook
Faces aren’t symmetrical and you become accustomed to the unique proportions of your mirrored impression over many years. A photograph shows your face without mirroring, and it can be unfamiliar and surprising with the two sides of your face swapped.
Advertisement
Of course, you could always spend a lot of time looking at photographs of yourself to get used to the non-reflected image of your face. Have fun with this.
Burcu Akten
Via Facebook
I know the answer in my own case. I have a better relationship with myself than I do with others. I’m worried about how others see me, but I’m not worried about how I see myself. So, when my photo is taken, I tense up and look uncomfortable and distressed under the gaze of others. In the mirror, I am kind to myself. So, I see a confident and happy person in the mirror, not a scared one.
Kittens brought up in a box containing only horizontal striped lines couldn’t see vertical objects in a normal environment
Lisa Munroe-Shields
Via Facebook
I look OK in the mirror. But I look like the love child of Hagrid and Worzel Gummidge in photographs! And the self-service cameras in supermarkets make me want to introduce a self-imposed ban on going in those particular shops!

articles.title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
articles.summary: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.  …
articles.full_text:
I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.  



While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level. 





Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans.Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.



What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second



Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.



So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.



There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.



The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.





With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations.



Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout. 



Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4. 



And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.



We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us. 



This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

articles.title: What I learned driving the Slate electric truck prototype
articles.summary: After 45 minutes behind the wheel, I am more optimistic about the $25,000 EV.
articles.full_text:
If my 45-minute drive yesterday morning is anything to go by, I think Slate Auto will have quite the hit on its hands. The startup had one of its prototype trucks in town and asked if I wanted to check it out—no jumping on a plane or having to spend yet another night in an interchangeable hotel room, just a drive from southwest DC to Rockville, Maryland. Easy-peasy.
The prototype truck had been well-used, with almost 6,000 miles (9,656 km) showing on the small and minimalist but very legible digital display that also shows your speed and, if you engage reverse, the backup camera. And while the cabin layout was representative of the production version, the surfaces most certainly weren’t—the prototype instead uses a lot of hard and shiny black plastic, with strips of Velcro here and there left over from when the interior had to be camouflaged when the vehicle was out in public.
Getting acquainted with the Slate was refreshingly easy. The Morris Marina-like door handles open with a pleasing mechanical action. The seat and steering column adjust manually but with plenty of reach, something many budget models used to leave out to save on cost.Read full article

articles.title: The DEA banned a drug some opioid users called a miracle
articles.summary: Researchers say the Schedule I ban could kill studies of a promising opioid treatment.
articles.full_text:
In 2012, as the driver of deaths in the opioid crisis began moving from prescription pills to heroin, Laura Bohn was tasked with finding safer drugs to manage pain.
Funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse, in 2017 she and other scientists revealed in the science journal Cell that several compounds—including a particularly promising one called SR-17018—could relieve pain in mice without causing respiratory depression. That’s a big deal, because respiratory depression is typically what causes people using opioids to stop breathing and die.
Bohn, senior associate vice president of research at University of South Florida Health, says her team filed a patent on SR-17018. They went on to discover that mice using the chemical did not develop a high tolerance for it and that mice already dependent on morphine—a powerful opioid—could consume SR-17018 to reset their tolerance without suffering from painful withdrawal symptoms.Read full article

articles.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
articles.summary: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s…
articles.full_text:
A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.








DOWNLOAD THE REPORT




This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.







Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

articles.title: California fights "preposterous" Trump admin demand to scrap state broadband laws
articles.summary: State tries to obtain broadband funds despite rejecting Trump admin condition.
articles.full_text:
California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration's demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations.
California's stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds.
The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects.Read full article

articles.title: NYT demands Brave shut down its paywall blocker and end deals with AI firms
articles.summary: Lawsuit calls Brave "supplier, dealer, and distributor" of stolen news content.
articles.full_text:
The New York Times and other newspaper companies sued Brave Software yesterday, alleging that the browser maker illegally bypasses paywalls and sells stolen news content to AI companies.
"Brave is the supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content for its own users and many of the most prominent GenAI companies, including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere," the NYT alleged in a lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Southern District of New York. Citing third-party revenue estimates, the suit claimed that "Brave has made more than $100 million by copying and reselling publishers’ work without consent or permission," while "publishers have received nothing."
The lawsuit said, "AI companies pay Brave to provide them with real-time online content from the Brave search index," and use content from the Brave index "to train their own AI models" and "to respond to specific user queries." The NYT lawsuit points to Brave's website, which says the Brave Search API is "used by some of the biggest names in AI, including Cohere, Mistral, Perplexity, and You.com."Read full article

articles.title: Buttons are back and storage is king when it comes to car interiors
articles.summary: We talk with Nissan designer Hiren Patel about how vehicle interior designs are changing.
articles.full_text:
As with interior design for houses, interior design for vehicles is also subject to fashion trends. And like any fashion trend, even the best ideas can become stale and played out with overuse. Some ideas weren’t the best, either, like demonstrably worse human-machine interfaces that add to driver distraction; yet, they still proliferated throughout the industry and across the cars offered for sale. But the good news is that the pushback seems to be working.
“When the trend of the Piano Black and the switchless interior was happening, it was during a time when designers and companies and engineers and everybody were thinking that, 'Hey, we can just get rid of all these switches on the interior. We can put it all in the software. It'll save money. It'll save us tooling up all these extra parts for unique cars and all this stuff and make the interior more like a software experience.' And it was done with those intentions,” said Hiren Patel, senior design manager at Nissan.
That resulted in cars with minimalist interiors that looked good in the dealership. But people drive their cars on roads; they don’t just sit inside them, parked inside a dealership. “So lots of people were complaining about it and saying, 'Hey, it takes my eyes off the road to change the temperature or to adjust my seat or do whatever.' It's not as easy as doing something on your phone where it's just right at your fingertips and intuitive,” Patel said.Read full article

articles.title: Google will let schools skip AI tools, but they have to give up search, too
articles.summary: Google will offer schools AI tools that purportedly don't give away the answers.
articles.full_text:
While Google is trying to move beyond Chromebooks, the ubiquity of these devices has made the company's education products huge in schools. Now, Google says it will let educators choose whether to allow its AI tools in the classroom. However, blocking AI tools also means giving up search, leaving schools with a difficult decision.
Google's new overarching approach to AI in K-12 classrooms sounds good on the surface. After consulting educators, researchers, and lawmakers, Google has decided that schools using its education products will be opted out of AI tools by default. It will be up to administrators to manually enable them when these changes roll out in the coming months.
When you look at what Google considers to be an AI tool, the nature of the Faustian bargain becomes clear. The affected products are Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search. There's no picking and choosing—you either allow all the AI or none of it.Read full article

articles.title: Another child dies of measles as CDC reportedly holds up health alert
articles.summary: NY governor pointed to Kennedy's long-standing anti-vaccine work as spurring outbreaks.
articles.full_text:
A child in New York has died of measles, health officials in the state announced late Monday. It marks the first reported measles-associated death in New York in more than 30 years. It is the seventh measles-linked death reported in the US this year; all six of the other deaths were reported in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing a dramatic measles outbreak that has stricken over 1,430 people this year. Prior to the deaths, Pennsylvania hadn't seen a measles-related death in 35 years.
The boom in vaccine-preventable outbreaks, cases,  and tragic deaths is being fueled by slipping vaccination rates nationwide as health misinformation and anti-vaccine sentiments have taken hold. One of the most prominent anti-vaccine activists in the US currently serves as the US health secretary; Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spent decades prior to taking office attacking vaccines and spreading misinformation. He and his anti-vaccine organization, Children's Health Defense, have been one of the most prolific sources of anti-vaccine content.
Since taking office, Kennedy has waged a multi-front war on vaccines that has included dismantling and obstructing federal vaccine recommendations; launching dubious studies to look for alleged, unspecified harms of vaccines; promoting alleged vaccine injuries; and continuing to spread misinformation about vaccines and vaccine-preventable illnesses.Read full article

articles.title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
articles.summary: Google has cut ties with the company behind the botnet campaign.
articles.full_text:
Google's Threat Intelligence Group says it has shut down a massive botnet called x.cpe. At its height, x.cpe ran on more than 1.3 million Android TV devices, and unusually, these were Google-certified boxes. Google says its screening process missed the malware due to "obfuscation techniques" employed by Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology.
In a detailed blog post, the Threat Intelligence Group explains how the x.cpe botnet evolved quickly from a single-stage dropper into a modular three-stage malware platform that sold access to third parties. Manufacturers must have their devices certified if they want access to Google apps and branding, a process that is supposed to catch threats like this. However, Videostrong's compromised boxes, mostly sold under the MECOOL brand, evaded detection by using a backdoor to remotely install the malware after the devices were set up and online.
After devices appeared online, a stub application called x.cpe or com.oemservice would phone home. This package did not have any malicious capabilities of its own, but it had the system-level permissions necessary to install malware modules at the operator's behest. It also disabled Play Protect, which would have otherwise flagged the silently installed packages as malicious.Read full article
