Why are we conscious? Nature investigates the theories
Scientists have yet to reveal how the human brain produces the subjective experience we perceive as consciousness, but research has pushed the field in exciting directions.
At first glance, human consciousness seems like the one thing we should never have to doubt. We know we are conscious because we experience the world in vivid detail: the small luxury of a piece of chocolate; a song imbued with sadness; or a childhood memory that takes us back to another place and time.
But for such a fundamental aspect of reality, what underlies consciousness — the experience of being aware of one’s own existence — has proved deceptively hard to pin down. Researchers and philosophers have spent centuries debating how and why physical processes in the brain result in the subjective, first-person experiences we all seem to have. This issue, known as the ‘hard problem’ of consciousness, continues to drive research today.
Scientists are still far from explaining how brain activity begets an entire inner world, but the field is making progress. The advances that researchers have made include the ability to reliably measure brain activity and connectedness and probe for signs of hidden awareness.
The emerging picture — based on insights from not just neuroscience, but also far-flung disciplines such as plant science, artificial intelligence and astrobiology — is not of consciousness as a single light that can be switched on, but as a coordinated condition that is potentially more widespread than previously thought. The rapid rise of AI, for example, has fuelled discussions over whether only humans can be conscious — and of whether a brain is even required for consciousness.
“People are often troubled by the fact that our understanding remains somewhat vague,” says Matthias Michel, a philosopher of cognitive science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. “However, it’s very important to note that definitions in the history of science come at the end of the scientific process, not at the beginning. I’d argue we’re now in the thick of it, which is an exciting place to be.”
The seed of consciousness
There is no direct test for evaluating human consciousness, but researchers have made advances in establishing what are known as neural correlates of consciousness (NCCs). These criteria, which can be a single metric or a combination of events, identify the minimum neuronal mechanism required to kickstart a conscious experience. Specific neurons might need to fire, for example, and particular brain activity patterns could signify an internal experience. Below these thresholds, a person might move through life not fully conscious of their behaviour — zoning out while driving, for instance, only to snap back to attention moments later.
Some NCCs have been determined by studying people in states we don’t typically associate with consciousness, such as those who are asleep, anaesthetized or in a coma. According to Melanie Boly, a neurologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, this type of research is crucial to help separate true NCCs from activities that merely signify being awake and responsive to our surroundings.
“That’s been a big breakthrough, isolating the true features of consciousness, rather than simply measuring something that is associated with or a consequence of the conscious experience,” Boly says.
Through that work, scientists know that about one-quarter of individuals who present as medically unconscious are, in fact, experiencing a type of covert consciousness in which they continue to perceive the world around them. In a landmark 2024 study, a subset of 241 people who had been left seemingly unresponsive by brain injuries were asked to imagine themselves engaging in activities such as playing tennis or opening and closing their hand. Dozens of patients’ brains became active on imaging scans during these challenges — calling into question whether consciousness persists in otherwise-inert states1.
In recognition of this finding, researchers have moved away from thinking of consciousness as a binary experience towards an understanding that consciousness is a dynamic process that exists on a continuum. From these principles, it has been possible to develop metrics that test the underlying scientific assumptions about consciousness. One of the most promising of these is called the perturbational complexity index (PCI)2.
PCI evaluates a person’s level of consciousness by assessing how their brain responds to a brief magnetic pulse, as measured by electroencephalography (EEG), which traces the brain’s electrical activity using electrodes. In a conscious brain, the neural response usually spreads while remaining complex and distinct from one brain region to another — features referred to as integration and differentiation, respectively. During sleep or under anaesthesia, the response becomes simpler and more repetitive.
“PCI is considered to be a very accurate correlate of consciousness that can be useful in many research settings,” says Johan Frederik Storm, a neurophysiologist at the University of Oslo. Widespread clinical adoption has unfortunately been hampered by the fact that it’s a laborious metric to gather, he adds, “but even still, it is gaining traction”.
Stress-testing theories
This growing understanding has led to the development of hypotheses that move beyond simply measuring aspects of consciousness towards a more foundational understanding of what it is. At present, there are more than 450 such theories, many of which share overlapping features even as they distinguish themselves by scale or focus. The two most popular are the global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT) and the integrated information theory (IIT).
The GNWT posits that most brain activity is restricted to specialized areas — visual regions process shapes and colours, for example, and language areas process words. Consciousness emerges when information becomes important enough to be broadcast across regions. A face whose representation remains inside the visual system might trigger a simple, unconscious reaction, but a face that triggers regions across the brain, collectively known as the global workspace, can be used by many systems to build a conscious experience.
The IIT tries to answer a different question: what is experience like? When we view the world or recall a memory, we experience a cohesive scene, not separate elements of colour, sound and touch. The IIT argues that consciousness depends on how strongly the parts of a system affect one another while still remaining distinct — there must be both integration and differentiation to give rise to diverse states and experiences. A conscious system must be more than a collection of independent parts, and it must form a whole that has a state that cannot be fully explained by looking at each part separately.
A major issue with proving such hypotheses is that researchers have often tested them in ways that lack true neutrality and rigour. A 2022 analysis of hundreds of experiments found that research into consciousness has often been done in ways that pre-emptively bias the results in support of a particular theory3. This has made it a challenge to directly compare studies of consciousness, according to Christof Koch, a consciousness researcher at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who has studied the topic for decades.
“People become very attached to their theories, and that confirmation bias can sometimes get in the way of an honest, collaborative effort,” he says.
Lucia Melloni, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Ruhr University Bochum in Germany, recently led a first-of-its-kind effort to force a direct comparison of the two schools of thought. She brought together proponents of both theories, as well as neutral participants, and asked them to agree in advance to a set of experiments and predictions. The group probed foundational assumptions of both theories4 using three measurement techniques — EEG; functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which tracks brain activity by detecting tiny changes in blood flow; and magnetoencephalography (MEG), which measures magnetic fields produced by the brain’s electrical currents.
One of the main differences between the two ideas is which part of the brain is considered most essential to the act of being. The GNWT predicts a sudden ‘ignition’ of widespread brain activity when a stimulus prompts a conscious experience, and so the prefrontal cortex is expected to play an important part because it uses information to form complex behaviours. ITT focuses instead on a ‘hot zone’ located towards the back of the brain that includes parts of the systems responsible for vision, hearing and touch, because it follows that this is where the relevant stimuli converge to generate a full experience.
The team found conscious information represented in both regions. However, the results also challenged important predictions of both theories. The long-lasting activity predicted by the IIT to occur in the back of the cortex was not clearly represented, and the ignition expected by the GNWT was limited. As such, the study did not settle the debate, instead suggesting that both theories might offer parts of an answer.
Melloni doesn’t see this as a failure, and considers such results the most exciting outcome. “I’m happy with what we found because neither theory was left untouched,” she says. “Having your predictions confirmed doesn’t leave you anywhere to grow, whereas having your thinking challenged makes you do better science.”

articles.title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8A two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven network material is constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into a triangular weave pattern, enabling an extra topological dimension to be used for the construction of functional materials.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Inspired by macroscopic weaving techniques1,2,3,4, molecular weaving, which interlaces molecular strands into ordered networks, has emerged as a powerful strategy for designing functional materials with emergent properties5,6. However, so far, molecular weaving has relied mainly on linear building blocks and biaxial structures. Higher-order weaving (≥3 axes) of nonlinear building blocks is expected to produce intriguing architectures and bring new and unforeseen functions to the resulting materials; however, their construction and property investigation remain underexplored. Here we report a two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven polymer network constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into the woven structure through dative B–N polymerization. The resulting material not only exhibits unique topological chirality and robust mechanical properties but it also serves as a porous material that permits the separation of representative aromatic/aliphatic compounds. This functional utility highlights how higher-order triaxial woven topologies can provide unique advantages in terms of regulating material properties and introduces an extra topological dimension for the construction of functional materials.

articles.title: Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11133-yRecent progress in photovoltaics has been investigated to translate state-of-the-art cells in the laboratory into deployable products suited to real indoor conditions, focusing on wide-bandgap absorbers, reduced non-radiative voltage losses and reshaping module design.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
The growing reliance on distributed electronics, such as Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, smart-home devices and portable consumer products, has intensified demand for indoor energy-harvesting technologies that reduce battery replacement and servicing.
Consequently, indoor photovoltaics (PVs) have advanced rapidly; however, translating state-of-the-art cells into deployable products requires design principles that reflect real indoor conditions.
Here recent progress in perovskite (bulk and quantum dot), organic, amorphous-silicon, III–V and dye-sensitized PVs is examined to identify bottlenecks that arise under low-light conditions and during scale-up.
This Review highlights how low-light operation favours wide-bandgap absorbers and reduced non-radiative voltage losses while reshaping module design: lower series-resistance (RS) penalties permit wider subcells and fewer interconnections, increasing geometric fill factor, whereas shunt and leakage pathways consume more of the weak photocurrent.
Measurement practices for credible cross-technology benchmarking are discussed, emphasizing the transparent reporting of spectra, illuminance/irradiance, stabilization and uncertainty.
Finally, the relationship between device performance and manufacturability and product integration is considered, including power-management requirements and chemical/regulatory constraints (for example, restricted substances and end-of-life handling).
These guidelines provide a practical framework for evaluating indoor PVs on the basis of delivered and retained power and for accelerating the transition from laboratory-scale demonstrations to reliable, visually adaptable products for the built environment.

articles.title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10956-zUsing high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double knockout screening, synergistic gene combinations to improve CAR-T cell therapy are revealed.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1,2,3,4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5,6,7,8,9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1–SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer.

articles.title: Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11225-9A programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator is used to explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits, revealing prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1,2,3,4.
Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics—which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5,6,7,8—is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10.
Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits.
By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes.
We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints.
We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances.
In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius–Clapeyron test.
Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.

articles.title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11209-9In Drosophila erecta, food odours initiate male sexual arousal, which is subsequently reinforced by the visual motion of other courting flies, creating a multisensory mechanism that synchronizes courtship in groups when conditions are favourable for reproduction.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners.
Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities1,2,3,4,5,6.
Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch.
We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group.
The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals.
D.
erecta’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster, where food odour can promote arousal7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship.
Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D.
erecta.
Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

Main
Social cues are essential for coordinating interactions between individuals, facilitating the emergence of group dynamics including mating, aggression and collective foraging8,9,10. Yet social interactions do not occur in isolation. Rather, they unfold in a broader environmental context that structures when, where and how social behaviours are expressed. Courtship and mating, for example, often take place at ecologically privileged locations—food sources1,2, prominent visual landmarks3,4 or suitable nesting sites5,6—where many individuals aggregate, either to increase their encounters with prospective sexual partners or to access key resources that promote reproductive success. In these settings, a central component of the environment is the social collective itself: the multisensory backdrop that emerges from the movement, sensory signals and interactions across all individuals in a group11,12,13,14. Social behaviours are therefore likely shaped by both the static properties of the physical environment and the dynamic features of the social landscape. Yet the neural mechanisms that integrate these distinct sensory streams to regulate social arousal states and structure interindividual interactions remain largely unknown.
The mating behaviours of Drosophila offer a powerful inroad to explore how animals adapt to complex ecological and social landscapes. Species in the Drosophila genus vary widely in their ecology and geographic distribution15,16,17,18,19,20, raising the possibility that mating strategies have evolved in concert with the diverse sensory environments in which reproduction occurs. Many species, including members of the Drosophila melanogaster subgroup, mate on their host plants, typically decaying ephemeral substrates where many individuals congregate17, creating a complex social backdrop for reproduction. Other species reproduce in more isolated social settings. Drosophila elegans, for example, establish individual territories and mate on their host flowers19, whereas species of the Hawaiian subgroup perform competitive lekking in the vegetation surrounding their hosts20. The evolution of Drosophila courtship behaviours may therefore have been shaped by the distinct sensory ecology of a species’ mating site and the structure and dynamics of the social groups that form there.
Reproduction and population density in Drosophila erecta, a close relative of D.
melanogaster, are tightly linked to the seasonal availability of its host fruit—the screwpine Pandanus21—creating a narrow window of opportunity for individuals to meet and mate22.
Such restricted access raises the possibility that D.
erecta has evolved behavioural adaptations that couple reproduction to sensory cues emanating from its host, allowing environmental signals not associated with sexual communication to shape mating behaviour.
Here we show that the olfactory volatiles emanating from a food patch exert both direct and indirect control over courtship in D.
erecta.
We find that food volatiles serve as a potent environmental trigger in this species, driving aggregation and serving as a stringent sensory gate to control a male’s sexual arousal.
In parallel, environmental food odours shape the visual landscape in which courtship unfolds by encouraging males to approach and sample prospective mates, amplifying visual motion to transform the sensory backdrop of the social scene.
D.
erecta males are highly sensitive to this increase in visual motion, in contrast to D.
melanogaster, pointing to the evolution of a multisensory feedback loop that coordinates male sexual arousal across members of the group, linking courtship to the broader social context.
We show that species-specific differences in the sensitivity to environmental cues seem to arise from variation in how olfactory information impinges on conserved components of the courtship circuitry, indicating a potential neural substrate for the rapid tuning of sensory thresholds that govern sexual arousal.
Together, these findings show how both ecological and social cues shape species-specific reproductive strategies.
Moreover, our observations underscore that the social landscape forms an integral part of the environment—both reflecting the collective dynamics of the group and actively shaping the sensory experience of each individual in it.

Odour cues gate D. erecta courtship
To investigate how environmental factors shape the reproductive decisions of species with different ecological preferences, we compared the dynamics of groups of D. erecta and D. melanogaster (five males and five females) provided with a small patch of agar perfumed with food volatiles (diameter 21.5 mm) at the centre of a large arena (diameter 190 mm), a configuration intended to mimic the presence of a localized feeding site (Fig. 1a). Although D. erecta and D. melanogaster have distinct hosts and divergent olfactory preferences16,23, both feed on the yeast microbiota that metabolize decaying fruits and thus display attraction to volatiles arising from fermentation15,24. We therefore used apple cider vinegar (ACV), a broadly appetitive fermentation product, as a generic ‘host’ odour to compare how the chemical environment influences mating behaviours. Flies were fed and maintained as virgins in these assays to minimize their motivation to track towards the odour source for purely metabolic needs or in search of an oviposition site.
We found that in the context of the localized ACV patch, these two ecologically disparate species displayed distinct patterns of behaviour.
D.
melanogaster broadly explored the arena, giving rise to a dispersed spatial distribution where individuals interacted mostly in pairs and only intermittently in larger groups (Fig.
1c, Extended Data Fig.
1a–e and Supplementary Video 1).
By contrast, D.
erecta individuals rapidly approached the central ACV patch and remained there for extended bouts (Fig.
1b,e and Extended Data Fig.
1a,b), forming dynamic clusters of three or more interacting flies (Extended Data Fig.
1c–e).
D.
erecta did not congregate on a patch composed of agar alone (Fig.
1b,e, Extended Data Fig.
1b,f,g and Supplementary Video 1), indicating that food volatiles act as a potent aggregation cue in this species.
Consistent with the notion that aggregation serves a social function in D.
erecta, more than 90% of their copulations occurred on the ACV patch, in comparison to the spatially dispersed mating observed in D.
melanogaster (Fig.
1d,f and Extended Data Fig.
1h).
Comparable differences in aggregation and mating behaviour were also apparent when D.
erecta and D.
melanogaster were presented with a food patch made from the ripe pulp of D.
erecta’s native host Pandanus candelabrum (Extended Data Fig.
1i–l), aligned with evidence that ACV shares several key volatiles with the bouquet of fermenting Pandanus fruit25,26,27.
Notably, D.
erecta refrained from mating entirely in the absence of ACV or Pandanus (Fig.
1f), highlighting the importance of the food patch as a site of reproductive opportunities in this species.

The ACV patch could facilitate mating in D.
erecta by simply aggregating individuals, creating a dense social landscape where interactions between males and females are enhanced by proximity.
Alternatively, ACV may directly elevate the sexual arousal of males or females on their arrival to the patch.
To differentiate between these possibilities, we assessed the courtship dynamics of groups of five males and five females confined to a smaller chamber (diameter 38 mm, 4% area of the large arena; Fig.
1g), allowing us to decouple the effect of spatial proximity from the influence of the chemosensory environment.
D.
melanogaster males courted vigorously in this arena, independent of the presence of ACV (Fig.
1h and Supplementary Video 2).
By contrast, D.
erecta males courted only when ACV was present but rarely in its absence, despite the high density of flies (Fig.
1h,i and Supplementary Video 2).
Indeed, D.
erecta remained dispersed on an agar-only patch (Fig.
1k and Extended Data Fig.
2a), with males rarely approaching or pursuing individuals of either sex (Fig.
1m and Extended Data Fig.
2b,c).

articles.title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11148-5The X-ray visualization platform TomoSAXS, demonstrated here on intervertebral spinal discs, can visualize nanoscale to macroscale mechanics in intact biological organs and fibrous materials.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Fibrous materials, ranging from connective tissues1,2,3,4 to engineered composites5,6,7,8, are vital to many biological and man-made systems, optimized to withstand complex in operando or in vivo loading.
The load-bearing capacity of intervertebral discs (IVDs) of the spine depends on a hierarchical extracellular matrix, where plywood-like lamellae of collagen fibres in the annulus fibrosus contain nanometre-scale fibrils built from staggered triple-helical monomers4,9,10.
How intact IVDs couple fibril-scale mechanics to fibre-scale organization under load remains unresolved.
Here we introduce TomoSAXS, a full-field 3D small-angle X-ray scattering tomography that maps fibril-to-fibre mechanics across an intact tissue.
We show that intrafibrillar molecular pre-strain (D-period stagger) is lamellar textured and tightly correlated with microscale fibre strain.
Pre-strain is inversely related to fibril strain and its variability, consistent with load-sharing through molecular unwinding.
Radial strain bridges and high-curvature zones at the annulus fibrosus–nucleus pulposus interfaces emerge as critical regulators of local mechanics.
These findings reveal concerted fibril–fibre interactions that sustain mechanical equilibrium in the IVD, preserving elasticity and shape.
More broadly, TomoSAXS establishes a platform to visualize nanoscale-to-microscale matrix mechanics across biological and synthetic fibrous materials, with applications in ageing and disease, therapeutic evaluation and the design of bio-based and bio-inspired materials.

Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Fibrous materials provide critical functions across biological and engineered systems. Biological tissues achieve remarkable properties through hierarchical structuring from the nanoscale or molecular scale to whole-organ scales, offering design principles for advanced synthetic materials5,6, such as nanostructured polymer composites7. Collagen-rich tissues such as tendon, cartilage and bone underpin vertebrate biomechanics, with function emerging from complex, hierarchically structured assemblies of collagen fibrils (typically type I or type II)9,10,11 and non-collagenous components, including hydrated glycosaminoglycans12. Distinct features at each hierarchical level, such as nanoscale pre-strain gradients1 and microscale variations in fibre orientation and curvature4, contribute to tissue performance. However, the complex architecture across scales presents major challenges in isolating the respective effects of each hierarchical element and understanding how they collectively support tissue function.
A clinically important example is the IVD, a sophisticated composite structure in the spine that must balance flexibility with efficient distribution of load13. IVD injury and age-related degeneration disrupts the mechanical environment and is a key driver of back pain14, the leading global cause of years lived with disability and a major economic burden15. Although emerging therapies such as synthetic disc replacements hold promise16, their development is hindered by an incomplete understanding of IVD structure–function relationships across length scales.
Our aim is to develop a technique to measure full-field molecular-to-macroscale biophysics of fibrous tissues and uncover new insights into IVD biomechanics. Here we introduce TomoSAXS, a correlative, multiscale X-ray imaging approach that integrates phase-contrast computed tomography (pCT)17 at the microscale with small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS)18 at the nanoscale. We applied this technique to intact rat IVDs under physiologically relevant loading to investigate structure–function relationships across multiple length scales. We then extended the technique to intact human IVDs in static conditions.
The IVD consists of a central nucleus pulposus—a hydrated proteoglycan-rich matrix that redistributes mechanical loads—surrounded by the annulus fibrosus, a fibrous outer ring that provides structural support and stability19 (Fig. 1a, first panel). Within the annulus fibrosus, concentric lamellae tens of microns thick are composed of collagen fibres (1–20 μm in diameter) with alternating orientations between adjacent lamellae (Fig. 1a, second panel), forming an architecture believed to convert nucleus pulposus-derived hydrostatic pressure into circumferential tensile stress13,19. An inter-lamellar network, composed of a non-fibrillar matrix, elastic fibres and trans-lamellar cross-bridges, further stabilizes this structure by anchoring adjacent lamellae20.
Imaging of this fibrous microstructure across the whole organ is challenging due to the similar density of fibres and the surrounding matrix, and fibre analysis of the IVD has generally been limited to small (less than 0.5 mm) regions of interest4,21. The phase information revealed by pCT, combined with digital volume correlation (DVC)4,21,22,23,24, is uniquely suitable to resolve the low-contrast fibre structure (Fig. 1c) and volumetric in situ deformation and strain at the microscale. Recent applications of the DVC have revealed intricate, region-specific strain patterns, with tissue compliance linked to fibre curvature and orientation4,21. These complex patterns depend crucially on the intrinsic structural properties of the fibres.
At the nanoscale, collagen fibres are composed of fibrils (approximately 20–100 nm; Fig. 1a, fourth panel), which are in turn formed of microfibrils of staggered tropocollagen molecules with a mean periodicity (D-period) of approximately 65–67 nm (ref. 9) (Fig. 1a, fifth panel). This axial staggering gives rise to characteristic SAXS diffraction patterns with Bragg peaks at integer multiples of 1/D (Fig. 1a, sixth panel), which act as an internal gauge of fibrillar strain, orientation and diameter (Fig. 1d). In other fibrous tissues—such as bone, tendon and cartilage—two-dimensional (2D) transmission-based SAXS has been used to identify nanoscale deformation mechanisms, including fibrillar pre-strain gradients and hydration-induced alteration in diameter in cartilage1, nanoscale response to in situ loading in tendons25 and altered mineral-collagen shear-transfer in ageing bone26. 2D SAXS analysis of the IVD has demonstrated that energy dissipation occurs through fibril reorientation and stretching27, but interpretation has been limited due to a lack of 3D information.
Linking 3D deformation of fibrous structures across scales using SAXS and pCT poses major challenges. Standard SAXS analysis is based on 2D convolutions of combined 3D reciprocal scattering from multiple fibres encountered along individual X-ray beam paths. As fibre scattering is anisotropic, the 2D pattern depends on fibre orientation at each scattering voxel1, invalidating traditional scalar tomographic methods for macroscopic specimens with complex fibre texture28. To overcome this, tensor tomographic methods have been developed that use multi-axis rotation and spherical basis functions to reconstruct 3D nanostructure in a voxel-wise manner in undeformed structures29,30,31,32. The number of angular projections required for reconstruction increases scan times and limits the scalability of the technique to large samples, and the need for multi-axis rotation makes in situ experimentation complex. There remains an unmet need for methods to reconstruct both microstructure and nanostructure of individual fibres and track their heterogenous deformation within the broader context of microscale-to-macroscale analysis.
The main experiment presented here uncovers nanoscale-to-macroscale biomechanics of rat IVD during in situ mechanical loading. Here TomoSAXS uses fibre tracing of collagen fibres in the annulus fibrosus from pCT reconstructions and their volumetric registration with tomographic SAXS data to allow deconvolution of the 3D scattering from individual fibres in each SAXS beam path. The IVD is an excellent biological exemplar due to its lamellar fibrous texture allowing deconvolution of contribution from different fibrils under rotation. Instances through the SAXS tomography where fibres are predicted to provide sufficient portions of independent scattering intensity are sampled and fitted with 3D fibre-diffraction models to estimate their individual nanoscale properties (mean and variation in D-period and fibril diameter). Registration between SAXS and pCT volumes allow these to be volumetrically mapped onto pCT reconstructions, alongside DVC measurements of tissue and fibre deformation. In addition to the in situ experimentation, we have provided proof of concept of the technique through reconstruction of simple tendon (uniaxial fibre orientation) constructs, and demonstrated the scalability of the TomoSAXS technique to large samples through analysis of an intact human IVD.
The main advantages of this technique are: (1) the isolation of nanoscale properties of individual collagen fibres; (2) the estimation of per-fibre nanoscale strain through tracking the location of fibres in their unloaded and loaded states; and (3) the spatial mapping of nanoscale properties facilitating hierarchical structural and mechanical analysis from the nanoscale to macroscale. In addition, the low number of angular projections required for SAXS reconstruction enables scalability of the technique to intact human organs, and major advantages in terms of acquisition speed and X-ray dose compared with existing techniques.
Our analysis reveals new insights into hierarchical IVD mechanics, providing an important case study for the coupled nanoscale–microscale characterization of other collagenous tissues, such as arteries and cartilage, and engineered fibrous materials, such as carbon-fibre composites. TomoSAXS opens new avenues for linking collagen structure to function in health, disease, ageing and tissue engineering, and for advanced characterization of next-generation composites from biomedical to aerospace applications.

articles.title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11238-4Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, atom probe tomography provides experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution across different FCC phases, consistent with theoretical predictions of hydrogen affinity, revealing hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies1, but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale2,3,4,5,6. This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction4,5,6. Here we address whether interstitial hydrogen in solution in materials can be distinguished from defect-trapped hydrogen in APT. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Hydrogen (H) and hydrogen-containing compounds such as ammonia offer promising routes for low-carbon energy storage and utilization, supporting global decarbonization efforts1. Developing hydrogen energy technologies requires a fundamental understanding of how hydrogen interacts with materials. Hydrogen embrittles high-strength alloys in transport and storage systems2,7,8; its behaviour in metals determines the capacity and reversibility of solid-state storage9; hydride formation in zirconium-alloy cladding threatens fission reactor integrity10; and isotope retention is critical to fusion viability11. Across all of these applications, knowing where hydrogen resides in materials is essential.
Hydrogen in crystalline materials exists in three principal states: dissolved as an interstitial solute in solid solution8, bonded to hydrogen-affinitive elements as thermodynamically stable hydrides (for example, titanium hydride)12,13 or trapped at crystal defects, including vacancies14,15, dislocations3,16 and grain boundaries3,17. Experimentally, these states can be analysed by APT2,4, which uses time-of-flight mass spectrometry to identify hydrogen with nanoscale spatial resolution. In practice, deuterium (2H or D) is often introduced instead of protium to distinguish genuine hydrogen signals from background hydrogen in the instrument, which is predominantly 1H (refs. 4,5).
Among the three states, hydrides and defect-trapped hydrogen have been investigated more extensively by APT. Hydrides are identifiable through their characteristic stoichiometries12,13 and defect-trapped hydrogen can often be co-localized with solute-decorated defects (for example, Cottrell atmospheres such as that of carbon)3,16. When defects are not decorated with identifiable elements, associating hydrogen with defect traps becomes challenging because such defects are ‘invisible’ in APT, unless correlative techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) are used16,18.
By contrast, characterizing hydrogen in solid solutions is particularly challenging for several reasons. First, the solubility of hydrogen is generally low in many alloys; for example, body-centred cubic (BCC) iron typically contains only a few tens of atomic parts per million (at. ppm) of hydrogen2,7,8, which approaches the APT detection limit6,19. Second, unlike hydrogen in stable hydrides, interstitial hydrogen is highly mobile and can diffuse to the surface and desorb before analysis20,21; cryogenic sample transfer (cryo-transfer) for APT mitigates, but does not eliminate, such signal loss4,20,22.
A further complication arises from the methods used to introduce hydrogen into the needle-shaped APT specimens. Electrochemical charging is commonly used2,4, but it can impose extremely high hydrogen fugacity on the specimen and generate large numbers of vacancies—so-called ‘superabundant vacancies’14,23. Further artefacts can be introduced during specimen preparation: electron-beam or ion-beam irradiation in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) or focused ion beam (FIB) can also create vacancies that subsequently trap hydrogen15. Careful interpretation of APT hydrogen maps is therefore required whenever SEM-FIB processing has been used.
In this study, we use a series of FCC alloys as model systems to address this challenge. Compared with BCC alloys, FCC lattices offer higher hydrogen solubility and lower diffusivity7,24, improving signal-to-noise ratio and reducing diffusion-related losses. Our results provide experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in FCC metallic solid solutions and establish a methodological basis for robust, artefact-aware APT characterization of hydrogen in materials.
Deuterium in precipitate-free FCC MPEA lattice
Throughout this study, APT tip specimens were electrolytically charged with deuterium, which saturates specimens more efficiently than gaseous charging, while reducing corrosion concerns3,4. Voltage pulsing rather than laser pulsing was used for all APT analyses to minimize ambiguity in deuterium signal identification against instrumental background hydrogen4,6. Full experimental details are provided in Methods.
As shown in Fig.
1, we first present results from an equiatomic CoCrNiFeMn MPEA, first developed by Cantor et al.
25.
This alloy is known to have a locally distorted lattice, which can more effectively hinder hydrogen diffusion and thus reduce signal loss26.
Immediately after D charging, we spent approximately 3 s to remove the D-charging electrolyte and then quenched the charged tips in liquid nitrogen (LN2) to ‘freeze’ the deuterium in the MPEA.
Once LN2 evaporation stopped—indicating thermal equilibration between the tips and LN2—the specimens were transferred into the APT system using the cryo-transfer procedure described previously3.
As shown in Fig.

The overall D concentration reaches 1.

Figure 1b presents the three-dimensional reconstruction of the APT dataset and 30-nm-thick two-dimensional slices showing the spatial distributions of the major elements, together with H in light blue and D in red.
The H map shows a hydrogen-rich cap at the specimen apex, which arises from the field-induced migration and evaporation of ambient hydrogen adsorbed on the tip surface during APT analysis4.
By contrast, the D map shows a relatively homogeneous and random distribution, consistent with what is expected for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution.
To confirm reproducibility, we repeated this experiment on a second tip and obtained a comparable result, as shown in Extended Data Fig.

Because deuterium can segregate to defects that are not visible in APT (ref. 16), we carefully evaluated whether the observed deuterium distribution is truly random. We performed nearest-neighbour analyses of deuterium atoms, as shown in Fig. 1c,d, for the first and fifth nearest deuterium neighbours, respectively. This approach detects clustering by comparing interatomic distances between deuterium atoms in the experimental dataset with those in a randomized dataset of equivalent size19,27. A marked shift towards shorter distances indicates clustering, whereas agreement with the random distribution is consistent with deuterium occupying a large population of equivalent interstitial sites27.
Figure 1c shows the distribution of deuterium–deuterium pair distances for the first nearest neighbour. The most probable pair distance in the experimental data is close to that in the randomized dataset (both approximately 0.8 nm), indicating that the deuterium atoms are randomly distributed. We repeated the analysis for the fifth nearest deuterium neighbour (Fig. 1d) and obtained a consistent result, with a larger most probable distance of about 1.2 nm, as expected when a more distant neighbour is considered. These results are consistent with interstitial deuterium (as a proxy of hydrogen) in solid solution. Notably, hydrogen solution in the CoCrNiFeMn matrix is not highly thermodynamically favourable according to our first-principles calculations, for neither octahedral nor tetrahedral interstitial sites (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Figure 1 therefore suggests the effectiveness of cryo-APT for preserving the charged D atoms and enabling observation of their distribution in solid solution. Random D distributions were also consistently observed in solution-treated CoNiV and (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 alloys (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 1), supporting the generality of this observation among FCC MPEAs.

articles.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11177-0Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression.
Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9,10,11,12,13.
Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas.
Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma.
The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment.
Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates.
We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity.
MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo.
Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression.
These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

The capacity of cancer cells to switch phenotypic states, also called cellular plasticity, is a hallmark of cancer and is involved in tumour initiation and progression, including therapeutic resistance1.
Glioblastoma (GB), the most common primary brain tumour in adults, is characterized by profound cellular heterogeneity and a dismal prognosis2,3.
Although the genomic landscape of GB has been catalogued extensively, actionable genetic drivers remain scarce, and clinical responses to targeted therapies have been minimal4,5,6.
Longitudinal studies have underscored the limited contribution of therapy-induced genetic evolution in GB and revealed remarkable clonal stability despite treatment7,8, suggesting that non-genetic mechanisms, such as epigenetic plasticity and transcriptional reprogramming, are central to adaptation and treatment resistance in GB.
Seminal single-cell transcriptomic studies have shown that malignant GB cells occupy a continuum of cellular states resembling developmental progenitors (for example, oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-like and neural progenitor cell (NPC)-like), as well as astrocytic and mesenchymal-like phenotypes9,10.
Patient-derived xenograft models have demonstrated that individual GB cells can give rise to multiple states, implying substantial plasticity10,11.
However, whether these state transitions follow stereotyped routes or variable trajectories12,13, and how gene-regulatory mechanisms promote or constrain them, remain poorly understood.

Here, and in a companion study14, we address these questions by integrating single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility (single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing; snATAC-seq) profiles from more than one million cells from isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wild-type primary GBs.
Using a computational approach (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference; scDORI) and systematic transcription factor (TF) perturbations, we decode enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks (eGRNs) at single-cell resolution and map the regulatory landscape that underlies the identity and plasticity of GB cells.
Specifically, we model the gene-regulatory processes that govern GB cell states, identify key transcriptional regulators for each state, elucidate their roles in driving cell-state conversions and reconstruct a hierarchical roadmap of GB transitions.
Our analyses reveal a structured landscape of GB state transitions shaped by epigenetic ‘highways’ and ‘barriers’.
Neuronal-like cells emerge as a constrained, low-plasticity state stabilized by a network of transcriptional repressors that actively silences alternative malignant fates.
We identify MYT1L as the key repressor in this network: gain-of-function of MYT1L restricts plasticity and induces a neuronal-like identity in patient-derived GB cells, and reduces tumour growth after transplantation in mice; by contrast, removal of MYT1L enhances plasticity and malignant features.
These findings suggest that enforcing repressive barriers could lock GB cells into less adaptive states, and identify plasticity restriction as a potential therapeutic strategy.

Together with our companion study mapping spatio-temporal trajectories in GB tumours14, our findings reveal a conserved, epigenetically controlled hierarchy of cell states and transition routes in GB. Our work establishes transcriptional repressors as key suppressors of plasticity and underscores the potential of targeting the epigenetic foundations of state switching in brain cancer.
State-specific epigenetic plasticity in GB
To characterize the regulatory landscape of GB, we generated a multiome snRNA–snATAC-seq atlas (see the companion study14), spanning parallel gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility profiles of more than one million cells collected across multiple sites (4–15) from 12 IDH-wild-type primary GB tumours, including peritumoral regions. In line with previous studies10, malignant GB cells exhibited vastly heterogeneous transcriptional profiles, ranging from developmental-like (OPC-NPC-like, OPC-like, OPC-neuronal-like, NPC-neuronal-like and astrocyte (AC)-progenitor-like) to glial injury response and hypoxia-associated (AC-gliosis-like, gliosis-like and hypoxia) phenotypes, as well as cycling signatures (proliferative) (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a).
First, we investigated the epigenetic plasticity of GB cells, assuming that accessible gene regions without active transcription indicate epigenetic plasticity. Inspired by a previous study15, we quantified how well accessibility profiles of cell-state markers predict transcriptionally defined cell states (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1b,c, Supplementary Table 1 and Methods). Cells whose chromatin profiles yield uncertain predictions are scored as more epigenetically plastic. Our analysis revealed that malignant cells exhibit greater epigenetic plasticity than non-malignant tumour microenvironment (TME) cells and analogous neurodevelopmental cell types (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1d–f), with chromatin accessibility in malignant cells often being compatible with multiple cell states (Fig. 1d). However, the extent of this plasticity varied significantly across GB cell states (Fig. 1e), and NPC-neuronal-like and OPC-neuronal-like cells stood out as the least plastic states. The variations in epigenetic plasticity could not be explained by differences in global coupling between gene expression and accessibility, were robust to differences in cell numbers per state and were consistently observed across patients (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1g–j). These data suggest that specific regulatory mechanisms underlie GB plasticity and govern cell-state heterogeneity.
Regulatory architecture of GB heterogeneity
To determine the specific gene-regulatory processes that underlie the observed differences in epigenetic plasticity, we aimed to identify relevant TFs, cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their interplay across GB states using eGRNs. Established eGRN inference methods are not designed for the heterogeneity of a single-cell tumour atlas like ours16,17,18,19,20,21,22. Specifically, existing methods assume discrete, predefined cell-types and therefore cannot capture the continuous, cell-state-specific variation in eGRNs that defines malignant heterogeneity. Many also scale poorly to datasets of this size23. Moreover, previous methods focus mainly on signatures of transcriptional activation, despite the growing recognition of gene repression as a key regulator of cell identity and plasticity in cancer24,25.
To address these limitations, we developed scDORI, a computational approach for inferring continuous eGRNs and their relationships across cell populations using single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and scATAC-seq multiome data (Fig. 2a and Methods). articles.title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11212-0A high-throughput CRISPR-interference platform allows the mapping of interactions between essential genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing many previously unknown genetic interactions and providing insight into gene function and drug–target relationships that could enable the development of new therapies for tuberculosis.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen1.
Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development.
Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations2,3.
Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria.
We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection.
Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M.
tuberculosis.
These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets.
By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations.
Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting.
Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

Main
Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the world’s leading infectious cause of death1, is among the bacteria that have been most extensively sequenced, but the functions and interactions of many of its genes remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap limits our understanding of the genetic foundations of tuberculosis (TB) and hinders the development of effective therapies.
Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful approach for deciphering the functional relationships between genes2,3. It involves systematically assessing how perturbing one gene modifies the phenotype associated with perturbing a second gene. A GI is defined as a combined phenotype that deviates from the expectation based on single-gene perturbations. Positive interactions occur when dual perturbation produces a milder phenotype than expected, whereas negative interactions—including synthetic lethal effects—result in a more severe phenotype. Applied at scale, GI mapping yields quantitative interaction profiles that serve as high-resolution phenotypes3. These profiles can generate functional hypotheses for uncharacterized genes, reveal surprising roles for genes of known function and identify connections between distinct biological pathways3. Moreover, they can highlight potential synergistic and antagonistic drug–target relationships, informing combination therapies5.
GI mapping in Mtb has historically been constrained by biological and technical challenges, including slow growth, biosafety requirements and limited early genetic tools. The development of high-density transposon mutagenesis libraries combined with hybridization- or sequencing-based readouts (TnSeq)6,7 constituted a major advance, permitting genome-wide identification of conditionally essential genes8 and GI mapping in deletion mutants9. However, such approaches are typically restricted to non-essential genes, excluding most antibiotic targets. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) has since emerged as a complementary technique10,11,12,13, enabling conditional and tunable knockdown of both essential and non-essential genes. In bacterial systems, dual-gene knockdowns have been used to identify GIs among small gene sets14, and larger-scale efforts have paired individual deletion or knockdown strains with genome-wide libraries15,16. Dual-CRISPRi and dual-TnSeq approaches for comprehensive GI mapping have been implemented in Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae17,18,19. However, technical limitations have thus far precluded the development of a comparable system in Mtb.
To enable high-throughput GI mapping in Mtb, we developed a dual-single-guide RNA (sgRNA) CRISPRi platform for mycobacteria. Addressing key challenges in library construction and data analysis, we devised a robust experimental and statistical pipeline for high-confidence detection of GIs. Using this platform, we mapped GIs among nearly all essential genes in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm) and Mtb, prioritizing this technically demanding class of genes because of their centrality to cellular processes and importance as antibiotic targets. These maps recapitulate known biological relationships, validating the platform, and also uncover thousands of novel GIs. We further performed AlphaFold3 co-folding for all gene pairs (approximately 600,000) represented in the GI maps, identifying GIs that are likely to reflect physical associations and offering a basis for mechanistic hypotheses. Finally, we validated selected predictions from the maps, including drug–drug interactions and roles in the electron transport chain (ETC) for several genes of unknown function. Together, these maps constitute a powerful resource for elucidating Mtb biology and guiding the rational design of combination therapies.
Optimal sgRNAs for GI mapping
To enable dual-sgRNA CRISPRi-based GI mapping in Mtb, we adapted the Combinatorial Genetics En Masse (CombiGEM) framework20 to the Mtb CRISPRi platform10, assigning each sgRNA a barcode, and using a cloning workflow that preserves sgRNA–barcode linkage and positions paired barcodes in close proximity (Extended Data Fig. 1a). This design permits accurate quantification of dual-sgRNA strain abundance by barcode sequencing, facilitating high-throughput GI mapping.
GI detection for essential genes requires sgRNAs that impose a precise fitness cost: sufficient to reveal interactions, yet not so severe as to mask additive or synergistic effects. Compounding this challenge, the combinatorial scale of dual-sgRNA libraries necessitates selecting only a small number of sgRNAs per gene. To define the optimal fitness cost for GI detection, we performed a pilot screen in Msm using a panel of 16 genes that are predicted to interact. We selected up to 24 sgRNAs per gene (Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Table 1) spanning a broad range of fitness costs, cloned a dual-sgRNA library containing all pairwise permutations and performed a GI screen using the workflow planned for larger-scale studies (Extended Data Fig. 1b). The resulting data allowed us to identify the sgRNA strength window that best supports GI detection under these conditions: an approximately 8% reduction in fitness per generation (Extended Data Fig. 1c–h and Supplementary Discussion).
Essential-gene GI map in Msm
To establish feasibility, we built a comprehensive essential-gene GI library in Msm. Guided by the pilot screen, we selected up to two sgRNAs per gene with reproducible, intermediate fitness costs (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). The library contains 1,524 sgRNAs targeting 787 genes, plus 10 non-targeting (NT) controls, yielding about 2.3 million sgRNA permutations. Target genes included those that are essential for Msm fitness and those that are non-essential in Msm but essential in Mtb; the latter were targeted by the predicted strongest sgRNAs10. The library was cloned in Escherichia coli, validated by deep sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 2a) and transformed into an Msm strain containing a chromosomally encoded Streptococcus thermophilus (Sth1) dCas9 expression cassette. This yielded a pooled library in which each bacterium carries a single integrated guide plasmid expressing two sgRNAs. We subjected this library to competitive growth, tracking dual-sgRNA strain abundance over time by barcode sequencing. Strain depletion was modelled using a piecewise linear regression10, providing a quantitative readout of fitness.
Growth phenotypes were highly reproducible across biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). As expected, strains with two NT sgRNAs showed minimal depletion, single-targeting strains exhibited moderate depletion and dual-targeting strains showed the greatest depletion (Fig. 1b). sgRNA position within the plasmid had little effect on fitness, indicating consistent activity from both expression cassettes (Fig. 1c).
To identify GIs, we compared the observed fitness of each dual-targeting strain to the expected outcome under a null model of no interaction (Fig. 1d,e). Deviations from this expectation were quantified and corrected for floor effects (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e), and then aggregated at the gene-pair level to generate a GI score. Gene pairs with greater-than-expected depletion were assigned negative GI scores, and those with less-than-expected depletion yielded positive GI scores (Fig. 1d). To assess confidence, GI scores were modelled as a mixture of typical deviations (normal distribution) and deviations outside the norm (uniform distribution). Gene pairs with interaction probabilities of 0.5  0.95 confident interactions.
The Msm GI map revealed nearly 8,500 interactions (p > 0.5), with negative GIs outnumbering positive ones (Fig. 1g–i and Supplementary Table 2). This 2.7% hit rate across gene pairs aligns with previous GI studies3. Most genes interacted with fewer than 15 partners, but a subset exhibited high connectivity, consistent with hub-like behaviour that has been observed in other organisms, such as yeast3 (Fig. 1i). Out of 787 targeted genes, 64 (8.1%) showed no interactions under these conditions. articles.title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11226-8Rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation is used for the formation of highly ordered, conformal self-assembled molecules, enabling the fabrication of high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells on rough textured substrates are at present limited by a critical trade-off in self-assembled monolayer (SAM) design because increasing molecular conjugation enhances conductivity but often leads to unfavourable aggregation that impairs conformal coverage1,2. Here we overcome this challenge using a rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation that incorporates tailored intramolecular distortion to suppress excess π–π stacking without sacrificing charge-transport efficiency. This steric regulation facilitates the formation of a highly ordered, conformal SAM across rough pyramidal textures. By reconciling molecular packing with interfacial coverage, the tailored interface provides optimized energy-level alignment for ultrafast charge extraction, enables improved defect passivation through adaptive conformational adjustment and acts as a robust template for high-quality perovskite film growth. Making use of this interface, the optimized tandem device achieves a notable fill factor (FF) of 85%, yielding a certified stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 35.1%. Furthermore, the device demonstrates outstanding stability, retaining more than 94% of its initial performance after 1,500 h of ageing under the ISOS-L-1 protocol. Our findings provide a clear molecular engineering route to reconcile conductivity and film uniformity while maximizing the performance of tandem photovoltaics on textured silicon substrates.

articles.title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11200-4Codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting is a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Ribosomal frameshifting, an uncommon translational recoding event, is best known for its regulatory roles in viral gene expression1,2, whereas its physiological relevance in mammals remains poorly understood.
Here we show that specific codon pairs trigger efficient −1 frameshifting preferentially in cancer cells.
Mechanistically, this recoding arises from ribosomal pausing associated with tRNA and amino acid availability, and is amplified by impaired ribosome quality control and sustained phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6.
We found that this codon-pair-specific frameshifting represents an intrinsic state of translational dysregulation, which is prevalent across cancer cells and reshapes protein synthesis.
Taking advantage of this frameshifting-permissive state in cancer cells, we engineered a frameshifting-activated synthetic therapeutic circuit (FAST) that conditionally expresses the pyroptotic effector gasdermin D.
FAST is activated across diverse cancer cell types, inducing potent and selective pyroptosis, while sparing normal tissues from detectable toxicity.
As a proof of concept, systemic AAV9-mediated delivery of FAST in mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer elicited pronounced tumour regression, robust immune activation and synergistic effects with immune checkpoint blockade.
Collectively, these findings reveal codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting as a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells and establish translation-coupled gene circuits as a strategy for cancer-selective therapy.
