articles.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11198-9Genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals are analysed, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which alternative archaeological and linguistic models for the origin and spread of Celtic fit reconstructed demographic histories.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age1,2,3.
How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested4, with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes.
Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories.
We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal.
First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken.
Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade.
Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts5,6,7,8.
Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic.
Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Europe’s present-day linguistic landscape is dominated by Romance, Germanic and Slavic languages, which expanded relatively recently during the Iron Age10,11,12,13. Before these events, Celtic languages were prominent across Europe1,2,3: Lepontic has been documented in northwestern Italy (2600–2100 bp), Celtiberian in central-northeastern Iberia (2200–1900 bp) and Gaulish across present-day France, central Europe, northern Italy and the Balkans (2500–1400 bp)14,15 (Fig. 1a). In the modern era, Celtic languages have retreated to the northwestern Atlantic fringe, where they persist as two groups: the Goidelic languages Irish, Manx and Scottish Gaelic; and the Brittonic languages Welsh, Cornish and Breton.
All Celtic languages diverged from an undocumented ancestral language, Proto-Celtic (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a). This language is defined by a series of linguistic innovations present in all Celtic languages, but absent from the other Indo-European languages, including closely related Italic and Lusitanian (Supplementary Note 5). Whereas there is widespread agreement that Indo-European dialects, including the one ancestral to Proto-Celtic, spread across Europe from the Pontic Steppe after 5000 bp (refs. 16,17,18,19), the centre and timing of the subsequent dispersal of Celtic within Europe remain contentious4. Existing hypotheses generally fall within one of the following four models:
- 
                (1)
                
                  The Bell Beaker model associates the Celtic split and dispersal with the Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age Bell Beaker Complex (roughly 4750–4500 to 4000–3800 bp)20,21,22,23, which spanned much of western and central Europe. Under this model, Celtic diverged largely in situ over the millennia following the Bell Beaker expansion. By contrast, the following three models place the formation of Proto-Celtic after 4000 bp.
- 
                (2)
                
                  The Celtic-from-the-West model (Fig. 1a) claims that Proto-Celtic emerged from relatively undiversified Indo-European dialects within long-distance maritime networks of the Atlantic Bronze Age Culture (3300–2700 bp)24, connecting Atlantic Iberia, parts of France, Ireland and Britain. It further posits a subsequent eastward expansion of a Gaulish–Brittonic–Goidelic Celtic subgroup into central Europe during the Hallstatt C period (2750–2600 bp), traced archaeologically through the distribution of Gündlingen swords25.
- 
                (3)
                
                  The Celtic-from-the-Centre model, in turn, posits that Proto-Celtic emerged neither along the Atlantic seaboard nor from eastern central Europe (next model). Instead, it situates this ancestral language in inland France and possibly northwestern Italy 4000–3000 bp, with a subsequent spread in many directions, including to Britain, Italy and Spain, after 3000 bp (refs. 26,27,28) (Fig. 1a). This model rejects overly strong archaeological–linguistic correlations and is instead supported by a relative density of Celtic toponyms and personal names in France.
- 
                (4)
                
                  Finally, the longstanding Celtic-from-the-East model places the formation of Proto-Celtic in eastern central Europe (Fig. 1a) and associates its diversification with the Late Bronze Age Urnfield Culture29,30, the subsequent Hallstatt Culture and La Tène archaeological horizon5,6,7,8, or a combination of these. The documentation of Lepontic Celtic inscriptions in the Urnfield-derived Alpine Golasecca Culture (2850–2350 bp) has been taken to support this model30. In addition, under this model (as well as models (2) and (3)), the geographic distribution of the Iron Age La Tène Culture, extending from France to the Balkans, broadly coincides with the distribution of Gaulish and closely related Celtic dialects31.
These models differ in their proposed centres and chronologies for the formation and spread of Celtic and imply conflicting proposals of human mobility. We therefore test to what degree each model is supported by past population genomic data, similar to approaches that have proved to be illuminative in other historical-linguistic debates11,12,16,17,32,33,34,35. We note, in this context, that the terms ‘spread’ and ‘population movements’ are used as purely descriptive terms that do not speak to the social mechanism driving them.
We expand on the results of a parallel study on the Germanic languages32, leveraging a filtered dataset of 4,587 imputed ancient human genomes that temporally and geographically encompasses the regions in which early Celtic languages have been historically documented (Fig. 1d,e and Supplementary Table 1.1). In addition, we assembled an auxiliary dataset including individuals from Urnfield contexts in Iberia, Celtic-associated contexts in Britain and southwest Germany, and Bronze Age northern Italy (Supplementary Table 1.4). We used identity-by-descent (IBD) mixture modelling and qpAdm, as well as an updated version of chromopainter together with Sourcefind (Methods), to distinguish population continuity from directional gene flow and to test whether proposed linguistic dispersals require additional, unsupported demographic events.
Steppe sources of Indo-European dialects
Current evidence suggests that the Indo-European dialect ancestral to the Celtic languages entered Europe along with a ‘massive migration’ from the Pontic Steppe16,17. In western Europe, the earliest Steppe ancestry appears in people of the Bell Beaker Complex36, whose cultural package in northwestern Europe includes Maritime Beaker influence from Iberia, and All-Over-Corded and All-Over-Ornamented Beaker influence from the Corded Ware region to the east37. Western and eastern contributions are also represented genetically, with Bell Beaker individuals deriving ancestry in various proportions from western Neolithic and eastern Steppe sources. To test whether their Steppe ancestry persisted in the four proposed formative regions for Proto-Celtic, we performed IBD mixture modelling (Methods). In brief, a palette is created for every ancient individual in the dataset, representing the proportion of IBD segments of DNA shared with all 386 clusters in the dataset. The palette of each ‘target’ individual is then modelled as the best-fitting combination of the palettes of the ‘source’ groups, using non-negative least squares in the R package limSolve (v.1.5.6)38. Full IBD mixture modelling results, including source-set definitions, spatial and temporal distributions, alternative source models and sensitivity analyses, are provided in Supplementary Note 1, Supplementary Figs. 1.1–1.58 and Supplementary Tables 1.1–1.6.
As sources, we included groups of individuals from Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related contexts, together with a series of earlier source groups (Supplementary Figs.
1.
1 and 1.
2 and Supplementary Note 1).
For source individuals, we prioritized early Bell Beaker and Corded Ware individuals to measure the persistence of their ancestry through time.
We also prioritized individuals with high Steppe ancestry and minimal Neolithic Farmer ancestries as sources, to allow more Farmer ancestry in later individuals to be detected.
As we are interested specifically in the spread of Steppe ancestry, we refer to these ancestry sources as Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related ancestry, while acknowledging that many Neolithic-related sources also contributed to Corded Ware and Bell Beaker populations32,39.
When including a single, early Steppe source (Yamnaya-related), we find Steppe ancestry appearing in eastern and northern Europe between 5000 bp and 4500 bp (Supplementary Fig.
1.
31a), spreading to western and southern Europe between 4500 bp and 4000 bp, consistent with expectations16,17,39.
When including the two other sources with high Steppe ancestry (Bell Beaker-related and Corded Ware-related, Extended Data Fig.
2c), we find that Steppe ancestry of individuals in the Corded Ware region of northern and eastern Europe is now modelled with Corded Ware-related ancestry (Fig.
2, Supplementary Fig.
1.

articles.full_text:
Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!
Weight-Space Programming
Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.
spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.
I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.
The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:

The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.

The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:

breakout/prompt.txt
freeway/prompt.txt
pacman/prompt.txt
pong/prompt.txt

I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.
Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models
The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro
This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro, which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.
But how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.
I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:
LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b
(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)
After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace):

Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.
Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.
Confidence: 72%

This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning) in 1h 4m 54s:

Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.
Description:
The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.
Confidence:
75%

And Breakout (reasoning) in 52m 25s:

Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.
Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.
Confidence: 88%

Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally".
The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample:

What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?

That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.
It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.
    
        Tags: machine-learning, ai, generative-ai, local-llms, llms, qwen, paper-review
